boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has kept at it. The 737 line is steady at 57 a month, the 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and the balance sheet is where we said we'd put it. That's the base we build the future on.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable. Rates stay tied to the data, and we agree them with the FAA, the same way we always have.

On widebodies, the 787 and 777X lines are stable, and we'll keep putting our effort into the airplanes our customers fly today.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we've been doing the work on three fronts: the market, the technology and our own readiness. Two of those have come a long way. The engine technology is maturing, and our balance sheet is ready. The business case isn't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane until it is. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. I'm not going to give you a date. When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source, and the entry-into-service date will have headroom built in.

In the meantime we're keeping our engineering team and our supply base ready, so that when the time comes we can execute. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION. I order Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold', at -0.28 / -0.03 / -1.74 / -0.28 (S1-S4).
- fps hold, code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold, fps_site new_site.
- No order differs from the default, so no item goes to the Board for approval. The full case still goes with the package.

TEAM RULE.
- Malave's buffer veto binds on all 12 fps rows. The floor is Do Nothing's S4 less $2B, -2.28. The best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -4.23 (short 1.95). The 10-year at Renton alone is -5.56 (short 3.28), the 7-year at Renton -7.72, and via Embraer at Renton -16.52. I accept the veto, and it matches my own reading.
- The KPI doctrine: Pope searched the brief and found no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate value offered.
- Everything else is mine to decide, so the re787 call is mine.

FPS: HOLD. Two of the three work streams have converged [BX-1296, B-2303].
- Technology: GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so code 7 gives three sources from a 2042 EIS.
- Boeing: net debt is $0.0B in base and stress, and the 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547].
- The market has not converged. The cheapest launch, the 10-year at Renton, is $5.20-5.28B below Do Nothing in every column. That is beyond H8's $2B cap, so the 50/50 and incumbency objectives cannot carry it.
- When the fps comes, it comes Solo on the 10-year ramp. Its worst column is $2.20B better than the 7-year's (-6.94 against -9.14), its bill is smaller, and it enters service after the 2039-43 capacity-binding years.
- NGSA's date does not set ours [B-2313].

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD, BY MY OWN DECISION. This is the crux, and I own it.
- The grid item is +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00. It passes every test but one:
  - Malave's buffer (S4 +1.72, clear by 4.00);
  - stress net debt $0.0B;
  - Fundable when the 777X turns;
  - H3's second half, in force and not triggered;
  - H4, with 0 years of overlap;
  - Pope's readiness, on two conditions: GE commits privately, and the amended type certificate comes before conversion.
- The one test it hangs on is how likely a same-round A350 Re-engine is (S3).
- In my frame I set the test before the memos came in, and I said I meant it: if my independent check [BX-1316] put that chance above about one in four, the edge would fall inside epsilon, and doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] would take hold.
- Malave's number is about 30%, in a range of 25-35%. He gave his reasons both ways:
  - for: on the board's 20-year window, 2035 is Airbus's best remaining shot; its overlap with NGSA development falls to 2 years; our own 2030 line said we would keep the 787 as it is;
  - against: Airbus held in 2030, and RR has launched no widebody engine.
- On my arithmetic (work/r2_calc.txt) the item is worth 2.00 - 3.64p:
  - +0.91 at 30%;
  - +0.79 at one-third, my own 2030 weight;
  - +1.09 only at the bottom of his range.
- With one conservative reset planned in, as I plan every development [BX-1318, BX-1275], the edge is about +0.6 at 30%. It clears epsilon only if the A350 risk is below about one in five (18%), and nobody at this table can get it there.
- Within epsilon, the worst column decides: -1.74 against -3.38, so hold is better by 1.64.
- What changed since 2030: the upside fell from +3.30 to +2.00 faster than the downside narrowed (from -2.48 to -1.64). At my 2030 weight the edge was +1.37; now it is +0.79.
- In the frame I said I would not park a ready program to dodge an A350 move. I am not doing that. I am holding because the expected value, weighted on my CFO's number, does not clear my own bar. This is not a reply to Airbus and not timed to them. It is the size of a bounded loss in a column we cannot rule out [BX-1279].
- The Board told me it would veto the item again on the same column. Its veto would have landed in the same place, but I would rather own the call than hand it to the Board.
- Cost, stated plainly. Holding gives up $2.00B in S1, S2 and S4, and it is likely for good: Malave puts a 2045 relaunch at +0.3 to +0.74, inside epsilon. It saves $1.64B if Airbus re-engines this round.

PREMIUM (H8). The hold is my choice, so it is a management doctrine premium (doing less, better, and the higher-confidence plan), not the Board's constraint.
- $0.91B on my expected (weighted) column; $2.00B on S1 alone, exactly at the cap.
- Nothing else is logged: no objective premium, and the fps hold and rate hold are grid-best. The H8 total is within $2B on either measure.

BOARD PACKAGE.
- Submitted row: 'fps: hold + 787: hold', -0.28 / -0.03 / -1.74 / -0.28. With no Board item, no default comparison is needed.
- For reference:
  - 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine': +1.72 / +1.97 / -3.38 / +1.72 (item +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00);
  - beside a 10-year fps the item is +1.33 / +1.34 / -2.31 / +1.33;
  - the 10-year at Renton against Do Nothing is -5.20 / -5.25 / -5.20 / -5.28.
- S4 is -0.28 against the -2.28 floor: a pass.
- Malave's results: buffer pass; stress net debt $0.0B in all columns; Fundable when the 777X turns, pass.
- Pope's written results: no live problem; Re-engine executable on her two conditions; strain counts 0 / 2 / 5; via Embraer fails invest-or-partner; no operational reason to move the site now.
- Rulings:
  - H1: lifted in 2030, and the ruling stands. The 777X has been delivering since 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 are in service [BX-1299], and net debt has been $0 since 2029 [B-2327]. The fps fails here on market and buffer, not on H1.
  - H3: first half lifted; second half in force and not triggered.
  - H4: overlap counts are 0 with the Re-engine alone, 2 beside a 10-year fps, and 5 beside a 7-year fps (struck).
  - H5 and H6: nothing in play.
  - H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger.

WRITTEN FRANCHISE VIEW FOR THE BOARD.
- The narrowbody run-down is real, and it is already in Do Nothing's numbers:
  - preference goes from 40% to 31% in 2045, 26% in 2050 and 16% in 2060;
  - delivered share is 22.1% in 2050 and 0% in 2060, as the MAX is phased out.
- 2045 is the last round in which an fps can enter service (2052 or 2055) while the MAX still builds 214-342 a year to hand over (Pope).
- Waiting has shrunk the loss in 2026 dollars, from -6.51 to -5.20, but at half the pace of discounting. It has not changed the sign. The business case needs a swing of more than $6B (Malave).
- So we keep the option warm at no cost on the grid: workforce, suppliers, engines, the Renton plan, and no concurrency. We decide on the 2045 grid against Malave's bar. I will not launch at a loss beyond the cap to defend a share target. I would rather report an honest decline than book an unfunded promise.

DOCTRINE AGAINST MY RECORD.
- My record drove: KPI gating [BX-1259]; debt first [BX-1305]; the three work streams [BX-1296]; no concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed price [BX-1262]; one conservative reset [BX-1318]; doing less, better [BX-1239]; the CFO as independent check [BX-1316]; no fps date [B-2315].
- Doctrine drove: the dual-source requirement; H3 and H4; Malave's 30%, which comes from doctrine and inference, as he says himself; the workforce-readiness move.

priorities: Safety and production readiness first. No launch reaches us without Pope's written results on KPIs, suppliers and strain. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, and her memo must confirm that from the brief, not assume it. For any 787 Re-engine she must also confirm two things. First, a widebody engine ready by its 2040 EIS (the GEnx upgrade on the public record has been ready since 2033; she should confirm it qualifies). Second, the amended type certificate before the line converts [BG-0043, BG-0025, BX-1263].

Protect the repaired balance sheet and the rating. Net debt is $0 in the base and stress cases through 2050 on Do Nothing. Every plan must pass the buffer test in the risk-case column S4: no more than $2B below Do Nothing (-0.28), a floor of -2.28. Every fps row fails it. The best, the 10-year ramp at Renton with the Re-engine, sits at -4.23 and is $1.95B short. The 10-year ramp at Renton alone sits at -5.56 [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327].

A business case and a bounded downside before any commitment. A launch must add more than $1B in the expected column, and no item may lose more than $1B in any plausible column. All four columns are plausible. The cheapest fps launch is -5.20 against Do Nothing. The 787 Re-engine is +2.00 in S1, S2 and S4 but -1.64 in S3 (a same-round A350 Re-engine) [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581].

The next airplane comes when the market, the technology and Boeing are ready. Two of the three are now met. Technology: GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) are on the public record, so code 7 fits three engine sources at any fps EIS from 2042. Boeing: net debt is $0 base and stress. The market leg fails on this grid in every column. The fps waits for a grid that carries it, not for Airbus's date [BG-0068, B-2303, B-2313].

One development at a time, and no announcement ahead of this Board. A Solo fps and the Re-engine may overlap by at most 2 years: a 10-year fps with the Re-engine passes (2 years), a 7-year fails (5 years). Management does not announce a programme before our approval [B-2167, B-0438, B-0521].

recommendations.text: Hold the fps this round and bring it back in Round 3 (2045) on that round's grid. The technology leg is now met: GTF2 and UltraFan NB are on the public record. The Boeing leg is met: net debt is $0, base and stress. The market leg fails: the cheapest launch, the 10-year ramp at Renton, is $5.20-5.28B below Do Nothing in every column. That is beyond H8's $2B cap, so the 50/50 and incumbency objectives cannot carry it as an objective premium. When an fps comes, prefer the 10-year ramp. Its worst column beats the 7-year's by $2.20B, more than epsilon, and its bill is smaller ($60.32B against $65.00B). Give no date in public before launch, and set a conservative EIS at launch.

On the 787 Re-engine, we speak plainly. On this grid we would veto it again on the Downside test: -1.64 in S3. Last round the CEO said the same-round risk would recur, and it has, though the loss has narrowed from $2.48B to $1.64B. Our limit is on the size of the loss in a plausible column, not on certainty that Airbus holds. If management still brings it, bring the full case: a widebody engine committed and ready by the 2040 EIS (the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033), the amended type certificate before the line converts, and no fixed-price development. Never pair it with a 7-year fps. If we veto, log the value given up ($2.00B in S1, S2 and S4) as the Board's constraint, not a management premium. If the A350 is re-engined this round, H3's second half closes the question for good. Otherwise we will test it again in 2045 on that grid's numbers.

The dual-source enabler is now within reach. With GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, code 7 fits CFM, P&W and RR at any fps EIS from 2042, and codes 5 or 6 fit two. Code 7 is not a barred pair against NGSA's code 7. Keep the public dual-source requirement, keep the second-source talks private, and name no maker in public before launch. At launch, choose a code naming makers ready by EIS. Do not rely on code 4 while no Joint Venture has formed.

Public statement: no fps date and no programme announced ahead of this Board. NGSA's launch is now public, and no Boeing order or date should be presented as a reply to it. Rates stay KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. Say nothing on returning cash to the owners. Net debt is $0 in base and stress through 2050, but that question is reserved to this Board, which will take it up once the rating is confirmed as solid investment grade.

We are a long-cycle business, and the narrowbody franchise needs a written view, not a default. On Do Nothing, preference falls from 40% to 26% by 2050, and MAX deliveries run from 641 in 2045 to none in 2060. At horizon 3 we grant no extra downside for a long-term position, but we ask management to prepare the 2045 decision now. Plan a Renton reassignment against the phase-out, with Pope's readiness result. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot. Plan no production-certification concurrency. In 2045, show how a launch then (EIS 2052 or 2055) compares on that grid. Keep fps_site at new_site until a launch.

In the package, show the following. The submitted row and each item row across S1-S4. S4 against Do Nothing (-0.28; floor -2.28). Malave's buffer, stress net-debt and 'Fundable when the 777X turns' results. Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results in writing. The status of H3's second half and the H4 overlap count. Every premium logged against H8's $2B cap.

frame.question:
It's 2035. Airbus launched NGSA in 2030 (EIS 2037). Nobody has re-engined a widebody. We launched nothing last round: the Board vetoed the 787 Re-engine on its Downside test, and we took its alternative, hold. Two questions this round.
(1) Does any fps launch now pass the three work streams, Malave's buffer test and the business case? Two of the three streams have now converged. Technology: GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so code 7 gives three sources at any EIS from 2042. Boeing: net debt is $0 in base and stress. Has the market converged?
(2) Do we bring the 787 Re-engine back as the Board asked? It is the only item ahead of Do Nothing: +2.00 in S1, S2 and S4, and -1.64 in S3 (a same-round A350 Re-engine). On my arithmetic this is the last round it clears epsilon, and the Board has said it would veto it again.
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2035 bulletin)
- NGSA launched in 2030 for an EIS in 2037, on the Alt plan, with A320 lines kept longer through the NGSA ramp.
- NGSA engine selection is RR, PW and CFM (code 7). P&W GTF2 Solo (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB Solo (ready 2037) both launched in 2030. The GEnx upgrade launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2033.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. My expected column last round (NGSA launched, A350 not re-engined) is what happened.
- Our final 2030 orders were Do Nothing. Our public statement gave no fps date and restated the dual-source engine requirement.
- Observed NB share was 39.4/60.6 through 2034, with deliveries of 664/1,020 in 2034. WB share is 58.8/41.2.

OUR POSITION (brief §1)
- Do Nothing is -0.28 against the status quo. The firm backlog runs out in 2035 (133 left), and from then all demand is new customers.
- After NGSA's EIS, with no fps, we lose 1 pp of preference a year. Preference reads 40% in 2035, 52.6% in 2040 (Airbus slack in its transition), 31% in 2045, 26% in 2050 and 16% in 2060.
- Capacity binds in 2039-43, with 225-402 customers waiting. The 737 MAX is phased out whatever we order: 641 in 2045, 428 in 2050, none in 2060.
- Delivered NB share falls to 22.1% in 2050 and 0% in 2060. Without an fps the narrowbody franchise runs out in the 2050s. That is a real question, but the grid has to carry it.

OBJECTIVES (brief §2)
- Not met: 50/50 split; incumbency (worst year 26%, newly not met because of NGSA); dual-source engines on our narrowbody (the 737 MAX flies CFM only).
- Met: balance-sheet repair (2029), and keeping it repaired in base and stress through 2050; three NB engine makers in 2045 and 2050.

KPIs
- The brief reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem.
- The FAA-process gate passes, and H7 has no trigger.
- The only rate value offered is hold.

GRID, S1-S4. S1 rivals hold; S2 Airbus returns to the A320 base plan; S3 Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine; S4 is the risk case, covert Delay Tactics. For rows without an fps, S4 equals S1.

  - Best fps row: the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, -4.23 in S4, short by 1.95.

Jay, you are my independent check on the estimates [BX-1316]. Please bring me the following.

(1) Buffer test, S4 against Do Nothing -0.28 (floor -2.28), on rows A-H. Confirm that:
- every fps row fails (best D -4.23, short 1.95; C -5.56, short 3.28);
- B passes at +1.72, by 4.00.

(2) For the Board: the submitted row and the same row with each Board item at its default, across S1-S4.
- Re-engine item: +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00.
- Also the Re-engine beside a 10-year fps (+1.33 / -2.31 in S3), so the Board sees why pairing makes it worse.

(3) Stress-case net debt by plan, from the brief's objective table.
- Confirm $0.0B for B and for the 10-year rows.
- Flag the 7-year at new sites ($0.7B), the 7-year with the Re-engine ($1.8-3.2B) and Embraer ($1.4-6.3B).

(4) Debt penalty: the grid already nets it, so don't subtract it again. Quote the undiscounted scale only: Re-engine $0.6B; 10-year $19.1B; 7-year $22.0B; via Embraer $52.5B.

(5) Cash timing on the standard curve:
- Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40;
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over its development years;
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over its development years.
Then your 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result for each. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547].

(6) Slip leg for the Re-engine. If its 5-year development needs one conservative reset of one or two years [BX-1318, BX-0553], does B still clear your buffer, and is it still above epsilon in S1? Last round you put a two-year reset at about $1.0B in 2030 money. What is it now?

(7) The crux: S3. Airbus did not re-engine the A350 in 2030, and it has NGSA in development to 2037.
- What chance do you put on a same-round A350 Re-engine?
- My arithmetic: the item's expected value is zero at 55%, +$1B at 27.5%, +0.79 at one-third and +1.09 at one-quarter.
- If your evidence puts it above about one in four, the edge is within epsilon, and doing less, better and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] would favour hold. I want your number, not mine.

(8) Cost of waiting on the Re-engine. A 2045 launch (EIS 2050) on discounting alone is about +0.74 / -0.60 (10 years at 10.5%; my rough inference). Check it, including whether the board's horizon cuts it further. If it holds, 2035 is the last round the Re-engine clears epsilon, and holding now gives up about $2.00B in S1, S2 and S4 for good.

(9) The fps for 2045: will waiting make the case better or worse?
- Each year of delay adds 1 pp to Airbus's lasting edge.
- Against that, the MAX phase-out shrinks what an fps would cannibalise.
- What would the 2045 grid have to show for a launch (EIS 2052 or 2055) to beat Do Nothing by more than epsilon and pass your buffer?

(10) Your expected column, and your premium view: if I held the Re-engine by my own choice rather than under a veto, that would be a $2.00B premium, exactly at the H8 cap.

Board risk to note: the Board says it would veto re787: launch on its Downside test, and every fps launch. Your numbers are the case it will judge [BG-0022].

tests.name: Meet and beat: 787 Re-engine, B against A (CEO asks 7 and 10)
tests.threshold: Among plans within epsilon ($1B) on the expected column, prefer the one with the higher worst column (inference)
tests.numbers: My expected column: S4 as the baseline, which equals S1 for every row without an fps, with S3 weighted by the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. Breakevens confirmed: the item's expected value is 2.00 - 3.64p, which is 0 at 54.9%, +1.00 at 27.5%, +0.79 at one-third and +1.09 at one-quarter. My number is about 30%, in a range of 25-35%. It comes from doctrine and inference, not my record; I have no evidence on Airbus. What raises it: (1) 2035 is Airbus's best remaining window, since an EIS in 2040 earns a full 20-year window and a 2045 move earns far less on the same board; (2) its overlap with NGSA development falls from 5 years in 2030 to 2 (2035-37); (3) doctrine expects an A350 attempt and reads the widebody as a Chicken game [B-2446]; (4) our 2030 statement that we keep the 787 line as it is tells Airbus it would move alone. What lowers it: (1) Airbus held in 2030; (2) it stresses a disciplined, self-funded transition with the NGSA ramp running to about 2045; (3) RR, the A350's engine maker, has launched no widebody engine and puts time on wing first. I cannot get it below one in four. At 30% the edge is +0.91 (A -0.72, B +0.19), inside epsilon. The worst column then decides: A -1.74 against B -3.38, so hold is better by 1.64. If I carry a one-year reset as the conservative baseline, the edge falls to about +0.6.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip: 787 Re-engine, one conservative reset (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Cost the delay in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost) once, then re-run the buffer test and epsilon
tests.numbers: Same method as 2030: the lost discounting on the item plus an assumed 20% overrun on the $5B bill (my inference). One-year reset (EIS 2041): 0.19 + 0.22 = about $0.41B; B S4 about +1.31; item in S1 about +1.59. Two-year reset (EIS 2042): 0.36 + 0.20 = about $0.56B; B S4 about +1.16, which clears the -2.28 floor by about 3.4; item in S1 about +1.44, still above epsilon by 0.44. Last round's $1.0B scales by 1.105^-5 to about $0.6B now. In S3 a slip costs more: the A350 would enter service first and keep its gains, so the item would fall to about -2.4 (inference). Cross-check on the brief's widebody figures ($180M a 787 at 20%, re-engined 25.21%, +1 pp a year): my model reproduces the item at +1.83 against the grid's +2.00.

tests.name: Full cost of a delay: Re-engine held to a 2045 relaunch (CEO ask 8)

tests.numbers: On discounting alone: 2.00 x 1.105^-10 = +0.74 in S1, S2 and S4, and -0.60 in S3. Confirmed. On the horizon: the grid's +2.00 at EIS 2040 is exactly 2030's +3.30 at EIS 2035 discounted five years (3.30 x 0.607), so the board counts at least to 2059. The brief's tables stop at 2060; if the board stops there too, a 2050 EIS earns only 11 of its 20 years while the bill is booked in full, and my model puts the relaunch at about +0.3. Either way it is inside epsilon, and doctrine would not take it. So 2035 is the last round the Re-engine clears epsilon. Holding gives up $2.00B in S1, S2 and S4 for good, and saves $1.64B if Airbus re-engines this round.

tests.name: fps for 2045: does waiting help? (CEO ask 9; advice)
tests.threshold: A 2045 launch must beat Do Nothing by more than $1B in the expected column, sit within $2B of Do Nothing in S4, hold stress net debt at $0.0B, and keep overlap at 2 years or less
tests.numbers: Lag: a 2045 launch enters service in 2055 on the 10-year ramp (18 years behind NGSA, long-run split 32/68) or 2052 on the 7-year (35/65), against 42/58 and 45/55 today. Preference on Do Nothing is 26% in 2050 and falls 1 pp a year. Cannibalisation: by then the MAX builds 342 (2052), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060). Most fps sales would fill empty capacity at about $14.1M a unit ($55M x 25.64%), against about $3.8M for a MAX. Trend: in the comparable column (NGSA on the Alt plan), the 10-year at Renton went from -6.51 in 2030 to -5.20 now; pure discounting would have given -3.95, so the growing lag ate about half the relief. On discounting alone the gap would reach about -1.9 in 2045, inside the buffer. On trend it reaches about -2.6 to -3.9 (inference), and a 2060 horizon would make it worse. Waiting shrinks the loss in 2026 dollars but does not change its sign: the business case needs a swing of more than $6.2B. The 2045 grid would have to show the best fps row above Do Nothing + $1B in the expected column, S4 at or above Do Nothing - $2B, and stress net debt $0.0B. Franchise view for the Board: the run-down is real and is already in Do Nothing's numbers. Keep the option warm at no grid cost and decide on the 2045 grid.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (option B)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto. B passes my buffer test (S4 +1.72 against the -2.28 floor, by 4.00) and keeps stress net debt at $0.0B, so if Ortberg orders it I concur on my ground. Advice only: I put a same-round A350 Re-engine at about 30%, which leaves an expected edge of +0.91, inside epsilon. On that tie, my Meet and beat rule takes the better worst column (A -1.74 against B -3.38), and Balance sheet first takes the plan with no added penalty. Holding by choice is a $2.00B premium on the grid, at the H8 cap, and it closes the Re-engine for good.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Re-engine: evidence that puts a same-round A350 Re-engine below one in four would change my advice to launch, which already passes my buffer. At one in four the edge is +1.09, outside epsilon. Examples would be an Airbus public commitment of its engineering to the NGSA ramp through 2040, or Rolls-Royce declining a new A350 engine. A ruling that the board counts no value beyond the brief's 2060 horizon does not change this, since it only makes waiting worse. Against the Re-engine, I would harden my advice if Pope finds no qualified widebody engine for 2040 or any production-certification concurrency, or if a reset larger than two years is in view. fps: a grid on which the best launch sits within $2B of Do Nothing in S4 and more than $1B ahead in the expected column, with stress net debt at $0.0B. Today the best fps plan is $1.95B short of the floor, and the cheapest launch is $5.20-5.28B below Do Nothing.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran every row with the risk case, S4, as the baseline. Do Nothing is -0.28, so the floor is -2.28.

fps: every launch fails, so my veto stands on all of them, and the team rule makes it binding. The best, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -4.23, $1.95B short; the 10-year at Renton alone is -5.56. Funding is not the gate: the 777X has been cash-positive since 2029, and the 10-year rows hold stress net debt at $0.0B. The market is. Waiting has helped at half the pace of discounting: the comparable gap went from -6.51 to -5.20 in five years. Hold.

Re-engine: it clears my buffer at +1.72, by $4.00B, holds stress net debt at $0.0B, and survives one conservative reset. Two years costs about $0.56B, leaving +1.44 in S1. No veto from me. Your numbers check, with one caution: if the board stops at 2060, a 2045 relaunch is worth about +0.3, not +0.74. Either way this is the last window.

One number decides it. On doctrine, not my record, I put a same-round A350 Re-engine at about three in ten, and I can't get it below one in four. That puts the edge at +0.91, inside epsilon, and on a tie I take the better worst column, -1.74 against -3.38. Holding by choice is a $2.00B premium on the grid, at the cap, or $0.91B on my column.

While disappointing, hold is the higher-confidence plan, barring evidence that Airbus stands still.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase, my veto (doctrine). Answers CEO ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem is live. Rate steps of 5 a month at least 6 months apart, agreed with the FAA. Supplier readiness is a hard gate
tests.numbers: I searched round2.md for FAA, quality, inject, certif, crunch, bottleneck, escape, scrutiny, grounding, strike, KPI, supplier, supply chain, problem and shortage. The only hits are public statements: our own line ('Our KPIs are stable', 57 a month), the Airbus and CFM/GE statements of principle, and Airbus's supply-security move for its own lines. P&W's note that its GTF fleet 'still has work ahead' concerns the A320neo engine; the 737 flies CFM only. None is a reported Boeing quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. That is confirmed from the brief, not assumed. rate_737 offers only hold, because the Rate Increase option expired in 2030, so the veto has nothing to bind on. Watch item, not a live problem: Airbus has publicly secured titanium, rare earths and LEAP-1A/GTF supply for its own lines to about 2045. We secure our own LEAP-1B and materials for the MAX tail and the widebody base, and we attribute nothing to Airbus (doctrine). One caution: the public line 'KPIs are stable' rests on the brief reporting no problem, because the board carries no KPI data

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (my record, applied to airplanes by inference). Answers CEO ask 2 in part
tests.threshold: Can the plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S4 (covert Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value rests on the nominal date
tests.numbers: For rows without an fps, S4 equals S1: Do Nothing -0.28, Re-engine row +1.72. Delay Tactics act only from an fps EIS, so no part of the Re-engine's +2.00 depends on the risk case. The fps rows lose only 0.05-0.20 from S1 to S4: 10-year at Renton -5.48 to -5.56; 10-year at new sites -5.72 to -5.92; 7-year at Renton -7.67 to -7.72; best row D -4.15 to -4.23. They fail on value, not on date. The board does not price the slip that matters, a derivative slip. Company slip priors (profile.md, doctrine): Re-engine +2 years central, range +1 to +4; clean-sheet fps +3 central, +2 to +5. My estimate from discounting alone at 10.5% (inference; the slip leg is Malave's): the item's +2.00 becomes about +1.81 at a 1-year slip, +1.64 at 2 years and +1.34 at 4 years. It stays above +$1B in S1, S2 and S4. The board's 20-year horizon cut is not tested here

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness, 2035-40 (doctrine plus inference). Answers CEO ask 2 (a)-(e) and the Board's two conditions
tests.threshold: A widebody engine ready by the 2040 EIS; the amended type certificate before the line converts (no production-certification concurrency); 787 line stable with capacity; engineering capacity free; widebody supply base hot
tests.numbers: Pass on two conditions. (a) Engine: the GEnx upgrade, launched 2030 and ready since 2033, is ready 7 years before a 2040 EIS. It qualifies on timing and is the only widebody engine work on the public record. It is an upgrade of today's 787 engine. The board prices the Re-engine without naming an engine, so it does not test the margin step from 20% to 25.21% against the engine (inference). A single GE source is acceptable on durability only if GE commits privately to capacity and to time on wing proven in service before EIS. With 7 years of fleet data by 2040, it can be. RR has launched no widebody engine. Under the public rules, a Trent 1000 upgrade launched this round would be ready in 2038, in time; an UltraFan WB launched this round would be ready in 2041, a year late. Today's 787 is dual-source (WB engines GEnx 42% / Trent 58%), so a GEnx-only Re-engine narrows supply (inference); keep the RR door open privately. (b) Plan: 5-year development over 2035-40. Design and ground test 2035-38, then flight test and the amended type certificate by 2039. The line converts only after the amended type certificate, with no re-engined 787 built at rate before it, and no fixed-price development. The board does not price concurrency. (c) 787 line: the brief holds widebody deliveries at 100 a year (8.3 a month) and reports no 787 problem. The item gains 1 pp a year from 2040, which is 134 a year (11.2 a month) by 2060; the 85% cap is 144.5 a year (12.0 a month). The Charleston expansion (completion targeted around 2028) aims at rates in the teens, so capacity covers it. (d) Engineering: the 777X has delivered since 2027, the MAX 7/10 are in service and no fps is in development, so this is one major development at a time. The trained workforce is not on the board (ExCo judgement). (e) Supply base: the brief reports no widebody supplier problem. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot. The growth is gradual, about 1.7 aircraft a year

tests.numbers: A 2035 Re-engine develops over 2035-40. Alone: 0 years, $0. With a 2035 10-year fps (EIS 2045, window 2038-45): 2 years (2038-40), $1.2B undiscounted, H4-legal. On the grid the Re-engine beside it is worth +1.33 / +1.34 / -2.31 / +1.33, against +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00 alone. With a 2035 7-year fps (EIS 2042, window 2035-42): 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach; the item drops to +0.77 / +0.78 / -2.86 / +0.77. Against a 2045 fps (7-year window 2045-52; 10-year window 2048-55): 0 years, because the Re-engine finishes 5-8 years earlier. Counts confirmed: 0 / 2 / 5

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7-year or 10-year (inference)

tests.numbers: The fps holds this round; recorded for 2045. 10-year: EIS 2045 for a 2035 launch or 2055 for a 2045 launch, a $60.32B bill, 2 years of strain beside a same-round Re-engine. 7-year: EIS 2042 or 2052, a $65.00B bill, 5 years of strain (H4 out). A 7-year fps enters service in 2042, inside them (385 waiting in 2042, 321 in 2043). The 10-year is the ramp operations can deliver predictably

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (my record, applied by inference). Answers CEO ask 5
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP; via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks (capital, capacity or IP the board credits)
tests.numbers: Via Embraer is $10.96B below the Solo 10-year in every column: at Renton -16.44 / -16.24 / -17.90 / -16.52 against -5.48 / -5.28 / -6.94 / -5.56, and the same gap at new sites. It has the same 2045 EIS and the same strain window on the board, so it brings no capacity relief. The bill is $100B against $60.32B, and the undiscounted debt penalty is $52.5B against $19.1B. The 787 Re-engine builds on our own airframe IP, so we invest

Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, about $1.0B a year; net debt $0.0B in base and stress in every column; undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B, already netted in the grid. fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2035-45, $6.0B a year on average, peaking at 14% (about $8.4B) in 2041, which is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow; stress net debt $0.0B. fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2035-42, $9.3B a year (67% of base, 101% of stress); stress net debt $0.7B at new sites (fails) and $0.0B at Renton, rising to $1.8-3.2B with the Re-engine. Via Embraer: $100B over 2035-45, $10B a year, peaking near $14B, above base free cash flow; stress net debt $1.4-6.3B. At a launch, Renton avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex, in full if chosen 3 years or more before EIS. The recommended plan (fps hold plus Re-engine) passes

tests.name: Narrowbody engine readiness for a future fps (inference). Answers CEO ask 4
tests.threshold: A real second or third engine source ready by fps EIS, with capacity and durability, not only on paper
tests.numbers: The fps holds and the code is null. On the board the sources are real. GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) launched in 2030 and are on the public record. The brief's table fits CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB under code 7 at a 2045 EIS, and the fps rows show 3 sources in 2050. (7,7) is not a barred pair. The ready dates sit 6-9 years before a 2042-45 EIS and 15-19 years before a 2052-55 EIS. Three operational caveats, none priced. Durability: P&W says its GTF fleet 'still has work ahead', and our customers want durability; NGSA service from 2037 gives 5-8 years of fleet data by 2042-45. Capacity: the same three makers supply NGSA (code 7) through its ramp, rate 100 about eight years after its 2037 EIS (about 2045), plus the A320 tail contracted to about 2045, and CFM capacity is already shared. Commitment: P&W and RR set their own test-driven dates. The result is real on technology and unproven on capacity. Keep warm privately: second-source talks with P&W and RR for capacity slots and durability data, with the CFM LEAP derivative as the floor. Name no maker in public

tests.name: Renton or new site, readiness (inference). Answers CEO ask 6
tests.threshold: Any operational reason to reassign Renton now; readiness of a Renton reassignment at an fps launch

ops.memo:
My seat runs mostly on Boeing's operations doctrine. My own record is Global Services, and I say so. Three results, ranked.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I searched the 2035 brief: it reports no quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. My KPI veto has nothing to bind on; the only rate offered is hold. The 787 Re-engine is executable over 2035-40. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, seven years ahead of EIS. Engineering is free. Charleston's expansion for rates in the teens covers the item's growth to about 11 a month by 2060. My two conditions stand: GE commits privately on capacity and durability, and the amended type certificate comes before the line converts. On my estimate, a two-year slip leaves it near +$1.6B. Its -$1.64B in S3 is a market call for Kelly, Jay and the Board, not mine.

Second, engineering capacity. Re-engine alone: zero overlap. Beside a 10-year fps: 2 years, $1.2B, legal. Beside a 7-year fps: 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Hold the fps. The cheapest launch is $5.20B below Do Nothing, and every fps row fails the S4 floor on value, not on date. When it comes: Solo, 10-year, code 7. Via Embraer costs $10.96B more and adds nothing we lack. Renton fits a 2045 launch, as the MAX runs down to 214 a year by 2055. Sensitivity: every $1B a year of programme spend is 7% of base and 11% of stress free cash flow.

At launch we will choose a code naming makers ready by EIS: code 7 (CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB) fits three sources at any EIS from 2042, and codes 5 or 6 fit two. We will not rely on code 4 while no Joint Venture has formed. No maker and no date named in public.

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago I said we'd get the basics right first, and the team has kept at it. The 737 line is steady at 57 a month, the 777X and the 737-7 and -10 are in service, and the balance sheet is where we said we'd put it. That's the base we build the future on.

On the 737, we're staying at 57 a month. Our KPIs are stable. Rates stay tied to the data, and we agree them with the FAA, the same way we always have.

On widebodies, the 787 and 777X lines are stable, and we'll keep putting our effort into the airplanes our customers fly today.

On a new single-aisle airplane, we've been doing the work on three fronts: the market, the technology and our own readiness. Two of those have come a long way. The engine technology is maturing, and our balance sheet is ready. The business case isn't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane until it is. We'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. I'm not going to give you a date. When we do launch, the airplane will carry more than one engine source, and the entry-into-service date will have headroom built in.

In the meantime we're keeping our engineering team and our supply base ready, so that when the time comes we can execute. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. I order Do Nothing, the row 'fps: hold + 787: hold', at -0.28 / -0.03 / -1.74 / -0.28 (S1-S4).
- fps hold, code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold, fps_site new_site.
- No order differs from the default, so no item goes to the Board for approval. The full case still goes with the package.

TEAM RULE.
- Malave's buffer veto binds on all 12 fps rows. The floor is Do Nothing's S4 less $2B, -2.28. The best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -4.23 (short 1.95). The 10-year at Renton alone is -5.56 (short 3.28), the 7-year at Renton -7.72, and via Embraer at Renton -16.52. I accept the veto, and it matches my own reading.
- The KPI doctrine: Pope searched the brief and found no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate value offered.
- Everything else is mine to decide, so the re787 call is mine.

FPS: HOLD. Two of the three work streams have converged [BX-1296, B-2303].
- Technology: GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so code 7 gives three sources from a 2042 EIS.
- Boeing: net debt is $0.0B in base and stress, and the 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547].
- The market has not converged. The cheapest launch, the 10-year at Renton, is $5.20-5.28B below Do Nothing in every column. That is beyond H8's $2B cap, so the 50/50 and incumbency objectives cannot carry it.
- When the fps comes, it comes Solo on the 10-year ramp. Its worst column is $2.20B better than the 7-year's (-6.94 against -9.14), its bill is smaller, and it enters service after the 2039-43 capacity-binding years.
- NGSA's date does not set ours [B-2313].

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD, BY MY OWN DECISION. This is the crux, and I own it.
- The grid item is +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00. It passes every test but one:
  - Malave's buffer (S4 +1.72, clear by 4.00);
  - stress net debt $0.0B;
  - Fundable when the 777X turns;
  - H3's second half, in force and not triggered;
  - H4, with 0 years of overlap;
  - Pope's readiness, on two conditions: GE commits privately, and the amended type certificate comes before conversion.
- The one test it hangs on is how likely a same-round A350 Re-engine is (S3).
- In my frame I set the test before the memos came in, and I said I meant it: if my independent check [BX-1316] put that chance above about one in four, the edge would fall inside epsilon, and doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] would take hold.
- Malave's number is about 30%, in a range of 25-35%. He gave his reasons both ways:
  - for: on the board's 20-year window, 2035 is Airbus's best remaining shot; its overlap with NGSA development falls to 2 years; our own 2030 line said we would keep the 787 as it is;
  - against: Airbus held in 2030, and RR has launched no widebody engine.
- On my arithmetic (work/r2_calc.txt) the item is worth 2.00 - 3.64p:
  - +0.91 at 30%;
  - +0.79 at one-third, my own 2030 weight;
  - +1.09 only at the bottom of his range.
- With one conservative reset planned in, as I plan every development [BX-1318, BX-1275], the edge is about +0.6 at 30%. It clears epsilon only if the A350 risk is below about one in five (18%), and nobody at this table can get it there.
- Within epsilon, the worst column decides: -1.74 against -3.38, so hold is better by 1.64.
- What changed since 2030: the upside fell from +3.30 to +2.00 faster than the downside narrowed (from -2.48 to -1.64). At my 2030 weight the edge was +1.37; now it is +0.79.
- In the frame I said I would not park a ready program to dodge an A350 move. I am not doing that. I am holding because the expected value, weighted on my CFO's number, does not clear my own bar. This is not a reply to Airbus and not timed to them. It is the size of a bounded loss in a column we cannot rule out [BX-1279].
- The Board told me it would veto the item again on the same column. Its veto would have landed in the same place, but I would rather own the call than hand it to the Board.
- Cost, stated plainly. Holding gives up $2.00B in S1, S2 and S4, and it is likely for good: Malave puts a 2045 relaunch at +0.3 to +0.74, inside epsilon. It saves $1.64B if Airbus re-engines this round.

PREMIUM (H8). The hold is my choice, so it is a management doctrine premium (doing less, better, and the higher-confidence plan), not the Board's constraint.
- $0.91B on my expected (weighted) column; $2.00B on S1 alone, exactly at the cap.
- Nothing else is logged: no objective premium, and the fps hold and rate hold are grid-best. The H8 total is within $2B on either measure.

BOARD PACKAGE.
- Submitted row: 'fps: hold + 787: hold', -0.28 / -0.03 / -1.74 / -0.28. With no Board item, no default comparison is needed.
- For reference:
  - 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine': +1.72 / +1.97 / -3.38 / +1.72 (item +2.00 / +2.00 / -1.64 / +2.00);
  - beside a 10-year fps the item is +1.33 / +1.34 / -2.31 / +1.33;
  - the 10-year at Renton against Do Nothing is -5.20 / -5.25 / -5.20 / -5.28.
- S4 is -0.28 against the -2.28 floor: a pass.
- Malave's results: buffer pass; stress net debt $0.0B in all columns; Fundable when the 777X turns, pass.
- Pope's written results: no live problem; Re-engine executable on her two conditions; strain counts 0 / 2 / 5; via Embraer fails invest-or-partner; no operational reason to move the site now.
- Rulings:
  - H1: lifted in 2030, and the ruling stands. The 777X has been delivering since 2027 [BX-0550], the MAX 7/10 are in service [BX-1299], and net debt has been $0 since 2029 [B-2327]. The fps fails here on market and buffer, not on H1.
  - H3: first half lifted; second half in force and not triggered.
  - H4: overlap counts are 0 with the Re-engine alone, 2 beside a 10-year fps, and 5 beside a 7-year fps (struck).
  - H5 and H6: nothing in play.
  - H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger.

WRITTEN FRANCHISE VIEW FOR THE BOARD.
- The narrowbody run-down is real, and it is already in Do Nothing's numbers:
  - preference goes from 40% to 31% in 2045, 26% in 2050 and 16% in 2060;
  - delivered share is 22.1% in 2050 and 0% in 2060, as the MAX is phased out.
- 2045 is the last round in which an fps can enter service (2052 or 2055) while the MAX still builds 214-342 a year to hand over (Pope).
- Waiting has shrunk the loss in 2026 dollars, from -6.51 to -5.20, but at half the pace of discounting. It has not changed the sign. The business case needs a swing of more than $6B (Malave).
- So we keep the option warm at no cost on the grid: workforce, suppliers, engines, the Renton plan, and no concurrency. We decide on the 2045 grid against Malave's bar. I will not launch at a loss beyond the cap to defend a share target. I would rather report an honest decline than book an unfunded promise.

DOCTRINE AGAINST MY RECORD.
- My record drove: KPI gating [BX-1259]; debt first [BX-1305]; the three work streams [BX-1296]; no concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed price [BX-1262]; one conservative reset [BX-1318]; doing less, better [BX-1239]; the CFO as independent check [BX-1316]; no fps date [B-2315].
- Doctrine drove: the dual-source requirement; H3 and H4; Malave's 30%, which comes from doctrine and inference, as he says himself; the workforce-readiness move.
decision.expected_scenario: Weighted. S1 (rivals hold) is the most likely single column, at about 70%. S3 (a same-round A350 Re-engine) is carried at about 30%, Malave's number (range 25-35%), which I adopt as I said I would in the frame. For rows without an fps, S4 equals S1 and S2 is within 0.25 of it. The weighted column reads Do Nothing -0.72 and 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine' +0.19.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: On the weighted column, 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine' is highest (+0.19 against Do Nothing's -0.72), but by +0.91, inside epsilon. With one conservative reset carried, the gap is about +0.6. In S1 alone it leads by 2.00 (+1.72 against -0.28). Within epsilon, the tie-break (doing less, better [BX-1239]; the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]; the better worst column, -1.74 against -3.38) selects 'fps: hold + 787: hold', which I order. Every fps row fails Malave's binding buffer test.
decision.premium_reason:
Doctrine premium, management's own choice: re787 is held even though the Re-engine row leads on the grid.
- $0.91B on my expected (weighted) column, with S3 at 30%.
- $2.00B in S1, S2 and S4 taken singly: exactly at the H8 cap, with no headroom.
- About $0.6B if one conservative reset is carried as the baseline.

Reason: within epsilon, doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] decide, and hold's worst column is better by $1.64B.

No other premium is logged:
- fps hold and rate hold are the grid-best rows;
- the objective premium for 50/50 and incumbency is $0, since the cheapest fps is $5.20B below Do Nothing, beyond the cap.

The H8 total is within $2B on either measure. What breaks the number: if Airbus holds the A350 this round, the full $2.00B is given up for good. If it re-engines, hold saves $1.64B.
decision.objective_note:
The orders serve the mission in objectives section 1 without trading PV for it beyond the logged premium. The Re-engine would not have moved the narrowbody objectives.
- 50/50 split: not met. Preference is 52.6% in 2040 (Airbus slack in its NGSA transition), then 31.0% in 2045 and 26.0% in 2050. The cheapest fps is $5.20B below Do Nothing, beyond H8's cap, so the objective premium is $0.
- Incumbency: not met. The worst year is 26% (2050).
- Balance-sheet repair: met. Net debt reached $0 in 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress), and holds at $0.0B through 2050 in every column.
- Engine-source enabler: dual sources on our narrowbody, not met (the 737 MAX flies CFM only). It is restated publicly as a requirement, with code 7 available at a future launch.
- Three narrowbody engine makers in 2045 and 2050: met.
- Widebody: the 58.8% position holds on the status-quo path.
decision.predictions:
Board: confirms Do Nothing (about 97%). No order is a Board item, and every order matches its would-approve list.

Airbus:
- NGSA enters service in 2037 as planned (likely).
- A same-round A350 Re-engine: about 30%, Malave's number. If it happens, hold saves $1.64B (-1.74 against -3.38), and H3's second half closes our Re-engine for good.
- No Delay Tactics while no fps is launched.

Engine makers:
- GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, as on the record.
- A Rolls-Royce widebody move is possible but not expected while no re-engine is launched.

Boeing:
- Narrowbody preference: 40% in 2035-36, 39% in 2037, 38% in 2038, then 53% in 2039 and 52.6% in 2040 on Airbus's slack. Deliveries are capped at 684 in 2039-43, with 225-402 customers waiting. Preference then falls to 31% in 2045 and 26% in 2050, and delivered share to 22.1% in 2050.
- Net debt $0.0B in base and stress through 2050.

Round 3 (2045):
- The fps is tested on that grid (Solo, 10-year, code 7, Renton). On Malave's trend it is likely still short of the bar unless the grid changes.
- If the A350 has not re-engined, the Re-engine is re-tested, likely inside epsilon.

Value: weighted, -0.72 (S1 -0.28, S3 -1.74).

airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. They frame every step our next-generation single-aisle aircraft takes towards entry into service.

The programme remains in development, and we continue to plan its entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Its timing follows a technology and production system we have been maturing, and we keep it on our own clock. We will report progress against milestones, in windows, and we will not trade safety or quality for speed.

We are preparing the Airbus of the 2030s while we keep delivering for our customers today. The A320 family stays at its present rate until the new aircraft enters service, and our production plan keeps A320 lines running longer through the new aircraft's ramp-up. The transition will be disciplined and controlled, rate by rate, with quality first: each step is taken only when the quality indicators for it are met. We will certify the aircraft's engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce in sequence, as each one matures.

The programme remains funded within our cash flow and preserves our financial flexibility and balance-sheet discipline; the case assumes no state support. We continue to secure our own supply base, from work packages to materials, and to invest in the people who will design and build this aircraft. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE (round 2, 2035)

I hold course. The orders are ngsa hold (NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037), engine code 7 kept, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none and a320_plan alt kept. Toepfer and Wagner recommend exactly these orders, and they are the Board's would-approve list. Every order is the default or the plan the Board approved in round 1, so there is no Board item this round. No override is used, and the game's one override stays in reserve.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted. Rule 4 bars it: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, 3.6 times net cash. Against the lean, one move is -15.68 / +0.83 / +0.48 / +0.39 / +0.83 / -15.69 / +0.83, and both moves -16.13 / +0.45 / +0.10 / -0.04 / +0.45 / -16.14 / +0.45. It falls short of $1B even in the fps columns. Its cash would also take 2035-2036 to $5.241B, over the line. Bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands, and I do not set it aside. This also deletes the A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics rows, the raw best in S2-S5.
- Every cancel row is deleted. Rule 7 bars it, and the grid agrees: against continuing it is -24.60 / -21.72 / -21.81 / -19.81 / -21.72 / -24.61 / -21.72, after a $25.37B write-off. Continuing never loses.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS OF BOTH TESTS
- The lean (NGSA hold, Alt, A350 hold) passes every test in both memos.
- The base-plan switch passes both memos, but Wagner gives it no safety ground and the Board vetoes it. It trails the lean by 1.31-1.45 in every column.
- NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (Alt) fails Toepfer's soft veto, which is binding. Peak cash is $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.674B in 2035-2036, $1.446B over $5.228B. The strain alone gives $5.674B, and no phasing on the board's terms cures it. It also fails his robustness test (item -1.21 in S6-S7). Wagner passes it at his capacity limit and holds no veto.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The lean is the highest-grid survivor in every column: +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86, or 8.46 on my weights. It is positive everywhere, with the worst plausible column S4 (fps 7-yr, entry into service 2042, a five-year NGSA lead) at +3.59.
- No survivor is within $1B (the base plan trails by more than $1.3B), so the tie-breaks are not engaged.

THE OVERRIDE I DO NOT TAKE
On the grid, the A350 Re-engine is +1.55 over the lean in S1 and +1.27 on my weights, so the team rule's $1B test would technically allow an override of Toepfer. I decline it for four reasons:
(a) The Board vetoes rea350 launch on balance-sheet grounds. Its override review fails on a Qualified Majority item that trails the best passing option by 1.21 in S6-S7. I have no override against the Board, so the order would revert to hold and burn the game's one override.
(b) It breaks the company's own guardrail, peak programme spend within one year's FCF (profile §9 step 7). My balance-sheet appetite is Low [AX-0022, AX-0102].
(c) Wagner's flag: it has no slip margin. His risk case, NGSA entering service in 2038, would make the overlap 3 years and the strain $1.8B, past rule 6's limit, and the grid could not show $1B in S6-S7.
(d) The item loses 1.21 in the 787 Re-engine columns.
For honesty on robustness: at plan level the A350 row's worst column is +4.65 (S7), above the lean's +3.59. Its weakness lies in the item and the cash, not the plan row.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Five pillars: nothing is covert. The public line gives windows, not a date. The wording now claims only 'a technology and production system we have been maturing', with no state money and no word of Delay Tactics [AX-0073, AX-0081].
(2) The ramp: the Alt plan is kept. The A320 stays at 85 a month to entry into service and never exceeds 82 after it. Each step-down is gated on quality KPIs, and Wagner's pacing measure is adopted, so the 2039-2040 gap is never closed by rushing NGSA [AX-0010, AX-0056].
(3) The 2030s: NGSA enters service in 2037, after the 2035 technology year (rule 1) [AX-0020, A-0409]. A one-year slip to 2038 stays inside 'the second half of the 2030s'.
(4) The Board: every order is on its approve list, and there is no item it would veto.

OWN CLOCK
Boeing made no move in round 1, and its line ('not there yet', no date) moves nothing. Its MAX phase-out from 2044 and its dual-source condition, now meetable, keep an fps this round plausible. Neither moves or cancels NGSA (rules 2 and 7). In S4, the worst case, NGSA still leads by five years.

ENGINE CODE
Code 7, final, on Wagner's recommendation. It gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050 at no payoff cost. Code 6 would put the three-maker enabler at risk. Code 5 would drop the maker that has margin. If a P&W and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture forms, codes 5, 6 and 7 behave alike, and 7 covers every case. Certification runs in sequence, and CFM is never dropped.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no item this round)
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass on peak cash ($5.074B against $5.228B), Alt phasing (nil in 2035-2036) and robustness. Net cash stays positive on the recommended 30% payout.
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, production readiness (an inference, since the brief gives no wing status), the ramp shield, supply crunch and engine code.
- Grid: +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86. Base row beside it: +10.19 / +4.95 / +5.65 / +2.14 / +4.95 / +9.70 / +4.47.

CORRECTION ACCEPTED
Toepfer's trigger is the right one. Five cash years are spent, so the overrun line is a bill of about $35.83B, not the $36.4-36.6B in my frame.

This round's statement uses the Board's wording and claims no more maturity than the record supports: Wagner's readiness pass is an inference, and the slip prior is 1-2 years.

board_response.recommendation: Round-1 review: Wagner to report to the twice-yearly safety review on NGSA readiness, the KPIs gating each A320 step-down and the A320neo engine-tail contracts.
board_response.response: Ongoing. The reporting is carried forward as described in the round-2 safety-oversight response above.

priorities: NGSA to entry into service in 2037, on its own clock. The order is ngsa: hold, which continues the programme and is not a Board item. Boeing has put no fps on the record and gives no date, and nothing in the bulletin calls for re-timing. Against continuing, a cancellation would lose 24.60 / 21.72 / 21.81 / 19.81 / 21.72 / 24.61 / 21.72 $B in S1-S7, after writing off about $25.4B of spend to date ($35.52B x 5/7).

Liquidity and the rating through NGSA's last two cash years. In 2035 and 2036 NGSA costs $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year. One year's FCF is about $5.23B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10/EUR), so headroom is $0.15B a year. Nothing else goes into those years. The A350 Re-engine waits until NGSA spend has rolled off, and the Alt-plan cash stays phased from 2037, as conditioned in round 1.

Integrity: Delay Tactics stay at none. No fps launch is on the public record, so any move would be naked. Against the same plan without it, one move loses 15.68 in S1 and 15.69 in S6, and both moves lose 16.13 to 16.14.

Safety, quality and the ramp through entry into service and the A320-to-NGSA transition. The Alt plan is kept, with each step-down gated on quality KPIs. Engines are certified in sequence, with CFM always fitted. The NGSA ramp is not rushed to close the 2039-2040 capacity gap.

Returns kept fundable and supply kept stable. Each dividend proposal stays inside the 30-50% policy and is calibrated so that net cash stays non-negative through 2036. No new buyback authority before NGSA cash ends, and no equity raise. Engine code 7 is kept, so that three makers are in the market.
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Averse, 4 of 5, unchanged. The Board funds NGSA alone through its last two cash years (2035-2036, $5.07B a year against a $5.23B line). It takes on no second programme and no covert move. It accepts no Board item that loses more than $2B in any of S1-S7: Boeing's public line points to S1, but the bulletin rules out no column.
would_approve: ngsa: hold (NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037). This is not a Board item, and the Board never vetoes it. The expected package row (NGSA hold, A320 Alt plan, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none) reads +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86 in S1-S7. It is positive in every column, with the worst at S4 (+3.59), and it is the best plan that passes the Board's tests in every column.

ngsa_engine_code: 7, kept. It rides with NGSA and does not change the payoff. With GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, every NGSA row shows 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050. No forbidden (fps, NGSA) pair involves NGSA code 7. A narrowing to 5 or 6 that keeps CFM, with its reason given, would not be vetoed: the code is never a veto ground.
rea350: hold and delay_tactics: none. These are the defaults, and the Board never vetoes them.
would_veto:
rea350: launch, on balance-sheet grounds. Plan-level failure means the added item is vetoed, never NGSA.
- A 2035 launch develops in 2035-2039 and overlaps NGSA development in 2035-2036.
- Spend in those years is $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain ($3B x 2/5 over two years) = $6.67B a year, $1.45B over the $5.23B line.
- Deferring the Re-engine's own spend does not cure it: the strain alone takes NGSA to $5.67B a year.
The other tests do not save it, but they are not the ground:
- Rule 6 is met at a two-year overlap.
- The downside test passes: +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 in S1-S5, and -1.21 in S6 and S7, within the $2B limit.
An override of the CFO's cash test would also fail Override review. This is a Qualified Majority item, and the plan trails the best passing option by 1.21 in S6 and S7. Acceptable alternative: hold.

delay_tactics: bottleneck or both, always, on integrity and abnormal-risk grounds. poaching this round as well: no fps launch is on the public record, so the move is naked (a $48.32B fine).
- One move, against the same plan without it: -15.68 / +0.83 / +0.48 / +0.39 / +0.83 / -15.69 / +0.83. It fails the downside test in S1 and S6, and even in the fps columns it falls short of the $1B poaching condition.
- The second move adds -0.38 to -0.45 in every column.
- Its $1B would also take most or all of NGSA's $0.15B headroom in 2035-2036.
Acceptable alternative: none.

ngsa: cancel, on the reactive-cancellation ground. Against continuing it is -24.60 / -21.72 / -21.81 / -19.81 / -21.72 / -24.61 / -21.72, so continuing never loses, let alone by $1B in every column. Any Boeing move would make no difference. Acceptable alternative: hold.

a320_plan: base, a change from the plan the Board approved in round 1. A blank field keeps alt, so the Board reads the switch as the Board item. Its item value is -1.43 / -1.40 / -1.31 / -1.45 / -1.40 / -1.44 / -1.39: it gains in no column, so it fails the downside test's requirement to gain in the expected scenario. The Board would approve it only if Mr Wagner's safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch results require it, because safety governs. Acceptable alternative: alt.

Any Board item Mr Wagner fails on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch, unless his own veto check shows it resolved, and any override of those tests. Any Board item carrying an ExCo objection that has been neither respected nor properly overridden, or a red-line flag that has been neither struck nor rebutted. Any plan that needs an equity raise or a dividend cut outside a crisis.

recommendations.text: Hold course on NGSA: order ngsa: hold, entering service in 2037, on the company's own clock. Boeing gives no fps date, so there is nothing to react to. If Boeing launches in this round, the column still favours continuing: S4 (fps 7-yr, entry into service 2042) gives NGSA a five-year lead and the package +3.59. Cancellation would lose 19.81 to 24.61 in every column. Only a reported technology or engine-maturity slip would re-time it, and the Board would hear of that before anything is committed.

Keep the A350 at hold in 2035, as the Board said in round 1. Any year that NGSA and the Re-engine share costs $6.67B, against a $5.23B line. The strain alone ($0.6B a year) breaks the line even if the Re-engine's own spend were deferred. The Board records what this costs: the item would gain +1.54 to +1.55 in S1-S5 and lose 1.21 in S6-S7. The Board gives that up for liquidity. The earliest clean development start is 2037, which on this calendar means the 2045 round, and only if Boeing has launched no 787 Re-engine and that round's grid passes the Board's tests. Please do not spend the game's one override on the CFO's cash test: it would fail Override review on the S6-S7 column.

Keep Delay Tactics at none. With no fps on the record, every Delay Tactics row is naked in S1 and S6 (-15.68 / -15.69 for one move). Even if an fps reaches the record later, bottleneck and both remain vetoed. Poaching would be considered only once, only with every condition met (at least $1B in the expected scenario included), and only with the CEO's setting-aside of the stricter ExCo condition recorded. On this grid one move gains no more than +0.83 in any fps column.

Keep NGSA engine code 7. All three makers have launched (GTF2 ready 2036, UltraFan NB ready 2037), so it gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050, and no forbidden pair can force it to change. Mr Wagner should report UltraFan NB's maturity, since it is ready in 2037 with no margin. Certify the engines in sequence and never drop CFM. Any narrowing should come to the Board with its reason. Dropping Rolls-Royce would put the three-maker enabler at risk, because Rolls-Royce has no other narrowbody on the record.

Keep the Alt plan, which gains +1.31 to +1.45 in every column, with the round-1 cash condition. On the transition: the brief shows NGSA preference at 47.0% in 2039 and 47.4% in 2040, against the 60% objective. Capacity then is 734+93 and 556+296 against demand of 1,931 and 1,972, and the slack goes to Boeing. The objective never changes the payoff, and the Board will not trade quality for it: no rate step ahead of its quality KPIs. Mr Wagner may propose quality-gated, unpriced measures as other_moves, reported to the Board.

Payout and balance sheet. Dividend proposals are reserved to the Board. The CFO should report net cash at end-2034 against his round-1 stress case. The 2035 and 2036 proposals should sit inside the 30-50% policy, set so that net cash stays non-negative until NGSA cash ends in 2036. No new buyback authority before 2037, and no equity raise. State money is upside, never in the case.

Public statement and scenarios. Present the package as the whole S1-S7 row, with the default rows, the worst plausible column and the CFO's peak cash. In public, report NGSA progress against milestones in windows, with no internal targets, no state money and no word of Delay Tactics. The Board's round-1 wording point is outstanding and should be answered in board_response: 'a technology and production system we have been maturing' rather than 'matured over the past decade'. Two years before entry into service, the line should claim no more maturity than the record supports.

frame.question: NGSA is two years from entry into service, and the next round (2045) comes after it. This is therefore our last chance to cancel or re-time NGSA, to change its engine code and to change the A320 plan. Do we hold course? That means: continue NGSA to 2037 on engine code 7 with the approved Alt plan, keep the A350 at hold and Delay Tactics at none, and put nothing else into NGSA's last two cash years, 2035-2036.

ngsa_engine_code: None, 1-7 (currently 7). It does not change our payoff, but it decides the engine-supply enabler. Because the next round (2045) comes after the 2037 entry into service, this is the last round to change it. No forbidden (fps, NGSA) pair involves NGSA code 7.

rea350: hold | launch. A 2035 launch enters service in 2040 and costs $5B, booked at entry into service. Development runs 2035-2039 and overlaps NGSA's in 2035-2036 (2 years), with strain of $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B. It is a Board item (Qualified Majority).
delay_tactics: none | bottleneck | poaching | both. Covert; $1B per move. A Board item. No fps is on the record, so any move ordered now is naked and draws the $48.32B fine if Boeing never launches.
a320_plan: alt | base (currently alt, approved in round 1). A blank field keeps alt. A switch to base is a Board item. This is the last round to change it before NGSA enters service.
Cancel options listed: ngsa: cancel only. rea350 has not been launched, so it cannot be cancelled.

red_lines: FIVE PILLARS (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security): no order or statement that fails them, and none is ever overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081]. A safety or quality slip of entry into service is acceptable; a rushed rate step is not [AX-0056].

RULES 2 AND 7, OUR OWN CLOCK: no Boeing move, recorded or expected, moves NGSA, and NGSA is never cancelled in reaction to Boeing [A-0364]. Cancel is deleted.

RULE 3: no A350 Re-engine after Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. It does not bind today (none is on the record). The S6-S7 column (-1.21 for the A350 item) is that risk priced. If Boeing launches one this round, the A350 path closes for good.

frame.asks_ops:

(1) SAFETY AND QUALITY. Report any safety or quality matter on the A320, the A350 or the NGSA programme. The brief reports none. Confirm that nothing in the lean or the public line fails the five pillars.

(2) NGSA PRODUCTION READINESS FOR 2037: the wing at rate, the production system, and engine maturity (GTF2 ready 2036; UltraFan NB ready 2037 with no margin; CFM always fitted). Give me:
- your slip prior;
- whether a one-year slip to 2038 is the risk case. It stays inside 'the second half of the 2030s';

(6) THE 2039-2040 TRANSITION. Capacity is 734+93 and 556+296 against demand of 1,931 and 1,972, and preference drops to 47.0% and 47.4%.

(7) A350 RE-ENGINE, for the record. Does a 2035 launch pass your engineering-capacity and A350F-absorption tests at the 2-year overlap? It fails the cash line in any case. If you hold a soft veto, say so.

frame.initial_lean:
My lean is to hold course on our own clock: NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037, and nothing is added to its last two cash years.

ORDERS:
- ngsa: hold;
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, subject to Wagner;
- rea350: hold;
- delay_tactics: none;
- a320_plan: alt, kept.

WHY, BY MY FOUR QUESTIONS:
(1) The five pillars: nothing is covert, and the public line uses windows, not dates [AX-0073, AX-0081].
(2) The ramp: the Alt plan keeps the transition 'disciplined and controlled' [AX-0010], with each step-down gated on quality KPIs.
(3) The 2030s: NGSA is on its clock for 2037, after the 2035 technology year [AX-0020, A-0409].
(4) The Board: every order is on its approve list, and there is no Board item.

THE GRID.
- The lean reads +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86. It is positive in every column, with the worst at S4 (+3.59).
- It is the best plan that passes in every column.
- It beats the base plan by 1.31-1.45 everywhere.

EXPECTED SCENARIO, revisited.
- Boeing's public line ('not there yet', no date; the 787 and 777X kept 'the way they are now') makes S1 my central case.
- The MAX phase-out from 2044, the 10-year gap to Boeing's next chance and its now-available dual engine sources keep the fps columns live.
- Weights: S1 40%, S2 25%, S3 10%, S4 10%, S5 5%, S6 5%, S7 5%. Expected ΔPV about +8.46.
- The choice does not depend on the column.

WHAT I GIVE UP, ON THE RECORD.
- The A350 Re-engine would add +1.55 in S1, about +1.27 on my weights, and lose 1.21 in S6-S7.
- It fails the company's peak-cash guardrail and Toepfer's line ($6.67B against $5.23B), and the Board vetoes it.
- It is removed on liquidity grounds, not traded as a doctrine premium. Against the best passing option the premium is 0.
- The A350 Re-engine returns in the 2045 round at the earliest, and only if Boeing has launched no 787 Re-engine and that grid passes.
- I do not spend the game's one override on it.

DELAY TACTICS: none. With no fps on the record, every move would be naked, and the team's stricter condition stands.

CANCEL: deleted. It loses 19.81-24.61 in every column, and rule 7 bars it in any case.

FOR THE BOARD:
- In board_response I will take up the outstanding wording point. The round-1 text should have said 'we have been maturing'; this round's statement will report progress against milestones in windows and claim no more maturity than the record supports.
- I will also answer each round-2 recommendation: payout, safety oversight, code 7 and the Alt-plan conditions.

OTHER MOVES I expect to renew (public, unpriced): recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s; supply security for our own lines; zero-for-zero advocacy [AX-0088]. Wagner may add quality-gated transition measures.

No override is planned.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: the lean in 2035-2036 (CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: Peak annual programme cash spend no higher than one year's FCF: EUR 4,753m x 1.10 = $5.228B (about $5.2B). Each bill is spread evenly over its development years (inference).
tests.numbers: NGSA costs $35.52B / 7 = $5.074B in each of 2035 and 2036 (development 2030-2036, entry into service 2037). With rea350 hold and delay_tactics none, nothing else falls in those years, so the peak is $5.074B. Headroom is $0.154B a year against the exact $5.228B line, or $0.126B against the rounded $5.2B. Spend to date (2030-2034) is 5 x $5.074B = $25.37B. What remains in 2035-2036 is $10.15B. From 2037, NGSA cash is nil in this view.

tests.name: Alt-plan cash phasing (round-1 Board condition)
tests.threshold: No more than about $0.13B of Alt-plan cash in any year to 2036, preferably nil; the roughly $0.75B is phased from 2037 as minuted
tests.numbers: The brief confirms that the board books the Alt cost at NGSA's 2037 entry into service. The Alt-plan component, -0.32, equals $0.75B x 1.08^-11 (0.429) = 0.322. The 2037 non-recurring line of $36.3B equals NGSA's $35.52B plus the Alt plan's $0.75B. Spread evenly over 2037-2044, the cost would have a PV of 0.25, not 0.32. Alt cash in 2035-2036 is therefore nil, and the 2035-2036 peak stays at $5.074B. Even if the full $0.75B fell in 2037, NGSA cash that year is nil in the cash view, far inside the line. I report the phasing at each Yearly Budget.

tests.name: NGSA bill against the line: overrun trigger (CEO ask 1, correction to the frame)
tests.threshold: The bill at which NGSA alone fails the peak-cash line. Any overrun goes to the Board before it is committed.
tests.numbers: The bill on the brief is unchanged at $35.52B: programme investment of -15.23 = $35.52B x 1.08^-11. No overrun is reported. tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA + A350 Re-engine launched in 2035 (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: No year with NGSA and A350 Re-engine both in development may exceed $5.228B (about $5.2B)
tests.numbers:
A 2035 launch develops in 2035-2039 and enters service in 2040. NGSA develops to 2036, so the overlap is 2 years. Strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B, or $0.6B a year in 2035-2036. The Re-engine's own cost is $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year. Peak: $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B = $6.674B, which is $1.446B (28%) over $5.228B. The strain alone gives $5.674B, $0.446B over. PHASING:
(a) Deferring the Re-engine's own spend to 2037-2039 still leaves $5.67B.
(b) Even spreading the $1.2B strain over all five A350 development years ($0.24B a year), with the own spend deferred, gives $5.314B, $0.086B over.
(c) No order on this board starts A350 development after 2035 within this round, because entry into service is launch + 5.
No phasing or structure brings it inside the line on the board's terms. The failure sits entirely in 2035-2036: in 2037-2039 the Re-engine alone is $1.0B a year. The earliest clean development start is 2037, which is the 2045 round on this calendar, subject to rule 3 and that round's grid.

tests.name: Net cash, payout, buyback and equity (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Net cash non-negative until NGSA cash ends (end-2036), inside the 30-50% payout policy; no equity raise; no new buyback authority before 2037 (Board guidance; inference)
tests.numbers:
The brief carries no balance sheet and no FCF. Actual end-2034 net cash and the payouts used in 2030-2034 are not on my record.

The round-1 stress case assumes $13.39B of net cash at the start of NGSA cash and flat FCF of $5.228B, with NGSA fully incremental, which leaves $0.154B a year. The payout is measured on 2025 net income of EUR 5,221m, or $5.743B.
- 30%: dividend $1.72B, draw $1.57B a year. Net cash is $5.54B at end-2034, $3.97B at end-2035 and $2.41B at end-2036.
- 48%: dividend $2.76B, draw $2.60B. Net cash is $0.37B at end-2034, reaches zero during 2035, and ends 2036 at -$4.83B.
- 50%: -$0.20B at end-2034 and -$5.63B at end-2036.

PROPOSAL: 30% for 2035 and 2036.
CALIBRATION RULE for the Yearly Budget: a payout p keeps net cash non-negative through 2036 only if audited end-2034 net cash is at least 2 x (p x $5.74B - $0.154B). That is $3.14B at 30%, $4.29B at 40%, $5.21B at 48% and $5.44B at 50%.

No equity raise is needed: gross cash is $29.9B (EUR 27.2bn), and the worst path, 50% throughout, troughs at -$5.6B. No new buyback authority before 2037.

Rating: the record holds no rating trigger [AG-0062], so I cannot put a number on the risk. On the 30% path net cash stays positive, which is the measure the company manages to [A-0401]. I do not convert the board's rising operating profit ($7.0-7.6B in 2033-2036) into FCF.
