cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would change my view if any of the following is shown:
(1) Mr Wagner fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the ramp shield or supply crunch. I would then recommend the base plan, which passes my cash tests at the same $5.074B peak.
(2) A reported NGSA overrun of more than about $0.31B lands in 2035-2036, taking the bill above about $35.83B, or FCF falls below the 2025 base. NGSA alone would then fail the line. It goes to the Board before commitment, and the remedy lies in the budget (payout at the policy floor, a draw on gross cash), never a cancel.
(3) Audited end-2034 net cash is below about $3.14B. Even a 30% payout would then take net cash negative before end-2036 on flat cash, and I would put that choice to the Board. If it is above about $5.4B, the policy room rises to 50%.
(4) A later grid shows an A350 Re-engine developing from 2037 or later, at least $1B ahead in every plausible column, with no 787 Re-engine launched.
(5) Otherwise: a grid gain of at least $1B over the best passing option, or a Board decision.
cfo.memo:
Test memo to the CEO and the Board, round 2 (2035). I concur with the lean: ngsa hold, a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, Delay Tactics none. Engine code: Mr Wagner's call; I expect 7.

Peak cash. NGSA is $35.52B / 7 = $5.074B in 2035 and in 2036, against one year's free cash flow, EUR 4,753m x 1.10 = $5.228B [AX-0104]. Pass, with $0.154B of headroom. The brief books the Alt plan's $0.75B in 2037; nil falls in 2035-2036. Correction: five cash years ($25.37B) are spent, so any overrun lands in the last two. The trigger is a bill above about $35.83B, not $36.4-36.6B.

Robustness. Positive in every column, worst S4 at +3.59. The Alt item is +1.31 to +1.45.

Balance sheet. The brief carries no balance sheet. On my flat-cash stress case, end-2034 net cash is $5.5B at a 30% payout, $0.4B at 48%. I propose 30% for 2035 and 2036, leaving about $2.4B at end-2036. No equity raise; no new buyback authority before 2037.

A350 Re-engine in 2035: soft veto, binding. $5.07B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.67B, $1.45B over. No phasing cures it: strain alone gives $5.67B, spread over five years $5.31B. Forgone: +1.55 in S1, +1.27 weighted, -1.21 in S6-S7. Earliest clean start: 2037, the 2045 round.

Delay Tactics and an NGSA cancel are red lines: the naked fine is 3.6 times net cash; a cancel writes off $25.37B.

A prudent risk approach [AX-0022]: one programme, inside cash flow.

tests.name: Safety, quality and the five pillars: the lean's orders and the public line
tests.threshold: No order, and no public explanation, that contradicts safety and quality. A slip of entry into service for safety or quality reasons is acceptable; a rushed rate step is not.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no safety, quality or supply event on the A320, the A350 or NGSA. Every order in the lean is a default, and none is covert.

Public line:
- The round-1 text kept 'matured over the past decade'. This round's statement should say 'a technology and production system we have been maturing'. My readiness pass is an inference: the brief gives no wing or production-system status.
- Keep 'the second half of the 2030s'. No 2037 date and no 'on track for 2037'.
- Do not promise three engines at entry into service. Say 'we certify them in sequence as each one matures'.
- Name no engine supplier as the cause of the 2025 reset.
- No word of Delay Tactics.

tests.name: Production readiness and rule 1: NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037
tests.threshold: NGSA enters service only once the wing is buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft. No entry into service before the 2035 technology year (rule 1). Only a reported technology or engine-maturity slip re-times NGSA, and only later.
tests.numbers:
- The bulletin shows NGSA in development, entering service in 2037. No slip is reported.
- 2037 is after the 2035 technology year, so rule 1 passes.
- The brief gives no status for the wing at rate or the production system, so this pass is an inference [A-0441, A-0225].

Slip prior, unchanged from round 1: 1-2 years at risk.
- The risk case is one year, to 2038. That is still inside 'the second half of the 2030s'.
- A two-year slip, to 2039, would also stay inside the window, but it would stack on the 2039-2040 transition.

Containment:
- Engines certified in sequence: CFM first (always available), then GTF2 (ready 2036), then UltraFan NB (ready 2037). This follows the A320neo precedent, with P&W certified in November 2015 and CFM in May 2016.
- An engine that is late joins later and never holds the entry-into-service date.
- The Alt plan's A320 lines cushion a slow NGSA ramp.
- Every NGSA rate step is gated on quality KPIs.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a slip, re-time NGSA so that entry into service stays at or after the new technology-ready year. Never cancel.
tests.numbers:
No inject this round. Readiness of each maker by NGSA's 2037 entry into service:
- CFM: always available.
- P&W GTF2: ready 2036, one year of margin.
- RR UltraFan NB: ready 2037, no margin.
- The P&W-RR Joint Venture: not formed.

Rule 8 cannot bind. A maker that is not ready is dropped from the fit; it does not delay NGSA.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (my recommendation, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: Keep CFM in the set plus at least one second maker: code 5, 6 or 7, and 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready. Narrow only if three-engine integration threatens the 2037 entry into service or quality.
tests.numbers:
Code 7 keeps CFM, P&W GTF2 and RR UltraFan NB. That is 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the code has no payoff effect.

The narrower codes:
- Code 6 (CFM and P&W): 2 sources. Rolls-Royce has no other narrowbody on the record, so the three-maker enabler is at risk.
- Code 5 (CFM and RR): 2 sources. It drops the maker that has margin (GTF2) and keeps the one that has none.

Integration:
- Three powerplant integrations mean more certification work than two. Sequencing contains it.
- Nothing in the brief shows that load threatening 2037 or quality, so there is no ground to narrow.

If P&W and Rolls-Royce form the Joint Venture this round (my reading of rules.md, an inference):
- GTF2 and UltraFan NB fold into it.
- The Joint Venture engine is ready 6 years after formation (2041), or earlier if a folded solo programme is further along. GTF2 would be ready in 2036.
- If it takes GTF2's 2036 date, code 7 fits CFM plus the Joint Venture engine. That is 2 sources, the Joint Venture engine counting as one, and P&W and Rolls-Royce hold equal shares.
- If it is not credited and is ready only in 2041, both makers drop at our 2037 entry into service, and NGSA flies on CFM alone.
- Codes 5, 6 and 7 behave the same in either case, so no code change fixes this. Code 7 covers every case. Code 4 drops CFM and is never acceptable.

ops.memo:
Round 2 (2035). My tests are role-derived; none of my record is in my own words (Very low confidence).

I concur: ngsa hold, code 7, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt.

Safety and quality: the brief reports no event on the A320, the A350 or NGSA. Nothing in the lean is covert.

NGSA readiness: the brief gives no wing or production-system status, so my pass is inference. Entry into service 2037, after the 2035 technology year. Slip prior unchanged: one year, to 2038, is the risk case, inside 'the second half of the 2030s'. CFM is always fitted; GTF2 is ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. Certified in sequence, no engine holds our date.

Code 7, kept: three sources, three makers. Nothing shows three-engine integration threatening 2037 or quality. A P&W and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture still fits under 7: CFM plus one Joint Venture source.

Alt plan: passes safety, quality, ramp shield and supply crunch. The A320 never exceeds 82 a month after entry into service. Nothing I hold requires base.

A350 Re-engine in 2035: passes my tests at the limit (2 years, $1.2B strain); no veto from me. No slip margin, though: NGSA in 2038 makes it three years and $1.8B. I prefer the 2045 round.

Delay Tactics and cancel: red lines, binding.

2039-2040: we build about 69 and 71 a month against 85 today. That is the plan, not a slip. Do not rush NGSA; pace each A320 step-down to NGSA's proven rate.

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. They frame every step our next-generation single-aisle aircraft takes towards entry into service.

The programme remains in development, and we continue to plan its entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Its timing follows a technology and production system we have been maturing, and we keep it on our own clock. We will report progress against milestones, in windows, and we will not trade safety or quality for speed.

We are preparing the Airbus of the 2030s while we keep delivering for our customers today. The A320 family stays at its present rate until the new aircraft enters service, and our production plan keeps A320 lines running longer through the new aircraft's ramp-up. The transition will be disciplined and controlled, rate by rate, with quality first: each step is taken only when the quality indicators for it are met. We will certify the aircraft's engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce in sequence, as each one matures.

The programme remains funded within our cash flow and preserves our financial flexibility and balance-sheet discipline; the case assumes no state support. We continue to secure our own supply base, from work packages to materials, and to invest in the people who will design and build this aircraft. We will keep working with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE (round 2, 2035)

I hold course. The orders are ngsa hold (NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037), engine code 7 kept, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none and a320_plan alt kept. Toepfer and Wagner recommend exactly these orders, and they are the Board's would-approve list. Every order is the default or the plan the Board approved in round 1, so there is no Board item this round. No override is used, and the game's one override stays in reserve.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted. Rule 4 bars it: no fps is on the record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, 3.6 times net cash. Against the lean, one move is -15.68 / +0.83 / +0.48 / +0.39 / +0.83 / -15.69 / +0.83, and both moves -16.13 / +0.45 / +0.10 / -0.04 / +0.45 / -16.14 / +0.45. It falls short of $1B even in the fps columns. Its cash would also take 2035-2036 to $5.241B, over the line. Bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands, and I do not set it aside. This also deletes the A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics rows, the raw best in S2-S5.
- Every cancel row is deleted. Rule 7 bars it, and the grid agrees: against continuing it is -24.60 / -21.72 / -21.81 / -19.81 / -21.72 / -24.61 / -21.72, after a $25.37B write-off. Continuing never loses.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS OF BOTH TESTS
- The lean (NGSA hold, Alt, A350 hold) passes every test in both memos.
- The base-plan switch passes both memos, but Wagner gives it no safety ground and the Board vetoes it. It trails the lean by 1.31-1.45 in every column.
- NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (Alt) fails Toepfer's soft veto, which is binding. Peak cash is $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.674B in 2035-2036, $1.446B over $5.228B. The strain alone gives $5.674B, and no phasing on the board's terms cures it. It also fails his robustness test (item -1.21 in S6-S7). Wagner passes it at his capacity limit and holds no veto.

STEP 3: CHOOSE
- The lean is the highest-grid survivor in every column: +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86, or 8.46 on my weights. It is positive everywhere, with the worst plausible column S4 (fps 7-yr, entry into service 2042, a five-year NGSA lead) at +3.59.
- No survivor is within $1B (the base plan trails by more than $1.3B), so the tie-breaks are not engaged.

THE OVERRIDE I DO NOT TAKE
On the grid, the A350 Re-engine is +1.55 over the lean in S1 and +1.27 on my weights, so the team rule's $1B test would technically allow an override of Toepfer. I decline it for four reasons:
(a) The Board vetoes rea350 launch on balance-sheet grounds. Its override review fails on a Qualified Majority item that trails the best passing option by 1.21 in S6-S7. I have no override against the Board, so the order would revert to hold and burn the game's one override.
(b) It breaks the company's own guardrail, peak programme spend within one year's FCF (profile §9 step 7). My balance-sheet appetite is Low [AX-0022, AX-0102].
(c) Wagner's flag: it has no slip margin. His risk case, NGSA entering service in 2038, would make the overlap 3 years and the strain $1.8B, past rule 6's limit, and the grid could not show $1B in S6-S7.
(d) The item loses 1.21 in the 787 Re-engine columns.
For honesty on robustness: at plan level the A350 row's worst column is +4.65 (S7), above the lean's +3.59. Its weakness lies in the item and the cash, not the plan row.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Five pillars: nothing is covert. The public line gives windows, not a date. The wording now claims only 'a technology and production system we have been maturing', with no state money and no word of Delay Tactics [AX-0073, AX-0081].
(2) The ramp: the Alt plan is kept. The A320 stays at 85 a month to entry into service and never exceeds 82 after it. Each step-down is gated on quality KPIs, and Wagner's pacing measure is adopted, so the 2039-2040 gap is never closed by rushing NGSA [AX-0010, AX-0056].
(3) The 2030s: NGSA enters service in 2037, after the 2035 technology year (rule 1) [AX-0020, A-0409]. A one-year slip to 2038 stays inside 'the second half of the 2030s'.
(4) The Board: every order is on its approve list, and there is no item it would veto.

OWN CLOCK
Boeing made no move in round 1, and its line ('not there yet', no date) moves nothing. Its MAX phase-out from 2044 and its dual-source condition, now meetable, keep an fps this round plausible. Neither moves or cancels NGSA (rules 2 and 7). In S4, the worst case, NGSA still leads by five years.

ENGINE CODE
Code 7, final, on Wagner's recommendation. It gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050 at no payoff cost. Code 6 would put the three-maker enabler at risk. Code 5 would drop the maker that has margin. If a P&W and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture forms, codes 5, 6 and 7 behave alike, and 7 covers every case. Certification runs in sequence, and CFM is never dropped.

BOARD-GATE LINE (package; no item this round)
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass on peak cash ($5.074B against $5.228B), Alt phasing (nil in 2035-2036) and robustness. Net cash stays positive on the recommended 30% payout.
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, production readiness (an inference, since the brief gives no wing status), the ramp shield, supply crunch and engine code.
- Grid: +11.62 / +6.35 / +6.96 / +3.59 / +6.35 / +11.14 / +5.86. Base row beside it: +10.19 / +4.95 / +5.65 / +2.14 / +4.95 / +9.70 / +4.47.

CORRECTION ACCEPTED
Toepfer's trigger is the right one. Five cash years are spent, so the overrun line is a bill of about $35.83B, not the $36.4-36.6B in my frame.

Briefing goal: 'Defend the 60/40 edge; protect the A320 family', with a stable engine supply as the enabler. The GM scores it; it never changes the payoff, and no PV is traded for it.

- 60/40 edge: not met. The worst year is 2040 at 47.4%; 2045 reads 69.0% and 2050 74.0%. The shortfall is the planned 2039-2040 transition gap (capacity of 734+93 and 556+296 against demand of 1,931 and 1,972), not a slip.
- A320 family before entry into service: met (60.0%).
- Engine-supply enabler: met. There are 3 sources (CFM + P&W GTF2 + RR UltraFan NB) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050.

Wagner's quality-gated pacing measure may soften the 2039-2040 gap, but I claim no figure and trade no quality for the objective. No rate step goes ahead of its quality KPIs, and NGSA is not rushed.

Risk to the enabler: if P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture this round and it is not credited GTF2's 2036 date, NGSA could fly on CFM alone at entry into service. No code change fixes that, and code 7 covers every case. The base-plan switch would cost 1.31-1.45 in every column and gains nothing on the goal.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: Airbus has launched its new single-aisle airplane and asked CFM to be on it. We don't have a birthright on that order. We'll earn it on the product and on durability. So CFM, with our partner Safran, is launching a new ducted engine for the airplanes that chose CFM, and we'll offer it to both airframers. It builds on the LEAP our customers fly today and carries what we've learned in RISE. I'll be plain about what it is and what it isn't. It's the right engine for these airplanes. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan.

We're also going to work with Embraer to bring a CFM engine to its airplanes. That adds to what we do for our two big customers, and it doesn't take anything away from them.

What we don't know yet is the date. You'll get one when our testing backs it, and not before. Durability comes ahead of the date: if the testing needs more time, it gets it. And job one hasn't moved. We keep LEAP and GEnx engines on wing longer for the customers flying them today.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. It's the same game as 2030: the installed base on the new narrowbodies, not share for its own sake [CX-0467, CX-0422, CX-0493]. The market moved. NGSA launched for a 2037 entry with code 7, and Airbus selected CFM. Two rival new engines are launched and selected on it, ready in 2036 and 2037. At hold we fly a LEAP derivative, and our NB share falls to 43.7% in 2045 and 39.1% in 2050. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. We win by keeping the place Airbus gave us with an engine that competes.

DECISION:
- ducted: launch, with partner_embraer: launch, as one defence. They stand or fall together, and neither can be cancelled after this round.
- open_fan: hold. lobby_emissions: hold. genx: hold (the upgrade is live).
- RISE stays all in as funded technology with Safran: no launch, no cancel for cost.
- Premium $0.0B. RISE allowance unused.

THE TESTS:
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Against hold, Ducted + Embraer (B) is +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50 (S1 / S2 / S3; rows -21.58 / -39.97 / -25.88 against -23.12 / -33.97 / -28.38).
- It is the best grid plan in S1 and S3, and $0.54B over epsilon in the expected column S1.
- S1 cost: none. It gains where rivals hold.
- Worst column S2: -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B R&D + $2B strain). The downside is bounded.
- The Ducted alone is -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41. It fails, and I'm not bringing it.
- Embraer next to the Ducted: +1.85 / 0.00 / +2.09, with no R&D and no added strain.
(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, because that is the public record: code 7 with CFM selected, the Alt plan, and Boeing 'not there yet'. I asked Rahul to push on S2 and he did, so I carry his 0.20 rather than my 0.15. Weights are S1 0.60 / S2 0.20 / S3 0.20. B against hold on them is +0.22, and the S2 breakeven at this mix is 22.9% (20.4% to 29.4% across mixes; the Board has 24-25%).
(3) Hard rule 3 [CX-0564, CX-0183]. The trigger I said would flip me is now on the public record, not just the grid: GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and selected on NGSA. I judged the Ducted on its row against hold. It's ready in 2041, four years after NGSA's entry, and still earns +10 pp from its ready year. This is the last window that counts, since a 2045 launch is ready in 2051.
(4) H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]. NGSA enters in 2037. A 2035 Open Fan is ready in 2045, eight years later in every column. The Open Fan alone is -20.85 / -10.00 / -22.16 against hold. The best Open Fan row is $20.28B or more behind B in S1, above even the $15B allowance. Held.
(5) 20% red line, restated [CX-0217]. It governs the next-generation product, RISE. A ducted engine has less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], so the Ducted can't be, and is never called, the next generation. It's an H3 defence. I rebut the line for it; I don't strike it. RISE keeps the 20% bar.
(6) Durability is not traded for fuel burn or for the date [CX-0208]. Ali raises no safety or durability flag: the gate is open, not failed. There are no turn-on/turn-off results on a ducted engine in our record, and I won't dress analysis up as test. What stands on test:
- the LEAP-1A hot-section kit, certified December 2024;
- more than 350 RISE tests, with dust testing on the compact-core HPT.
Our cross-functional answer is the named gate (other moves). Gate point (a) is met at launch, and (b) must pass on core or engine test before 2041 is used anywhere. If the gate fails, the date moves, not the durability [CX-0012].
(7) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. This is doctrine, not my record: the $2B strain is in the grid and paid for in S1 and S3. LEAP OE load falls 14% by 2041 and 44% by 2045 as a Ducted would ramp. Fleet kits, spares and OE keep priority over development parts. Capacity stays joint with Safran.
(8) Tie-break [CX-0658]. In the expected column B leads by more than epsilon. On weights it's a near tie: +0.22, about -0.10 with a one-year slip, and -0.52 with two. So I ran it:
- Safety: with the gate binding the date, there's no reason to prefer hold.
- Quality: the gate sets the bar at our best fleet standard.
- Delivery: we bring a competitive engine to the airframer that chose us, while LEAP OE, spares and kits keep first call.
- Cost: $1.0B a year, inside the payout floor.
None of the four reverses the value call.
(9) Three gates [CX-0433]:
- Foundation: fleet upgrades, the A-range rating and at least 70% returned.
- Partner: Safran, and Embraer non-exclusive.
- Market: an airframer has selected CFM on the record.
All three hold.

EXCO. Every Ghai test I rely on passes:
- pays-for-itself, B +1.54;
- volumes-first: code 7 is on the record, and Embraer rides NGSA;
- capex: $1.0B a year against about $2.55B of room;
- premium: $0.0B;
- terms: no price talk.
His binding vetoes cover only plans I am not bringing. Ali's date tests pass (2041, 2042, 2045 floor), and he raises no binding veto and no flag. No overrides.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity):
- Ducted: consent assumed. It's an H3 defence of the NGSA slot Airbus gave CFM, with rival engines launched and selected on the record. Half of that annuity is Safran's, and meeting an airframer's launch with an engine is CFM joint practice. Price and capacity stay joint.
- Embraer: consent assumed. It's a CFM engine for a third airframer, non-exclusive, on terms worked jointly.
- Open Fan and Lobby: held. A RISE product with no airframer path is outside joint practice.
- GEnx: GE alone.

AIRFRAMER FINDINGS. The brief carries no findings from the private talks, and I won't invent any. First-hand on the record: Airbus selected CFM in 2030 with no new CFM engine launched, so that code did not depend on a launch. Whether code 7 holds to 2037 is the S2 question, and I carry it at 0.20.

BIASES, NAMED:
- The installed-base lens likes this move [CX-0555]. I book none of the upside it suggests: no lower S2 odds for having launched, nothing past the board's 2056 window, no later fps win.
- Deference to airframers made us wait in 2030. Rahul scores that wait at about $0.4B.
- Ramp optimism: I haircut my own date, not the board's ramp. A one-year slip leaves S1 at +1.14 to +1.27; two years leave +0.61 to +0.89.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove Embraer and the supply read.

WHAT FLIPS ME IN 2045: a gate failure I can't answer on test, or evidence that S2 sat above the breakeven. "We don't want to be rash, but we need to get after this straight away" [CX-0237].

priorities: Safety and readiness first. If you bring us a Ducted, it will be ready in 2041 (2035 + 6). It must come with Ali's turn-on/turn-off results from the hot-and-harsh and dust test plan commissioned in 2030, a named cross-functional durability gate, and no safety or durability flag left standing. A Ducted only as a paid defence, and on this grid only paired with Partner Embraer. The hard-rule-3 trigger is now on the record: GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) are launched, and both are selected on NGSA (EIS 2037). Against hold, the Ducted alone is -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41 (S1 / S2 / S3) and clears the $1B epsilon in no column. Ducted plus Embraer is +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50, the grid's best plan in S1 and S3. No Open Fan product and no Lobby. 2035 is the last round in which an Open Fan could be ready by 2050, but NGSA enters service in 2037, before 2045. Keep the balance sheet and the payout whole. A Ducted plus strain is $6B over six years, or $1.0B a year, inside the roughly $2.5B left after returning at least 70% of free cash flow. The premium is $0.0B in S1 and S3. The game total is $0.0B of $4.0B, and no RISE allowance is used [CG-0022, CG-0063, CX-0645, CG-0064].

Price what cannot be undone. The next round is 2045, after the Ducted is ready (2041) and after Embraer counts (2042), so this $6B cannot be cancelled for a write-off. recommendations.text: Safety first. Bring us the Ducted durability evidence before any Ducted: turn-on/turn-off results in hot-and-harsh and dust conditions, signed off by a cross-functional team, with the gate named. Keep 2041 internal and publish it only once a test backs it. Do not trade durability for fuel burn or for the date.

If you bring a Ducted, bring it with Partner Embraer, as one defence. On our arithmetic the Ducted alone (-0.31 in S1) does not pay its $6B bill, and the pair (+1.54 in S1, +2.50 in S3) is the grid's best plan. The margin over epsilon in S1 is $0.54B, so show us the weights and the S2 breakeven (about 24-25%). Remember that after this round neither the Ducted nor Embraer can be cancelled.

Frame any Ducted publicly as CFM's engine for the airframes that chose CFM, offered to both airframers. It is a defence and is never the next generation; RISE keeps the 20% bar. Keep the Embraer partnership non-exclusive: no airframer is refused or locked out, Boeing's fps options included. Give the Safran reason for each CFM order in rationale.

RISE: keep it all in as a funded technology programme with Safran, with no product launch and no cancel for cost. Tell us and the record plainly that 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' cannot now be met. NGSA's 2037 entry puts any 2035 launch into the wait, and the one RISE allowance stays unused.

Report what the private airframer engagement found, which we asked for in round 1. Does either airframer's code depend on CFM having a new engine launched? Is Airbus's code-7 selection firm through NGSA's 2037 entry? That decides how much weight S2 deserves.

Cost and balance sheet. State premium_b in dollars against the best grid plan in the expected column ($0.0B for Ducted plus Embraer in S1 or S3), with the game total ($0.0B of $4.0B to date). Keep at least 70% of free cash flow returned and the A-range rating untouched; $1.0B a year of new R&D and strain fits. The grid does not price rival moves after this round, such as a P&W-RR Joint Venture (CFM -10 pp), so book expected_pv_b low.

Public statement: name no rival and blame no one. Give no Open Fan entry before 2045 and no Ducted ready date as a commitment. Never call the Ducted the next generation. No CFM price or capacity talk without Safran.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? It's the same game as 2030: the installed base on the new narrowbodies, not share for its own sake. What changed is that the market has moved. NGSA is launched for a 2037 entry, and Airbus has selected all three makers (code 7). Two new rival engines are launched and will be ready by that entry (2036 and 2037). At hold we fly a LEAP derivative on NGSA, and our NB share falls to 43.7% in 2045 and 39.1% in 2050. The fps has not launched. We have no birthright on that next order [CX-0564].

The question this round: do we put $6B behind a defensive Ducted, paired with Partner Embraer, to hold the NGSA place Airbus gave us? That is $4B of R&D plus the $2B strain, because the live GEnx upgrade counts as a project. This is the last round in which a Ducted can matter. A 2045 launch would be ready in 2051. And neither the Ducted nor Embraer can be cancelled after this round. On the grid, the pair earns $1.54B in S1 and $2.50B in S3, and loses its whole $6B bill in S2, the column where Airbus changes its code this round.

Second question, and I'll be candid about it: the 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' objective cannot be met. 2035 was the last window, and NGSA enters service in 2037, eight years before any Open Fan could be ready. RISE stays all in as technology. We get paid in dollars, not percentages [CX-0630]. Tell me what we know and what we don't [CX-0436].
frame.situation:
ROUND: decision year 2035, round 2 of 4 (2030, 2035, 2045, 2050). The next round is 2045, ten years out.

PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 2):
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, entry 2037, Alt plan (A320 lines kept longer through the ramp). Engine selection: code 7, RR + PW + CFM. Airbus can change the code until 2037, so in practice only in this round.
- Rival NB engines: the code-2 maker's GTF2 (Solo) launched 2030, ready 2036; the code-1 maker's UltraFan NB (Solo) launched 2030, ready 2037. Both are ready by NGSA's entry, so both will be fitted.
- Joint Venture: one maker says the door is open; the other has launched solo. Neither has committed. Not priced on our grid.
- Boeing: no fps launched and no date. It requires dual-source engines on its next narrowbody. It says it is 'not there yet', and its code stays null.
- Ours: GEnx upgrade launched 2030, ready since 2033, counting from 2042. WB share rises from 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042.

HARD RULE 3 TRIGGER: met on the public record, not only on the grid. Two rival new NB engines are launched and selected on NGSA. This is the trigger I said would flip me.

OUR POSITION AT HOLD (S1):
- dPV -23.12 against the status quo; yield 85.55%.
- NB share: 69.8% (2040), 43.7% (2045), 39.1% (2050). NB engines fall from 2,553 (2034) to 1,438 (2045) and 1,313 (2050).
- Engine value runs about $8-9B a year under the status quo from the mid-2040s.

OBJECTIVES:
- Dominate NB (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050): not met at hold (worst 39.1% in 2050).
- Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: not met, and out of reach after this round. A 2035 launch is ready in 2045, NGSA enters in 2037, and the wait penalty bites in S1 and S3.

GRID (dPV $B; S1 rivals hold / S2 Airbus switches NGSA to code 2, PW only / S3 Boeing launches fps 10-yr, code 7, entry 2045):
- Hold: -23.12 / -33.97 / -28.38.
- Ducted + Embraer: -21.58 / -39.97 / -25.88, i.e. +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50 against hold. Best plan in S1 and S3.
- Ducted alone: -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41 against hold.
- Embraer next to the Ducted: +1.85 / 0.00 / +2.09.
- Open Fan alone: -20.85 / -10.00 / -22.16 against hold.
- Best row with an Open Fan (Ducted + Open Fan + Embraer + Lobby): -20.28 / -9.00 / -21.64 against Ducted + Embraer.
- Best plan in S2: hold.
- S2 is the column where a rival takes our NGSA slot. No lever of ours buys it back: there the Ducted is pure bill.

CALENDAR:
- Ducted ready 2041, four years after NGSA's entry. Under the rules it still earns +10 pp from its ready year, since a new NB is in service. It is four years ahead of an S3 fps (2045).
- Embraer counts from 2042.
- Open Fan not before 2045.

PRIVATE AIRFRAMER ENGAGEMENT (the Board's round-1 ask): the brief carries no findings from our private talks, and I won't invent any. What the record shows first-hand: Airbus put CFM on NGSA in 2030 with no new CFM engine launched, on our public offer of 'LEAP-based or new, on a date our testing backs'. So the 2030 code did not depend on a launch. What I don't know: whether code 7 holds to 2037 now that both rivals have new engines and we have a LEAP derivative. That is the S2 question. Boeing has said only that it wants more than one source.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision):
- Would approve:
  - Ducted + Partner Embraer launched together, with S1 or S3 expected. Conditions: Ali's durability gate named and resolved cross-functionally on test evidence, my 20% rebuttal restated, and no binding Ghai or Ali veto standing.
  - Hold on every field (never vetoed), though it would ask why we give up $1.54B (S1) and $2.50B (S3).
- Would veto:
  - the Ducted alone;
  - Ducted + Embraer with S2 expected (-6.00, a $6.00B premium over the $2.0B cap);
  - Embraer with no CFM engine, or next to an Open Fan only (the two stand or fall together);
  - any Open Fan, in any combination;
  - Lobby;
  - any premium over $2.0B, and any RISE allowance this round;

  - Ghai's tests in numbers, and his confirmation that the live GEnx counts toward strain;
  - Ali's test results, a named gate, and any flag with my answer to it;
  - the Safran reason for each CFM order;
  - candour on both objectives;
  - a statement that the pair stands or falls together and cannot be cancelled after this round;
  - the airframer findings.

- That B is irreversible after this round.

(9) Objective. On the brief and the rules, estimate what B does to CFM's NB share in 2045 and 2050 against 43.7% and 39.1% at hold. Label it an estimate: the brief gives no year path for B. No objective premium is on the table.

(10) Booking. Guide low. B's weighted row is -25.20 on my weights and -26.33 on the low-case set, against hold at -25.80 / -26.61. I'd book about -26.5 until the NGSA code is locked. Tell me where you'd put it.

(11) Terms. Any public line carries no price, no capacity figure and no number before the airframer's volumes are agreed. Narrowbody price and capacity are joint with Safran.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding): it would approve B only with S1 or S3 expected and the premium at $0. It would veto C alone, B with S2 expected, Embraer without a CFM engine, any Open Fan, Lobby, any premium over $2.0B, any RISE allowance, and any launch with one of your binding vetoes still standing. It wants your three tests in numbers and the GEnx strain confirmation.
frame.asks_ops:
Mohamed, I need what the tests say, not the analysis. Turn it on, turn it off.

(1) Ducted durability. We commissioned the hot-and-harsh and dust turn-on/turn-off test plan in 2030. What results stand today, on test and not on analysis? Name the cross-functional durability gate, with who sits on it and what it must turn off before any ready date is used anywhere. Tell me whether you raise a safety or durability flag on a 2035 Ducted. If you do, bring it as a cross-functional call, since no single person makes a safety call [CX-0012], and tell me what evidence would clear it. If the evidence isn't there, I'd rather hear it now than in 2041.

(2) Ready years against the first new NB, in years of gap:
- Ducted: 2041 (2035 + 6) against NGSA 2037 (four years late, still earning +10 pp from its ready year) and an S3 fps 10-yr 2045 (four years early).
- Embraer: counting from 2042 (2035 + 7).
- Open Fan: not before 2045 against NGSA 2037.
Confirm the Open Fan is not ready no later than NGSA's entry in any column. What would slip the Ducted, and by how much? GE's demo dates have moved before.

(3) RISE. Where do the ground and flight tests stand, for the record and for the technology programme? I'm not asking for a product date. I'll say plainly that 'ready by 2050' is out of reach.

(4) Physics and my lines. Confirm that a ducted engine has less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain [CX-0183, CX-0180]. Then the Ducted is a defence, never the next generation, and RISE keeps the 20% bar. Confirm the Ducted does not trade durability for fuel burn or for the date [CX-0208].

(5) Supply load. Can the supply base carry a Ducted next to the live GEnx, LEAP OE, spares and the LEAP fleet durability upgrades, with spares never crowding out OE [CX-0529]? On the brief, our NB engine volume falls from 2,553 (2034) to about 2,190 (2041) and 1,438 (2045), so the LEAP load eases as a Ducted would ramp; check that against doctrine and the constrained suppliers. The board's strain is $2B either way. Capacity decisions stay joint with Safran.

(6) Dates in the public line. 2041 never goes out as a commitment. The Open Fan is 'not before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer'. Flag any date in my statement that a test doesn't back.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding): the Board vetoes any launch carrying an unresolved date, safety or durability flag from you. It wants your test results, the named gate, any flag and my answer to it on evidence, and your ready years set against NGSA 2037 and an fps 2045.
frame.initial_lean:
LEAN:
- ducted: launch and partner_embraer: launch, as one defence. They stand or fall together.
- open_fan: hold. lobby_emissions: hold. genx: hold (the upgrade stays live).
- RISE stays all in as a funded technology programme with Safran: no product launch and no cancel for cost.
- The RISE allowance is unused, and the premium is $0.0B.

EXPECTED COLUMN (provisional): S1, rivals hold. It is the public record: NGSA selected CFM next to two rival engines, and Boeing says it is not there yet. Weights: S1 0.65 / S2 0.15 / S3 0.20.

WHY:
- The trigger is on the record, not hoped for. Two new rival engines are launched and selected, and at hold our NB share falls to 39.1% by 2050.
- B is the best grid plan in S1 (+1.54) and S3 (+2.50).
- Its worst case, S2, is bounded at its $6B bill.
- $1.0B a year fits inside the payout floor.
- The three gates hold:
  - Foundation: the LEAP fleet upgrades and the balance sheet.
  - Partner: Safran, and Embraer non-exclusive.
  - Market: an airframer has selected CFM [CX-0433].
- A 2045 Ducted would be ready in 2051. Waiting is no longer a cheaper option; it's a decision not to defend.

WHAT KEEPS ME HONEST:
- The S1 margin over epsilon is $0.54B, and on weights B is within epsilon of hold (+0.60). Equal weights make it -0.65.
- The case rests on S2 being under about 20-25%, and it cannot be undone after this round.
- My installed-base lens likes this move [CX-0555], so I want Ghai to push on S2 rather than agree with me.

WHAT FLIPS ME TO HOLD:
- Ali raises a safety or durability flag I can't answer on test evidence with a cross-functional team.
- Ghai shows an honest S2 above the breakeven, or a binding test fails that I can't answer with evidence.
- A reason Safran would not agree.
- Within epsilon, safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order, decides. I won't trade durability for a date.

SAFRAN GATE:
- Ducted: consent assumed. It is a hard-rule-3 defence of the NGSA slot Airbus gave CFM, with rival engines launched and selected on the record. That slot is half Safran's annuity too, and meeting an airframer's launch with an engine is CFM's joint practice. Capacity stays a joint decision.
- Embraer: consent assumed once a CFM engine is launched. It is a CFM engine for a third airframer, non-exclusive.
- Open Fan: a RISE product launch with no airframer path is outside joint practice; held.
- Lobby: serves RISE; held.
- GEnx: GE alone.

OBJECTIVES, CANDIDLY:
- 'Open Fan ready by 2050' cannot be met.
- 'NB share of at least 50%' is not met at hold. B lifts 2045 and 2050, but I won't claim it clears 50% until Ghai estimates it.
- No objective premium.

BOOKING: low, about -26.5, until the NGSA code is locked.

PUBLIC LINE:
- Safety first.
- CFM brings a new engine to the airplanes that chose CFM, offered to both airframers, as a defence and not the next generation.
- No ready date as a commitment, no rival named, no price or capacity talk without Safran.
- RISE all in as technology, 'not before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer'.
- 'It's that simple, ain't that hard.'

cfo.memo:
Larry, the short answer: B pays for itself on the record, but only just on weights.

Your arithmetic checks. B is +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50 against hold; the Ducted alone is -0.31 and fails. The live GEnx counts as a project: the Ducted alone is -6.00 in S2, the Open Fan -10.00. Embraer adds no strain. $1.0B a year fits inside about $2.5B of room after the 70% payout. Premium $0.0B. No Open Fan fits the $15B allowance: the best is $20.28B behind B in S1.

Volumes: code 7 and Airbus's production plan are on the record, so the Ducted passes. Embraer's launch is not a volume agreement. Its +1.85 rides on NGSA, where we're already selected, so it passes on the board, but no Embraer number goes out until we've worked the volumes with them.

You asked me to push on S2. I carry 0.20, not 0.15: that column stands for any single-source call, code 1 included, and we're the only maker on NGSA without a new engine. That's under the 23% breakeven, so it doesn't flip me, but B is only +0.22 on my weights. A one-year Ducted slip takes it to about zero; two years, below. We've been proven wrong on dates before.

But the good news is the downside stops at the $6B bill, and B lifts 2045 share to about 53%. 2050 is about 49%: at the line, not cleared.

Book -26.5 and raise once the code locks. No price talk without Safran.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: Ducted ready year (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than launch + 6, the board's development time. If an order's value depends on an earlier year, it fails. This is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Launched 2035, ready 2041 (2035 + 6). The grid rows rest on 2041 and on nothing earlier: Ducted -23.43 / -39.97 / -27.97, and Ducted + Embraer -21.58 / -39.97 / -25.88. Against hold: the pair is +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50 and the Ducted alone -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41. Only the board's development time backs 2041. The brief has no turn-on/turn-off result on a ducted engine. What could slip it, on my record: the near-term fixes that had test behind them landed on time (fuel nozzle in production 2024; LEAP-1A HPT hardware certified December 2024). The longer dates moved. The LEAP-1B kit was promised for 2025 and is now 1H 2026, about a year late. The RISE fly demo went from 'by the middle of this decade' to 'this decade'. If the gate turns on a failure the design does not turn off, there is a redesign-and-retest loop. My estimate for that is 1 to 2 years (2042-2043). It is an inference from the LEAP-1B precedent, not a test number. A 2045 launch would be ready in 2051.

tests.numbers: Embraer launched 2035 counts from 2042 (2035 + 7). Its engine, the Ducted, is ready in 2041, one year earlier. Next to the Ducted, Embraer is worth +1.85 / 0.00 / +2.09 on the grid, and that rests on 2042. GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033, counting from 2042 because no Re-engine is on the record. WB share goes from 42.0% to 44.8% and WB engines from 143 to 152 a year. The order is hold only. Slip interaction (advice): a two-year Ducted slip to 2043 would leave Embraer's 2042 count resting on an engine that is not yet ready. The board books 2042 regardless. Ghai should price that.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: Open Fan ready year, and RISE test status (Culp asks 2 and 3)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 10 and not before 2045. Any earlier year is my binding date ground (inference).
tests.numbers: A 2035 launch is ready in max(2035 + 10, 2045) = 2045. The grid's Open Fan rows are computed at 2045. The lean holds the Open Fan. The next round is 2045, and a launch then is ready in 2055, so 'ready by 2050' cannot be reached after this round. Where RISE testing stands: the brief carries no RISE ground or flight test results. My record stops at: over 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability; dust testing on the compact-core HPT blades, started October 2025, the earliest GE has ever started it; open-fan noise below today's LEAP, shown with Airbus; and ground and flight tests targeted for 'this decade', after the fly demo moved from mid-decade. What happened after October 2025 is not in my evidence. No product date follows from that. 2045 is a floor, not a promise.

tests.name: Test, not analysis: dates in Culp's frame and draft public line (Culp ask 6)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan entry before 2045, and no ready date before launch plus development years (binding ground 2, inference).
tests.numbers: Every date in the frame sits at launch plus development years and none is earlier: Ducted 2041, Embraer 2042, GEnx 2042, Open Fan 'not before 2045', S3 fps 10-yr 2045, a 2045 Ducted in 2051. The draft public line gives no Ducted date, no Embraer date and no price. For the Open Fan it says 'not before 2045, ten years from a launch with an airframer', which is my wording and sits at the floor. Advice: lead with 'ten years from a launch with an airframer'. With no launch this round, 2045 is now a loose floor, so never tighten it into an entry date. 2041 has no test behind it today. At step 4 I will veto, on binding ground 2, any statement or move that commits to 2041 or 2042 or gives an Open Fan entry before 2045.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Against NGSA (EIS 2037), the 2041 Ducted is 4 years late in S1 and S3, but still earns +10 pp from 2041 on the NGSA airframes where CFM is fitted. Against an S3 fps 10-yr (EIS 2045) it is 4 years early. The two rival new NB engines on NGSA are ready in 2036 and 2037, so ours trails them by 4 to 5 years through the NGSA ramp. In S2, code 2 drops CFM from NGSA. Being ready earlier would not change that: the Ducted is pure bill there, -6.00.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. If the Open Fan is ready after the first new NB's EIS, the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: NGSA (EIS 2037) is the first new NB in every column. A 2045 Open Fan is 8 years behind it in S1, S2 and S3 alike, so it is not ready by NGSA's entry in any column. The S3 fps (2045) comes second. Against hold: Open Fan alone -20.85 / -10.00 / -22.16, and with Lobby -21.85 / -11.00 / -23.16. Against Ducted + Embraer, the best Open Fan row is -20.28 / -9.00 / -21.64.

tests.name: Physics (Culp ask 4)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so a Ducted is never called the next generation. The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data. Wording check: the frame calls the Ducted 'a defence, never the next generation', and RISE keeps the 20% bar. Confirmed in my own words: a ducted engine 'has less than half the fuel burn improvements that can come from an open fan'. 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics.' RISE targets 'more than 20%'. On physics, then, a Ducted cannot meet Culp's 20% line. Whether he rebuts the line (it governs RISE) or strikes it is his call. The public line must never call the Ducted the next generation.

tests.name: Durability first (Culp asks 1 and 4)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or for schedule (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The plan passes as framed. It is not a result on the engine. The brief has no durability data and no ducted turn-on/turn-off results from the 2030 test plan, and I won't invent any. What does stand on test: the LEAP-1A durability kit (upgraded HPT blade, fuel nozzle) was certified in December 2024, is in all LEAP-1A deliveries and shop visits, and more than doubles time on wing, to the CFM56 level. On RISE, there are over 350 tests with an early durability focus and compact-core HPT dust testing. The yardstick is LEAP at about 4,800 cycles in harsh conditions against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56. The frame puts the gate ahead of the date: if the gate holds, the date gives way. The risk is that the pair's value rests on 2041 and 2042, and that puts pressure on the date. Culp should say in his rationale that the date moves, not the durability. The LEAP fleet kits reach the fleet at shop visits, 'years, not months', and they keep priority.

tests.name: Safety call: cross-functional Ducted durability gate (Culp ask 1)
tests.threshold: If a problem or an order touches safety or durability, a cross-functional team makes the call, not one person.
tests.numbers: The Ducted order touches durability, so I name the gate: the Ducted hot-and-harsh and dust gate. Who sits on it: engineering, quality and supply chain (one organisation since 2025); fleet support with field data; the safety review; and Safran engineering as the CFM partner (inference). The fixes must be accepted by the airframer and the regulator. What it must turn off: in hot-and-harsh and dust conditions, it turns on in test the failure modes behind the LEAP harsh-environment shortfall, which are hot-section/HPT blade distress and fuel-nozzle coking, and turns them off with the ducted design. Harsh-environment time on wing must be no worse than the mature LEAP-1A, with the CFM56 as yardstick (the threshold is my inference). Gate points: (a) at launch, named, staffed and with criteria set; (b) before 2041 is used in any public statement, customer commitment or the Embraer schedule, passed on engine or core test; (c) before EIS, accepted by the airframer and the regulator. Today only (a) can be met. I raise no safety flag and no durability flag on the launch: no failure has been turned on and left on, and the gate is open, not failed. A flag would come from a failure turned on in test that the design does not turn off.

tests.name: Supply load: Ducted + Partner Embraer next to the live GEnx (Culp ask 5; doctrine, not my record)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers: With the live GEnx this makes two projects, so the $2B strain is charged. The S2 row confirms it: -6.00 = $4B of R&D + $2B of strain. Net of strain, the pair against hold is +1.54 (S1), -6.00 (S2) and +2.50 (S3). The grid pays more than the strain in S1 and S3 but not in S2. Embraer adds no strain (+1.85 / 0.00 / +2.09 against the Ducted alone). Physical load: at hold, CFM NB engines fall from 2,553 (2034) to 2,191 (2041, -14%) and 1,438 (2045, -44%), so LEAP OE load eases as a Ducted would ramp. GEnx moves from 143 to 152 a year. The load that matters is qualifying new parts at the same constrained suppliers, where 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites. Priority: safety first, then LEAP fleet durability upgrades and spares, with spares never crowding out OE, and Ducted development parts after both. Capacity stays joint with Safran. No evidence in my own words: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load: Ducted alone (advice)
tests.threshold: A second project next to the live GEnx must pay its $2B strain on the grid (inference; doctrine).
tests.numbers: Against hold: -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41. It is below zero in S1 and S2 and inside the $1B epsilon in S3. It does not pay its strain in the expected column. If Embraer falls, hold the Ducted too.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the WB, prefer the upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the NB, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: WB: the GEnx upgrade is live on the GE90/GEnx architecture, with no flag, so hold. NB: at hold we fly a LEAP derivative on NGSA. A Ducted is a new engine, which my preference does not favour, but the hard-rule-3 trigger is Culp's ground and it is now on the public record. If launched, build it as a LEAP-lineage successor that carries RISE technology and the proven hot section. Keep the LEAP fleet upgrades flowing.

vetoes.plan: ducted: launch alone, without partner_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice only, on supply load (doctrine and the board's strain rule, not my record). The 2041 date passes my test, so there is no binding veto. Against hold the Ducted alone is -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41. It loads the same constrained suppliers as the live GEnx and LEAP and does not pay its $2B strain in the expected column. If the pair breaks, hold both.

vetoes.name: unused
vetoes.plan: ducted + partner_embraer if S2 is the expected column
vetoes.ground: Advice only, on supply load. In S2, where code 2 takes CFM's NGSA slot, the pair is -6.00 against hold: $4B of R&D plus $2B of strain, with nothing to show for it. The dates are not the problem: 2041 and 2042 pass my test, so this is not binding. The S2 weight belongs to Culp and Ghai.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in any combination (with or without lobby_emissions)
vetoes.ground: Advice only. The ready year, 2045 (2035 + 10, not before 2045), passes my date test, so this is not binding. But it is 8 years behind NGSA's 2037 entry in every column: -20.85 / -10.00 / -22.16 against hold, and -21.85 / -11.00 / -23.16 with Lobby. No RISE flight-test result in the brief backs a product commitment, and the fly demo has moved before. Keep RISE all in as a funded technology programme with Safran, with no cancel.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data only, never analysis. (1) Ducted, against: if a core or engine test under hot-and-harsh or dust conditions turns on a failure the ducted design does not turn off, I raise a cross-functional durability flag and the date moves, by 1 to 2 years on my LEAP-1B precedent. Ducted, for: if it turns them off, at harsh time on wing no worse than the mature LEAP-1A, I would back 2041 as a date, still kept internal until engine test confirms it. (2) Supply: if supplier capacity data shows the 9 constrained suppliers cannot qualify ducted hot-section parts without slipping LEAP OE, spares or the fleet durability kits, I would raise a supply flag and recommend holding the Ducted. (3) RISE: ground and flight-test results with durability and dust turned on and off would let me back '10 years from a launch with an airframer' as a commitment. Not mine to change: the S2 weight, launch timing and Embraer belong to Culp and Ghai, and my date test still reads 2041, 2042 and 2045 whatever they decide.
ops.memo:
What the tests say, not the analysis.

Dates. A Ducted launched now is ready in 2041, launch plus six: four years after NGSA enters in 2037, four ahead of a 2045 fps. Embraer counts from 2042. The Open Fan is not ready before 2045, eight years behind NGSA in every column. Every date passes my test. None goes out as a promise.

Durability. The Board asked for turn-on, turn-off results on a ducted engine. The brief has none, and I will not dress analysis up as test. What stands on test: the LEAP-1A hot-section kit, turned on, turned off and certified, and over 350 RISE tests, dust on the compact core. So I name the gate: hot-and-harsh and dust. Engineering, quality, supply chain, fleet support and Safran sit on it. No single person makes that call. Before 2041 is used anywhere, it must turn off hot-section distress and nozzle coking, at harsh time on wing no worse than the mature LEAP-1A. If it can't, the date moves, not the durability.

No safety flag. No durability flag on the launch: the gate is open, not failed.

Slip: a year on the LEAP-1B kit, more on the RISE demo. Two years puts the engine behind Embraer's 2042.

Physics: less than half the open fan's gain. A defence, never the next generation.

Supply, on doctrine: the pair pays its strain in S1 and S3, not S2.

Orders: Ducted and Embraer, following Culp; hold the rest. No binding veto.

other_moves.move: CFM's engine for the new single-aisle airplanes, offered to both airframers
other_moves.detail: CFM, with Safran, brings a new ducted engine to the airplanes that selected CFM, and offers it to both airframers on NGSA and the fps. It is a LEAP-lineage successor that carries the proven hot section and what RISE has taught us. It is a defence (H3), never called the next generation. No ready date, no price and no capacity figure are published. No airframer is refused or locked out, and Boeing's fps options stay open (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185, CX-0564]. Joint CFM practice: meeting an airframer's launch with an engine. Safran's consent is assumed.

other_moves.move: Partner Embraer, non-exclusive, terms joint with Safran
other_moves.detail: A CFM engine for a third airframer, in addition to our two customers and not in place of either; no one is locked out (H1). No Embraer volume, price or date goes public until the volumes are worked through with Embraer and Safran (Ghai's terms condition) [CX-0184]. The Ducted and Embraer stand or fall together, and neither can be cancelled after this round.

other_moves.move: Ducted hot-and-harsh and dust durability gate (gate before date)
other_moves.detail: Ali's named, cross-functional gate. Members: engineering, quality and supply chain; fleet support with field data; the safety review; Safran engineering. It must turn on, in hot-and-harsh and dust test, the failure modes behind LEAP's harsh-environment shortfall (HPT blade distress, fuel-nozzle coking) and turn them off in the ducted design. Bar: harsh time on wing no worse than the mature LEAP-1A, with the CFM56 as the yardstick. Gate points: (a) at launch, named and staffed with criteria set (met today); (b) passed on core or engine test before 2041 is used in any statement, customer commitment or the Embraer schedule; (c) accepted by the airframer and the regulator before EIS. If it fails, the date moves, not the durability [CX-0012, CX-0208, CX-0009].

other_moves.move: RISE kept all in as a funded technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: No cancel (H5) and no product launch (H2). Ground and flight testing continue jointly, with durability and dust first. It becomes a product only when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. The only public timing is 'ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045' (Ali's wording), a floor and never an entry date. Joint practice.

other_moves.move: LEAP and GEnx fleet durability upgrades keep first call on supply
other_moves.detail: Targeted component upgrades continue into the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B fleets, and the GEnx upgrade into the 787 fleet [CX-0607, CX-0422]. Supply priority: safety first, then fleet kits and spares, with spares never crowding out OE [CX-0529], and Ducted development parts after both. FLIGHT DECK at the constrained suppliers: lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. CFM narrowbody capacity decisions stay joint with Safran [CX-0184]. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Private engagement with both airframers on NGSA through EIS and on the fps
other_moves.detail: Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. Purpose: first-hand data on whether NGSA's code 7 holds to its 2037 entry, which is the S2 risk, and on Boeing's dual-source requirement for the fps. Show the Ducted's durability gate and test plan, not price. No launch-era pricing and no concession to keep a code or win one (Ghai's terms test) [CX-0930, CX-0184].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That hasn't changed, and it won't.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. What we know: Airbus has launched its new single-aisle airplane and asked CFM to be on it. We don't have a birthright on that order. We'll earn it on the product and on durability. So CFM, with our partner Safran, is launching a new ducted engine for the airplanes that chose CFM, and we'll offer it to both airframers. It builds on the LEAP our customers fly today and carries what we've learned in RISE. I'll be plain about what it is and what it isn't. It's the right engine for these airplanes. It isn't the next generation. That's the open fan.

We're also going to work with Embraer to bring a CFM engine to its airplanes. That adds to what we do for our two big customers, and it doesn't take anything away from them.

What we don't know yet is the date. You'll get one when our testing backs it, and not before. Durability comes ahead of the date: if the testing needs more time, it gets it. And job one hasn't moved. We keep LEAP and GEnx engines on wing longer for the customers flying them today.

RISE stays a technology program, and we're all in on it with Safran. On the testing we have today, an open fan comes ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045. It launches with an airframer, not ahead of one.

It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. It's the same game as 2030: the installed base on the new narrowbodies, not share for its own sake [CX-0467, CX-0422, CX-0493]. The market moved. NGSA launched for a 2037 entry with code 7, and Airbus selected CFM. Two rival new engines are launched and selected on it, ready in 2036 and 2037. At hold we fly a LEAP derivative, and our NB share falls to 43.7% in 2045 and 39.1% in 2050. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. We win by keeping the place Airbus gave us with an engine that competes.

DECISION:
- ducted: launch, with partner_embraer: launch, as one defence. They stand or fall together, and neither can be cancelled after this round.
- open_fan: hold. lobby_emissions: hold. genx: hold (the upgrade is live).
- RISE stays all in as funded technology with Safran: no launch, no cancel for cost.
- Premium $0.0B. RISE allowance unused.

THE TESTS:
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Against hold, Ducted + Embraer (B) is +1.54 / -6.00 / +2.50 (S1 / S2 / S3; rows -21.58 / -39.97 / -25.88 against -23.12 / -33.97 / -28.38).
- It is the best grid plan in S1 and S3, and $0.54B over epsilon in the expected column S1.
- S1 cost: none. It gains where rivals hold.
- Worst column S2: -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B R&D + $2B strain). The downside is bounded.
- The Ducted alone is -0.31 / -6.00 / +0.41. It fails, and I'm not bringing it.
- Embraer next to the Ducted: +1.85 / 0.00 / +2.09, with no R&D and no added strain.
(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, because that is the public record: code 7 with CFM selected, the Alt plan, and Boeing 'not there yet'. I asked Rahul to push on S2 and he did, so I carry his 0.20 rather than my 0.15. Weights are S1 0.60 / S2 0.20 / S3 0.20. B against hold on them is +0.22, and the S2 breakeven at this mix is 22.9% (20.4% to 29.4% across mixes; the Board has 24-25%).
(3) Hard rule 3 [CX-0564, CX-0183]. The trigger I said would flip me is now on the public record, not just the grid: GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and selected on NGSA. I judged the Ducted on its row against hold. It's ready in 2041, four years after NGSA's entry, and still earns +10 pp from its ready year. This is the last window that counts, since a 2045 launch is ready in 2051.
(4) H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]. NGSA enters in 2037. A 2035 Open Fan is ready in 2045, eight years later in every column. The Open Fan alone is -20.85 / -10.00 / -22.16 against hold. The best Open Fan row is $20.28B or more behind B in S1, above even the $15B allowance. Held.
(5) 20% red line, restated [CX-0217]. It governs the next-generation product, RISE. A ducted engine has less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], so the Ducted can't be, and is never called, the next generation. It's an H3 defence. I rebut the line for it; I don't strike it. RISE keeps the 20% bar.
(6) Durability is not traded for fuel burn or for the date [CX-0208]. Ali raises no safety or durability flag: the gate is open, not failed. There are no turn-on/turn-off results on a ducted engine in our record, and I won't dress analysis up as test. What stands on test:
- the LEAP-1A hot-section kit, certified December 2024;
- more than 350 RISE tests, with dust testing on the compact-core HPT.
Our cross-functional answer is the named gate (other moves). Gate point (a) is met at launch, and (b) must pass on core or engine test before 2041 is used anywhere. If the gate fails, the date moves, not the durability [CX-0012].
(7) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]. This is doctrine, not my record: the $2B strain is in the grid and paid for in S1 and S3. LEAP OE load falls 14% by 2041 and 44% by 2045 as a Ducted would ramp. Fleet kits, spares and OE keep priority over development parts. Capacity stays joint with Safran.
(8) Tie-break [CX-0658]. In the expected column B leads by more than epsilon. On weights it's a near tie: +0.22, about -0.10 with a one-year slip, and -0.52 with two. So I ran it:
- Safety: with the gate binding the date, there's no reason to prefer hold.
- Quality: the gate sets the bar at our best fleet standard.
- Delivery: we bring a competitive engine to the airframer that chose us, while LEAP OE, spares and kits keep first call.
- Cost: $1.0B a year, inside the payout floor.
None of the four reverses the value call.
(9) Three gates [CX-0433]:
- Foundation: fleet upgrades, the A-range rating and at least 70% returned.
- Partner: Safran, and Embraer non-exclusive.
- Market: an airframer has selected CFM on the record.
All three hold.

EXCO. Every Ghai test I rely on passes:
- pays-for-itself, B +1.54;
- volumes-first: code 7 is on the record, and Embraer rides NGSA;
- capex: $1.0B a year against about $2.55B of room;
- premium: $0.0B;
- terms: no price talk.
His binding vetoes cover only plans I am not bringing. Ali's date tests pass (2041, 2042, 2045 floor), and he raises no binding veto and no flag. No overrides.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity):
- Ducted: consent assumed. It's an H3 defence of the NGSA slot Airbus gave CFM, with rival engines launched and selected on the record. Half of that annuity is Safran's, and meeting an airframer's launch with an engine is CFM joint practice. Price and capacity stay joint.
- Embraer: consent assumed. It's a CFM engine for a third airframer, non-exclusive, on terms worked jointly.
- Open Fan and Lobby: held. A RISE product with no airframer path is outside joint practice.
- GEnx: GE alone.

AIRFRAMER FINDINGS. The brief carries no findings from the private talks, and I won't invent any. First-hand on the record: Airbus selected CFM in 2030 with no new CFM engine launched, so that code did not depend on a launch. Whether code 7 holds to 2037 is the S2 question, and I carry it at 0.20.

BIASES, NAMED:
- The installed-base lens likes this move [CX-0555]. I book none of the upside it suggests: no lower S2 odds for having launched, nothing past the board's 2056 window, no later fps win.
- Deference to airframers made us wait in 2030. Rahul scores that wait at about $0.4B.
- Ramp optimism: I haircut my own date, not the board's ramp. A one-year slip leaves S1 at +1.14 to +1.27; two years leave +0.61 to +0.89.
- Doctrine, not my record, drove Embraer and the supply read.

WHAT FLIPS ME IN 2045: a gate failure I can't answer on test, or evidence that S2 sat above the breakeven. "We don't want to be rash, but we need to get after this straight away" [CX-0237].

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed as binding on dates and as the condition on durability. It's a thin record: his own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, and his supply section is doctrine, which I checked against the board's strain rule.

Dates pass his test: Ducted 2041, Embraer 2042, GEnx counting from 2042, and the Open Fan no earlier than 2045, eight years behind NGSA in every column. None goes public as a commitment.

He named the cross-functional durability gate, with its members, criteria and three gate points, and raised no safety or durability flag: the gate is open, not failed. He was candid that there are no ducted turn-on/turn-off results on our record. I took that as is and made gate point (b) the condition before 2041 is used anywhere.

His 1-2 year slip estimate rests on the LEAP-1B kit precedent. It's an inference, not a test number, and I priced it through Ghai.

Physics confirms a ducted engine has less than half the open fan's gain, so the 20% line stays with RISE. On supply, his reading matches doctrine: the strain is paid in S1 and S3 and not in S2. Fleet kits and spares keep priority. Capacity stays joint with Safran.

I accepted his advice to hold the Ducted if Embraer fell, and his build preference for a LEAP-lineage successor carrying RISE technology.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. NGSA keeps code 7 through its 2037 entry, and Boeing does not launch the fps this round. That is the public record: Airbus selected all three makers in 2030 with no new CFM engine launched, says it will certify them in sequence as each matures, and contracted LEAP and GTF supply for the A320 tail to about 2045. Boeing says it is 'not there yet'. Weights: S1 0.60 / S2 0.20 / S3 0.20 (Ghai's, lower on S1 than my 0.65).
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: Ducted + Partner Embraer: -21.58 in S1, +1.54 against hold (-23.12). It is also best in S3 (-25.88). Hold is best only in S2 (-33.97).
decision.premium_reason:
$0.0B. The submitted plan (Ducted + Partner Embraer) is the best grid plan in the expected column S1, and in S3.
- Doctrine premium: $0.0B.
- Objective premium: $0.0B.
- RISE allowance: not used, $0.0B. No Open Fan fits it; the best Open Fan row is $20.28B or more behind B in S1, above the $15B allowance.
- Game total to date: $0.0B of $4.0B.
decision.objective_note:
Briefing goal, reported honestly, with no objective premium.

(1) NB share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Hold: 69.8% / 43.7% / 39.1%. Not met.
- Submitted plan (Ghai's estimate, not a grid number): 69.8% in 2040 (unchanged, since the Ducted is ready in 2041), about 53% in 2045 and about 49% in 2050.
- How: CFM's share of NGSA engines goes from 18.3% to 31.7% after re-normalisation, and NGSA is about 69% and 75% of NB deliveries in those years.
- Worst year: at the line, not cleared, within the error of the estimate. I don't claim it.

Bring gate point (b), passed on core or engine test in hot-and-harsh and dust conditions, before 2041 is used in any statement, customer commitment or the Embraer schedule. Public statement and public other moves: they pass our disclosure check. No rival is named, no one is blamed, there is no Ducted or Embraer date and no price talk. Take Ali's wording: say an open fan comes 'no sooner than ten years from a launch with an airframer, and not before 2045', so the floor never reads as an entry date. Never call the Ducted the next generation. In the public other-move texts, keep internal labels out (rule codes, 'defence', 'consent is assumed', 'cannot be cancelled').

Delivery and customers. Offer the Ducted to both airframers, including on any fps, and keep Embraer non-exclusive. Offer no launch-era pricing or concession to hold NGSA's code 7 or to sign Embraer. Embraer volume, price and capacity stay joint with Safran and stay out of public until agreed. LEAP and GEnx fleet kits and spares keep first call on the constrained suppliers, ahead of Ducted development parts.

Airframer findings, raised again. The private engagement has still reported nothing first-hand. In 2045, tell us whether code 7 held through NGSA's 2037 entry (which settles S2), where Boeing stands on the fps and its dual-source requirement, and whether the Joint Venture door has closed or formed. Raise the booking only when the NGSA code locks and gate (b) clears. In 2045, add a project only when the grid pays its strain, and keep at least 70% of free cash flow returned and the A-range rating untouched.

RISE. Keep it all in as a funded technology programme with Safran, with no product launch and no cancel for cost. We take on record the CEO's candour that 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' cannot now be met. A 2045 launch would be ready in 2055, long after NGSA's 2037 entry, so absent a change on the record there is no airframer path, and the one RISE allowance stays unused. other_moves.move: Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce: P&W commitment on the record, with its terms in principle
other_moves.detail: The commitment is public at once and standing. Terms: (1) risk and investment are shared, never core technology [P-1233]; (2) the gear and the GTF Advantage core enter as P&W-owned, P&W-designed, P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer; (3) both partners' solo programmes (GTF2, UltraFan NB) fold into one engine, so the partners are aligned on the same new engine [P-1875]; (4) equal shares, and each partner's own solo development spend counts toward its own share, which is how we credit the technology each side brings; there is no cash or balancing payment for technology, no partner carries the other's share, and P&W's economic share is not below half; (5) P&W modules are supplied into the Joint Venture at standard terms; (6) no money moves until Rolls-Royce has committed and the Joint Venture has formed. other_moves.detail: (T1) Any Joint Venture engine for an airframe entering service before 2041 is the GTF2 configuration as tested. The gear, core and hot section do not change before EIS, and Rolls-Royce content comes later as a block upgrade with its own durability campaign [PX-0116][PX-0088]. (T2) Gear and core stay P&W modules [P-1233][P-1240]. (T3) GTF2's durability campaign, test assets and test engineers stay with P&W. They are not re-planned for integration, and testing is never compressed: the date gives. (T4) Joint Venture integration is staffed from the Joint Venture and the partners, not from GTF fleet engineering [PX-0080]. (T5) Any GTF2 or Joint Venture production ramp is gated on GTF fleet spares, worked daily and reported to the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]. (T6) No public Joint Venture ready date, Rolls-Royce commitment or NGSA EIS. Eddy re-tests T1-T6 at every step. Mitchill's ground-3 line: a cash payment to Rolls-Royce, carrying its share, below-standard module terms or a P&W share below half triggers his binding veto, and we then resubmit or hold. GTF risk-sharing partners keep their existing proportions in the modules P&W brings and sit behind P&W's half. No dilution without their consent, no cash make-whole from P&W, and no partner money booked before formation [P-1563][PX-0037][PX-0038]. Eddy's 2035 durability re-test (severe-environment campaign against plan, core and gear on test, all life-limited parts at full life at EIS) goes to the Board's Governance and Public Policy committee [PG-0023]. If testing slips, we tell Airbus early.
