pratt_whitney.public_statement:
The bad news first. The GTF fleet still has work ahead of it, and that work comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into the fleet at shop visits, and we will keep doing it until the fleet is where it needs to be. Control what you can control.

GTF2 is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We offer an engine to an airframer only where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. A Joint Venture spreads risk and investment; it does not share technology. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core come in as Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. The partners hold equal shares, and each partner's own development work counts toward its own share. No partner buys the other's technology. GTF2 is what we bring. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself, and the Joint Venture forms only when both partners have committed.

We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates, and we will not get out ahead of them. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: commit; premium_b $0; overrides empty.

1. STARTING POINT. Eddy proposes hold / commit and Mitchill recommends the same, which was also my framing lean. Neither raises a binding veto against these orders. Mitchill's two binding vetoes are conditional: ground 3 on the Joint Venture terms and ground 4 on the words. I wrote the terms and the statement to stay clear of both, as tested below. Eddy's ground-1 veto on the commit is also conditional, on T1-T3 and T6, and none is triggered. Eddy's red-line flag (gear and core stay P&W modules) is met in the terms, so it is not a breach.

2. STRIKE. I strike rows C (cancel/hold) and D (cancel/commit). Neither is a binding veto ground: Mitchill objects on his return gate and his own 2035 cancel rule, and Eddy flags it as advice. The company red line strikes them. We do not exit a programme a customer has asked for [P-1342]. NGSA's code 7 includes P&W, and GTF2 is ready in 2036, before the 2037 EIS. Cancel would have to beat hold in every plausible column, and it trails in all four:
- C vs hold: -16.56 / -1.87 / -18.49 / -16.56;
- D vs A: -16.56 / -1.87 / -18.49 / -1.67.
Mitchill's 2035 rule says carry, and all three of his cancel conditions fail. Cancel books a $1.67B write-off (2 x 5/6) to save $0.33B, and the Board would veto it. 2035 is GTF2's last cancel window; I do not use it.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035]. Eddy's readiness check binds on me, and it passes:
- GTF2 ready 2036 against NGSA EIS 2037 (one year) and against fps 10-yr EIS 2045 in S3 (nine years);
- a Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2036 only because GTF2 folds in (2041 without it).
So T1 is the safety constraint on the commit: the 2037 engine is GTF2 as tested, the gear, core and hot section do not change before EIS, and Rolls-Royce content comes later as a block upgrade with its own campaign.

The 2035 re-test passes on the record: GTF2 shows ready 2036, unchanged since 2030, with no escape, no rising AOG and no ask to compress testing. Eddy's three round-1 triggers are not live, and parts and capacity pass.

The margin is thin, and I say so. One year nominal; -1.0 to -0.5 years after the company's derivative slip prior; about +0.25 years on Eddy's own record. My instinct says 2036 holds. My record says discount my dates: the GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087], though the H1 2025 date was met [PX-0078]. So the date gives and the testing never does. If it slips we tell Airbus early, and we slip and add testing; we do not cancel. The GTF2 ramp is gated on fleet spares, because the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

4. OPTIMISE, in $B, S1-S4, on the governing weights (Mitchill's): S1 0.65, S2 0.15, S3 0.10, S4 0.10.
- A hold/commit: -1.53 / -16.22 / +0.40 / +0.68; expected -3.32; worst -16.22 (S2).
- B hold/hold (default): -1.53 / -16.22 / +0.40 / -1.53; expected -3.54; worst -16.22.
- C cancel/hold: -18.09 in every column; expected -18.09.
- D cancel/commit: -18.09 / -18.09 / -18.09 / -0.99; expected -16.38.
Commit vs hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.21, worth +0.22 governing, +0.44 on my framing weights and +0.55 uniform. Its break-even p(S4) is 0. Commit adds no R&D: $1.67B spent plus 2035's $0.33B is $2.00B against P&W's $2B share, so the fold write-off is $0. It does not deepen the worst column. A is the best row on every weight set and weakly dominates B. My working is in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/dash-2050-phaseout/work/r2_decide_calc.py.

5. WHY I ADOPT MITCHILL'S WEIGHTS. The Board asked for one governing set, and I trust his numbers over my dates. I set S4 at 0.10, down from my framing 0.20. Rolls-Royce says it commits "once P&W's commitment is on the public record", and sealed orders mean it cannot see ours this round. That is timing, not refusal. S3 is 0.10: Boeing is "not there yet", gives no date, and I do not get ahead of an airframer [PX-0062]; that is also my incrementalism. S2 is 0.15: Airbus can change the code only this round, and a one-year margin is a selection risk. Against that, Airbus has contracted GTF supply for the A320 tail to about 2045.

6. MY TESTS.
- Safety and durability: pass, as in point 3.
- Visible demand: not in play. GTF2 is live on a code-7 selection on the public record, so neither launch nor launch_if_selected is on offer.
- Miss-a-cycle [PX-0071]: the S2 loss is $14.69B against S1, and no order prices it. Carrying GTF2 is what keeps us fitted and able to answer. Cancel would miss the cycle by our own hand.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no doctrine-favoured order trails, so the premium is $0. My doctrine (hold before a Joint Venture; architecture loyalty) and the objective (Capitalise) differ, and the objective's order wins at no cost.
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms. 2035 outlay is $0.33B, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope and 0.8% of $40B debt. Commit adds $0, no stretch is used and the one-time stretch stays in reserve. Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669].
- Value, not share: standard terms, no concession, and no technology concession to win Rolls-Royce's commitment.
- Objective status: see objective_note.

7. JOINT VENTURE, ON DOCTRINE AND NOT ON MY RECORD. I have no evidence of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low), so I follow doctrine [P-1233][P-1875] and take Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. My round-1 condition is met on the public record: live NGSA, not in service until 2037, carries code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce. In round 1 Mitchill vetoed commit on ground 4 because it cost $2.00B in a column. It now costs nothing in any column, and its S4 value is its own condition, not booked upside.

On the terms, ground 3 is clear on Mitchill's test. Equal shares; each partner's solo spend counts to its own share; no cash or balancing payment; no carrying Rolls-Royce's share; modules at standard terms; no money before formation. The gear and core stay P&W-owned and P&W-built, with no licence or transfer. Our GTF risk-sharing partners keep their proportions behind P&W's half [P-1563][PX-0038].

My bias, declared: architecture loyalty says GTF2 should stand alone; the GTF is "the architecture of the future" [PX-0014]. The grid says the commitment costs nothing in any column, and data moves me. GTF2 is what we bring, not what we give up.

8. DOCTRINE RELIEF, DECLARED AT $0 PV COST. The round-1 shared-source relief for code 7 stands [P-0746][PX-0058][P-1292]. A Joint Venture engine is shared by design; doctrine allows that for risk and investment, never for technology [P-1233].

9. BOOKED NUMBER AND WHAT IS NOT COUNTED. Booked: -1.53 (S1). The +0.68 in S4 is not booked until Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record. The following are recorded and not booked:
- the value of a standing commitment into 2045;
- what a Joint Venture might give if Airbus dropped P&W (S2 and S4 together);
- a later fps on code 4;
- early GTF2 OE margin;
- the 2045 exposures. If a ready GTF2 does not count toward our share, the low end is a new $2.00B share. The equal-share effect costs us wherever P&W is fitted on more new-type volume than Rolls-Royce.
Those exposures are in our control, because a commitment can be withdrawn before formation. The 2045 package brings the withdraw row.

10. TIE-BREAKS. The fleet beats a new engine: the GTF2 ramp is gated on spares and integration is staffed off the fleet (T4, T5). "Miss a cycle" applies on visible demand, and NGSA is visible: carry GTF2. A rival's discount never moves the answer.

frame.question:
Control what you can control. GTF2 is live: it launched in 2030 on NGSA's code 7 selection, is in its last development year, and is due ready in 2036. NGSA (EIS 2037) is coded 7, so CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce are all fitted if nothing changes.

Three things are outside our control: whether Airbus keeps us on the code until its EIS, whether Boeing launches fps, and whether Rolls-Royce commits. Three things are inside it:
- whether GTF2 is ready, durable and supported by its 2036 ready year;
- whether we carry it through 2035, its last cancel window;
- whether we put a Joint Venture commitment on the record, now that a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce.

So the question for 2035 is this. Do we order `gtf2_solo: hold` (carry GTF2 to 2036) with `jv_with_rr: commit`? Or does another grid row (hold/hold, cancel, cancel + commit) pay more inside the safety and durability constraint, Mitchill's gate, Eddy's two vetoes and the Board's would-veto list?

The bad news first. On a three-way NGSA, GTF2 earns +$0.47B of engine value against $2.00B of R&D. We sit at -1.53 and the Capitalise objective is not met. The one order on the grid that can lift it is the Joint Venture commitment, and only if Rolls-Royce commits.

frame.initial_lean:
Lean: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit`, `premium_b` 0. This is subject to Eddy's proposal and his durability and parts check, and to Mitchill's four-ground gate.

Why:
- Carrying GTF2 keeps us fitted on NGSA and meets the credibility objective. It costs about $0.33B more against a cancel that trails hold by $1.87-18.49B in every column. We do not exit a programme a customer has asked for [P-1342].
- The commitment is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +2.21). It adds no R&D, its fold write-off is $0, and it is the one order that can lift us to ΔPV >= 0 where we are not already (S4, +0.68). Doctrine and objective agree, so no premium.
- The condition I set in round 1 is met on the public record: live NGSA carries code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce says it moves once our commitment is on the record, so ours is what opens the route. Responsible bet, responsible payback [PX-0010].
- Biases, declared. My architecture loyalty says GTF2 should stand alone; the GTF is "the architecture of the future" [PX-0014]. The grid says the commitment costs nothing in any column, and data moves me. GTF2 is what we bring into the Joint Venture, not what we give up. I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low confidence), so on it I follow doctrine [P-1233][P-1875] and Mitchill's and Eddy's tests.
- Fallbacks. If Eddy fails the folded GTF2 on durability or parts, I go to `jv_with_rr: hold` (the Board's named alternative). If Mitchill's ground 3 bites on the terms, I resubmit on risk-and-investment-only terms or hold.
- Looking ahead to 2045: if Rolls-Royce does not commit, the commitment stands. We review it then on the withdraw row against the hold row, and I withdraw if my conditions have lapsed and withdraw is not worse.

Proposed disclosure, in my voice, to be checked by Mitchill on ground 4 and by Eddy on full life:
"The bad news first. The GTF fleet work is not finished, and it still comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into the fleet at shop visits. Control what you can control.
GTF2 is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We offer an engine to an airframer only where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service.
Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. A Joint Venture spreads risk and investment; it does not share technology. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core come in as Pratt & Whitney modules, built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. GTF2 is what we bring.
We compete on standard terms, on the product and the durability record. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."
The statement does not claim Rolls-Royce's commitment, a formed Joint Venture, a Joint Venture date or a time-on-wing figure, and names no NGSA EIS.

Proposed other moves:
1. Public: GTF fleet first. The Hot Section kit continues at shop visits, charged on standard terms.
2. Public: standard commercial terms on NGSA and fps. No discount or concession to hold the NGSA selection.
3. Public: Joint Venture terms in principle. Risk and investment shared; gear and core P&W-owned and P&W-built, with no licence or transfer; both solo programmes fold into one engine; no money moves before formation.
4. Private: gates.
- Eddy's 2035 durability re-test is reported to the Board's Governance and Public Policy committee.
- The GTF2 production ramp is gated on fleet spares.
- Equal-share crediting of contributions.
- GTF risk-sharing partners kept whole.
- A 2045 review of the standing commitment.

ops.proposal:
ORDERS PROPOSED: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: commit. Nothing technical calls for a premium; premium_b is Calio's and Mitchill's call.

WHY gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 is live. It launched in 2030, is in its last development year and is due ready in 2036 (bulletin programme table; brief section 1). NGSA (EIS 2037) is coded 7 and fits P&W if nothing changes. GTF2 passes both my grounds for that EIS. Cancel is not a durability or parts ground, and my record has no view on cancelling. So, per my rule, I propose hold as the default and flag the cancel test to Mitchill and Calio. GTF2 CAN still be ready by the EIS of a live airframe whose code includes P&W (2036 against 2037). Cancel against hold is -16.56 / -1.87 / -18.49 / -16.56 (round2.md section 3). Seat doctrine, not my record: a programme in trouble slips quietly and adds testing; it is not cancelled (profile section 5, row 10). A cancel would also throw away five years of severe-environment testing, and that durability record is what we sell on.

WHY jv_with_rr: commit. My rule is hold before any commitment, unless Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce. NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, so that gate is open. My job is the technical conditions, and they pass on the CEO's draft terms.
- If Rolls-Royce commits (S4), a Joint Venture formed in 2035 folds in GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037). It is ready in 2036, one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- If Rolls-Royce does not commit, nothing forms and GTF2 carries on solo to 2036. Commit against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.21 and adds no R&D, so it changes nothing technical.

Technical conditions for the commit. They should be written into the terms (private gates in other_moves), and I re-check them at the veto step.
- T1: Any Joint Venture engine for an airframe entering service before 2041 is the GTF2 configuration as tested. No change to the gear, core or hot section before EIS. Rolls-Royce content comes in later as a block upgrade with its own durability campaign, the way Block D and the Advantage kit did [PX-0116][PX-0088]. Otherwise 2036 is a date on paper only and the durability clock resets (ground 1).
- T2: The gear and the GTF Advantage core are P&W-owned, P&W-designed and P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer [P-1233]. The design team mirrors the product's architecture [P-1240], so owning our modules is how a Joint Venture engine works; it is not a concession.
- T3: GTF2's durability campaign, test assets and test engineers stay with P&W. They are not re-planned for integration, and testing is not compressed.
- T4: Joint Venture integration is staffed from the Joint Venture and the partners, not from GTF fleet engineering. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- T5: Any GTF2 or Joint Venture production ramp is gated on GTF fleet spares, worked at a daily cadence and reported to the ExCo weekly [PX-0131].
- T6: The statement claims no Joint Venture ready date, no Rolls-Royce commitment and no NGSA EIS.

ANSWERS TO THE CEO'S ASKS

(1) Proposal: as above.

(2) Readiness against each EIS.
- GTF2, ready 2036 (launched 2030 + 6):
  - against NGSA EIS 2037: one year of margin, pass;
  - against fps 10-yr EIS 2045 (S3, launched 2035 + 10): nine years, pass.
- Joint Venture formed in 2035 (S4):
  - With GTF2 folded in, ready 2036: pass, one year of margin (row hold/commit, S4 +0.68).
  - On UltraFan NB alone, ready 2037 (row cancel/commit, S4 -0.99): passes the rule with zero margin. Its durability rests on Rolls-Royce's test campaign, which I cannot test or vouch for. This is advice, not a veto.
  - With neither, ready 2041: fails NGSA 2037, meets fps 2045.
- Is the 2036 ready year the GTF2 configuration as it stands? On the board, yes: the earliest folded ready year counts. Technically, only if T1 holds. The CEO's draft ("GTF2 is what we bring"; gear and core as P&W modules) does not reopen the configuration, so it passes. I would invoke ground 1 if the terms, the rationale or the statement put a merged or changed engine on NGSA 2037, or a Joint Venture date ahead of the testing.

(3) The 2035 durability re-test.
- Status: on plan on the record. The bulletin and brief show GTF2 'in development; ready 2036', unchanged since 2030, with no slip, escape or compressed testing on record.
- Basis: the board models neither test hours nor parts, so I report against the 2030 gates instead of inventing a test count.
- The gates:
  - an Advantage derivative, with gear and core carried over and nothing clean-sheet;
  - a severe-environment endurance campaign, front-loaded, at no less than the Advantage's 2-3x the base programme's testing [P-0779][P-1095], with core and gear on test;
  - all life-limited parts at full life at EIS [PX-0128];
  - the golden rules: all development testing done before service, and every new feature instrumented [PX-0168][P-1214][P-1215];
  - testing not compressed; if anything gives, the date gives.
- Margin:
  - nominal: 1 year;
  - after the company's +1.5-2 year slip prior for derivatives: -1.0 to -0.5 years;
  - on my own record from one year out (in June 2023 I said mid-2024 certification; it came in H1 2025 [P-0779][P-0785], about 0.75 years late): about +0.25 years.
  Thin either way.
- On the record, Airbus says it will certify the three engines in sequence as each one matures (bulletin). That eases the pressure to compress testing. It is qualitative and not booked: on the board, an engine not ready by EIS is dropped. If the testing slips, we tell Airbus early.

(4) Pacing parts and capacity: pass.
- No live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem is in the bulletin or the brief. Our own line that the fleet 'still has work ahead of it' refers to the Hot Section kit going in at shop visits. That is continuing work, not an escape. These orders launch nothing new, so ground 2 is not engaged.
- My evidence has no 2035 AOG count or material balance. The last figures are:
  - 10% of the fleet AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120];
  - about 350 AOG on average, projected through 2026 [PX-0300];
  - about 30 pacing parts [PX-0123];
  - shops waiting on parts, not capacity [PX-0124].
- P&W NB engines (brief section 1): 816 (2034), 758 (2035), 752 (2036), 757 (2037), 612 (2038), 659 (2039), 672 (2040), 842 (2041).
- Airbus has contracted GTF supply for the A320 tail to about 2045, so GTF1 OE, fleet spares and the GTF2 ramp overlap from 2037 to 2045. NGSA ramps slowly (rate 50 about four years after EIS), and our NB engine count falls from 757 to 612 in 2038 as the A320 lines wind down. GTF2 production therefore largely replaces GTF1 OE on the same material (inference).
- Gate confirmed: the GTF2 ramp goes only as fast as fleet spares are covered, worked daily and reported weekly to the ExCo [PX-0131]. No capacity spike: the powder-metal escape came from ramp-driven capacity [P-1040].

(5) Engineering load.
- GTF2 is P&W's only development, and this is its last year. Commit adds no R&D, and on formation two programmes fold into one engine, so it stays one programme.
- Off the board, integration load is real: governance, supply chain, MRO networks, and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan work. Under T1-T4 it does not touch the 2036 configuration or fleet engineering.
- This board has no strain charge for P&W, so this is advice, not a veto.

(6) My veto check on both grounds.
- Ground 1: pass for hold and for commit as framed. My three round-1 triggers:
  - (a) a quality escape or rising AOG without containment: none;
  - (b) any ask to compress testing: none, and the frame says the date gives;
  - (c) data showing durability cannot be proven by 2037: none on record.
- Ground 2: pass.
- Commit conditions: ready by the EIS it serves (2036 against 2037 with GTF2 folded in), and our gear and core kept as P&W modules. Both are met by the draft terms.
- Standing commitment into 2045 (advice, for Mitchill to price): if Rolls-Royce commits after NGSA's EIS, the fold takes in a GTF2 fleet already in service. Its type design, fleet support and parts flow must not be reopened or change hands. I re-test this in 2045, beside the withdraw row.

STATEMENT CHECK: pass on full life.
- It says "due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch" and "every life-limited part at full life on day one".
- It says "if the testing needs more time, the testing gets it", and offers an engine "only where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service" (my round-1 note, taken).
- It names no NGSA EIS, no Joint Venture date, no Rolls-Royce commitment and no time-on-wing figure.
- Keep "GTF2 is what we bring": it is T1 in public words.

Joint Venture formed in 2035 (S4): ready 2036 with GTF2 folded in (pass, 1 year; row hold/commit S4 +0.68); 2037 on UltraFan NB alone (pass, 0 margin, on Rolls-Royce's test campaign; row cancel/commit S4 -0.99); 2041 with neither (fails NGSA 2037, meets fps 2045). hold/hold and hold/commit both keep GTF2 ready by 2037. P&W NB engines (brief section 1): 816 (2034), 758 (2035), 752 (2036), 757 (2037), 612 (2038), 659 (2039), 672 (2040), 842 (2041). tests.numbers: No quality escape in the 2035 bulletin or brief. If one appears before the GTF2 ramp (2036-37), the ramp waits on containment and a dated recovery.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
- GTF2 test data or a finding showing durability, with full-life parts, cannot be proven by a 2037 EIS. I would fail GTF2 for NGSA on ground 1, propose telling Airbus early, and keep gtf2_solo at hold (slip and add testing, not cancel). I would move jv_with_rr to hold, because a 2035 Joint Venture's readiness rests on GTF2's 2036 date.
- Joint Venture terms, rationale or statement that put a merged or changed gear, core or hot-section configuration on NGSA 2037, re-plan GTF2's testing for integration, or name a Joint Venture date ahead of the testing: ground 1 veto on the commit, and I would propose hold.
- Terms that license or transfer our gear or core: a red-line flag, and I would propose hold.
- A live quality escape or rising AOG in the bulletin without containment and a dated recovery: I would fail parts on the GTF2 ramp and gate it until contained.
- Any ask to compress testing or promise an earlier EIS: ground 1.
- If the NGSA engine came to rest on UltraFan NB alone (cancel + commit), I would want Rolls-Royce's severe-environment data before I could pass it. Mitchill's or Calio's weights do not change my technical view.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. GTF2 has one year of margin: ready 2036 against NGSA's 2037 entry into service. My record says discount my dates. In June 2023 I was a year out from GTF Advantage certification, mid-2024; it came in 2025. Slip GTF2 the same way and it lands just inside 2037. The testing sets the pace: the severe-environment campaign stays whole, every life-limited part is at full life at entry into service, and if anything gives, the date gives.

The 2035 re-test passes on the record: GTF2 still shows ready 2036, with no escape, no rising AOG and no ask to compress. The board models neither test hours nor parts; I invent no count.

I propose gtf2_solo: hold. GTF2 can be ready for an EIS whose code includes us. Cancel isn't my ground; I flag it to Neil and Chris.

I propose jv_with_rr: commit, on two technical conditions. One: the 2037 engine is GTF2 as tested. A Joint Venture formed this year is ready in 2036 only because GTF2 folds in; new gear, core or hot-section content before entry into service resets the clock, and I'd veto on durability. Two: our gear and core stay Pratt modules, designed and built by us.

Parts: Airbus has GTF supply contracted to about 2045, and the fleet still needs spares. The GTF2 ramp waits on fleet spares. The fleet comes first.

Where I'm thin: one event, before the recall; nothing of mine on a Joint Venture. That is seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF fleet first: continue the GTF Advantage Hot Section durability kit across the in-service fleet, at shop visits, charged on standard terms
other_moves.detail: No game-board effect. The fleet work comes before any new engine [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0080]. The kit is charged, not given away [PX-0100]. No time-on-wing figure is published beyond what is already proven (Mitchill ground 4; Board recommendation 7).

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms for any NGSA or fps engine campaign
other_moves.detail: No launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade to hold the NGSA selection or win the fps [PX-0055][PX-0100]. We hold the NGSA seat on readiness and the durability record. A rival's discount does not move this. We say nothing on any airframer's dates, rates or engine choice [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce: P&W commitment on the record, with its terms in principle
other_moves.detail: The commitment is public at once and standing. Terms: (1) risk and investment are shared, never core technology [P-1233]; (2) the gear and the GTF Advantage core enter as P&W-owned, P&W-designed, P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer; (3) both partners' solo programmes (GTF2, UltraFan NB) fold into one engine, so the partners are aligned on the same new engine [P-1875]; (4) equal shares, and each partner's own solo development spend counts toward its own share, which is how we credit the technology each side brings; there is no cash or balancing payment for technology, no partner carries the other's share, and P&W's economic share is not below half; (5) P&W modules are supplied into the Joint Venture at standard terms; (6) no money moves until Rolls-Royce has committed and the Joint Venture has formed. No Joint Venture ready date, no Rolls-Royce commitment and no partner money is claimed.

other_moves.move: Internal gates on GTF2 and the Joint Venture commitment (Eddy T1-T6, Mitchill terms, Board durability reporting)
other_moves.detail: (T1) Any Joint Venture engine for an airframe entering service before 2041 is the GTF2 configuration as tested. The gear, core and hot section do not change before EIS, and Rolls-Royce content comes later as a block upgrade with its own durability campaign [PX-0116][PX-0088]. (T2) Gear and core stay P&W modules [P-1233][P-1240]. (T3) GTF2's durability campaign, test assets and test engineers stay with P&W. They are not re-planned for integration, and testing is never compressed: the date gives. (T4) Joint Venture integration is staffed from the Joint Venture and the partners, not from GTF fleet engineering [PX-0080]. (T5) Any GTF2 or Joint Venture production ramp is gated on GTF fleet spares, worked daily and reported to the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]. (T6) No public Joint Venture ready date, Rolls-Royce commitment or NGSA EIS. Eddy re-tests T1-T6 at every step. Mitchill's ground-3 line: a cash payment to Rolls-Royce, carrying its share, below-standard module terms or a P&W share below half triggers his binding veto, and we then resubmit or hold. GTF risk-sharing partners keep their existing proportions in the modules P&W brings and sit behind P&W's half. No dilution without their consent, no cash make-whole from P&W, and no partner money booked before formation [P-1563][PX-0037][PX-0038]. Eddy's 2035 durability re-test (severe-environment campaign against plan, core and gear on test, all life-limited parts at full life at EIS) goes to the Board's Governance and Public Policy committee [PG-0023]. If testing slips, we tell Airbus early.

other_moves.move: 2045 review of the standing Joint Venture commitment
other_moves.detail: If Rolls-Royce does not commit in 2035, our commitment stands into 2045. The 2045 package brings the hold row against the withdraw row, including a column where Rolls-Royce commits. Mitchill prices: the equal-share effect wherever P&W is fitted on more new-type volume than Rolls-Royce; whether a GTF2 ready since 2036 still counts toward P&W's $2B share (low end: a new $2.00B share). Eddy re-tests whether an in-service GTF2 fleet can fold without reopening its type design, fleet support or parts flow. I withdraw if my conditions have lapsed and withdraw is not worse than hold in the columns we weight; the Board tests a withdrawal at a weighted item value of at least 0. Recorded, not booked.

decision.public_statement:
The bad news first. The GTF fleet still has work ahead of it, and that work comes before anything new: time on wing, parts, and our customers' aircraft back in the air. The GTF Advantage hot section keeps going into the fleet at shop visits, and we will keep doing it until the fleet is where it needs to be. Control what you can control.

GTF2 is in its last year of development and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Durability will be proven before entry into service, with every life-limited part at full life on day one. If the testing needs more time, the testing gets it. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We offer an engine to an airframer only where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. A Joint Venture spreads risk and investment; it does not share technology. Our gear and the GTF Advantage core come in as Pratt & Whitney modules, designed and built by Pratt & Whitney, and they stay ours. The partners hold equal shares, and each partner's own development work counts toward its own share. No partner buys the other's technology. GTF2 is what we bring. Rolls-Royce speaks for itself, and the Joint Venture forms only when both partners have committed.

We compete on standard terms, on the product and on the durability record. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates, and we will not get out ahead of them. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: commit; premium_b $0; overrides empty.

1. STARTING POINT. Eddy proposes hold / commit and Mitchill recommends the same, which was also my framing lean. Neither raises a binding veto against these orders. Mitchill's two binding vetoes are conditional: ground 3 on the Joint Venture terms and ground 4 on the words. I wrote the terms and the statement to stay clear of both, as tested below. Eddy's ground-1 veto on the commit is also conditional, on T1-T3 and T6, and none is triggered. Eddy's red-line flag (gear and core stay P&W modules) is met in the terms, so it is not a breach.

2. STRIKE. I strike rows C (cancel/hold) and D (cancel/commit). Neither is a binding veto ground: Mitchill objects on his return gate and his own 2035 cancel rule, and Eddy flags it as advice. The company red line strikes them. We do not exit a programme a customer has asked for [P-1342]. NGSA's code 7 includes P&W, and GTF2 is ready in 2036, before the 2037 EIS. Cancel would have to beat hold in every plausible column, and it trails in all four:
- C vs hold: -16.56 / -1.87 / -18.49 / -16.56;
- D vs A: -16.56 / -1.87 / -18.49 / -1.67.
Mitchill's 2035 rule says carry, and all three of his cancel conditions fail. Cancel books a $1.67B write-off (2 x 5/6) to save $0.33B, and the Board would veto it. 2035 is GTF2's last cancel window; I do not use it.

3. CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035]. Eddy's readiness check binds on me, and it passes:
- GTF2 ready 2036 against NGSA EIS 2037 (one year) and against fps 10-yr EIS 2045 in S3 (nine years);
- a Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2036 only because GTF2 folds in (2041 without it).
So T1 is the safety constraint on the commit: the 2037 engine is GTF2 as tested, the gear, core and hot section do not change before EIS, and Rolls-Royce content comes later as a block upgrade with its own campaign.

The 2035 re-test passes on the record: GTF2 shows ready 2036, unchanged since 2030, with no escape, no rising AOG and no ask to compress testing. Eddy's three round-1 triggers are not live, and parts and capacity pass.

The margin is thin, and I say so. One year nominal; -1.0 to -0.5 years after the company's derivative slip prior; about +0.25 years on Eddy's own record. My instinct says 2036 holds. My record says discount my dates: the GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087], though the H1 2025 date was met [PX-0078]. So the date gives and the testing never does. If it slips we tell Airbus early, and we slip and add testing; we do not cancel. The GTF2 ramp is gated on fleet spares, because the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

4. OPTIMISE, in $B, S1-S4, on the governing weights (Mitchill's): S1 0.65, S2 0.15, S3 0.10, S4 0.10.
- A hold/commit: -1.53 / -16.22 / +0.40 / +0.68; expected -3.32; worst -16.22 (S2).
- B hold/hold (default): -1.53 / -16.22 / +0.40 / -1.53; expected -3.54; worst -16.22.
- C cancel/hold: -18.09 in every column; expected -18.09.
- D cancel/commit: -18.09 / -18.09 / -18.09 / -0.99; expected -16.38.
Commit vs hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.21, worth +0.22 governing, +0.44 on my framing weights and +0.55 uniform. Its break-even p(S4) is 0. Commit adds no R&D: $1.67B spent plus 2035's $0.33B is $2.00B against P&W's $2B share, so the fold write-off is $0. It does not deepen the worst column. A is the best row on every weight set and weakly dominates B. My working is in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/dash-2050-phaseout/work/r2_decide_calc.py.

5. WHY I ADOPT MITCHILL'S WEIGHTS. The Board asked for one governing set, and I trust his numbers over my dates. I set S4 at 0.10, down from my framing 0.20. Rolls-Royce says it commits "once P&W's commitment is on the public record", and sealed orders mean it cannot see ours this round. That is timing, not refusal. S3 is 0.10: Boeing is "not there yet", gives no date, and I do not get ahead of an airframer [PX-0062]; that is also my incrementalism. S2 is 0.15: Airbus can change the code only this round, and a one-year margin is a selection risk. Against that, Airbus has contracted GTF supply for the A320 tail to about 2045.

6. MY TESTS.
- Safety and durability: pass, as in point 3.
- Visible demand: not in play. GTF2 is live on a code-7 selection on the public record, so neither launch nor launch_if_selected is on offer.
- Miss-a-cycle [PX-0071]: the S2 loss is $14.69B against S1, and no order prices it. Carrying GTF2 is what keeps us fitted and able to answer. Cancel would miss the cycle by our own hand.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: no doctrine-favoured order trails, so the premium is $0. My doctrine (hold before a Joint Venture; architecture loyalty) and the objective (Capitalise) differ, and the objective's order wins at no cost.
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms. 2035 outlay is $0.33B, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope and 0.8% of $40B debt. Commit adds $0, no stretch is used and the one-time stretch stays in reserve. Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669].
- Value, not share: standard terms, no concession, and no technology concession to win Rolls-Royce's commitment.
- Objective status: see objective_note.

7. JOINT VENTURE, ON DOCTRINE AND NOT ON MY RECORD. I have no evidence of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low), so I follow doctrine [P-1233][P-1875] and take Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test as my evidence. My round-1 condition is met on the public record: live NGSA, not in service until 2037, carries code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce. In round 1 Mitchill vetoed commit on ground 4 because it cost $2.00B in a column. It now costs nothing in any column, and its S4 value is its own condition, not booked upside.

On the terms, ground 3 is clear on Mitchill's test. Equal shares; each partner's solo spend counts to its own share; no cash or balancing payment; no carrying Rolls-Royce's share; modules at standard terms; no money before formation. The gear and core stay P&W-owned and P&W-built, with no licence or transfer. Our GTF risk-sharing partners keep their proportions behind P&W's half [P-1563][PX-0038].

My bias, declared: architecture loyalty says GTF2 should stand alone; the GTF is "the architecture of the future" [PX-0014]. The grid says the commitment costs nothing in any column, and data moves me. GTF2 is what we bring, not what we give up.

8. DOCTRINE RELIEF, DECLARED AT $0 PV COST. The round-1 shared-source relief for code 7 stands [P-0746][PX-0058][P-1292]. A Joint Venture engine is shared by design; doctrine allows that for risk and investment, never for technology [P-1233].

9. BOOKED NUMBER AND WHAT IS NOT COUNTED. Booked: -1.53 (S1). The +0.68 in S4 is not booked until Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record. The following are recorded and not booked:
- the value of a standing commitment into 2045;
- what a Joint Venture might give if Airbus dropped P&W (S2 and S4 together);
- a later fps on code 4;
- early GTF2 OE margin;
- the 2045 exposures. If a ready GTF2 does not count toward our share, the low end is a new $2.00B share. The equal-share effect costs us wherever P&W is fitted on more new-type volume than Rolls-Royce.
Those exposures are in our control, because a commitment can be withdrawn before formation. The 2045 package brings the withdraw row.

10. TIE-BREAKS. The fleet beats a new engine: the GTF2 ramp is gated on spares and integration is staffed off the fleet (T4, T5). "Miss a cycle" applies on visible demand, and NGSA is visible: carry GTF2. A rival's discount never moves the answer.

- His figures check against the brief: A -3.32, B -3.54, C -18.09, D -16.38; commit +0.22 weighted.
- I adopt his 2035 cancel rule (carry), his fold arithmetic ($0 write-off, no new R&D) and his cash by year: $0.33B a year for 2030-34, $1.67B to date, $2.00B at ready in 2036.

STATEMENT: PASS on full life.
- It says "due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch", "every life-limited part at full life on day one" and "if the testing needs more time, the testing gets it".
- My round-1 wording note is taken: "only where it can be ready by that airframe's entry into service".
- It names no NGSA EIS, no Joint Venture date, no Rolls-Royce commitment and no time-on-wing figure.
- "GTF2 is what we bring" is T1 in public words.
- The equal-shares line is a term in principle. It is Mitchill's ground, not mine.

GROUND 2, PARTS AND CAPACITY: PASS.
- The bulletin and brief show no live P&W escape, rising AOG or supply problem. "The fleet still has work ahead of it" refers to the Hot Section kit going in at shop visits: continuing work, not an escape. Contain first does not apply.
- No unconditional launch is ordered.
- The board does not model parts. I have no 2035 AOG count; my last figures are 10% AOG and about 30 pacing parts (June 2023) [PX-0120][PX-0123].
- P&W NB engines: 758 (2035), 752 (2036), 757 (2037), 612 (2038). GTF1 OE for the A320 tail runs to about 2045, so from 2037 GTF1, fleet spares and the GTF2 ramp draw on the same material. T5 gates the ramp on spares, the fleet comes first, and there is no capacity spike [P-1040].

NOT MY GROUNDS: cash, Joint Venture strategy, PV and the weights. Cancel is struck, and I took no view on it.

TRIGGERS I WILL RE-TEST IN 2040:
- GTF2 shown ready in 2036 with no slip;
- no quality escape or rising AOG without containment;
- T1 to T6 intact if the Joint Venture has formed;
- the GTF2 ramp running behind fleet spares.

Where I'm thin: one event, before the recall, and nothing of mine on a Joint Venture. The gates are seat doctrine and inference, not my record.

items.ground:
Every test that applies passes. I checked the figures against the round2.md section 3 grid in work/r2_review_calc.py.

(1) Unresolved objection: pass. Mitchill concurs. His two binding vetoes are conditional (ground 3 on the terms, ground 4 on the wording), and the submitted terms and statement trigger neither. Eddy concurs. His conditional ground-1 veto would apply to a merged or changed gear, core or hot section before 2041, re-planned testing, or a Joint Venture date. None of these is present, and T1-T6 are written into the private gates. Neither flags a red-line breach, and `overrides` is empty.

The +2.21 in S4 depends on the order's own condition, Rolls-Royce's commitment, so it is not booked upside. The booked number is -1.53 (S1). The statement claims no Rolls-Royce commitment, formed Joint Venture, Joint Venture date, partner money or time-on-wing figure.

(5) Durability first: pass. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2036 on the folded GTF2 (2030 + 6), one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS. Eddy passes ground 1: the re-test is on plan and none of his three triggers is live. He also passes ground 2: there is no live fleet problem, and the ramp is gated on spares. T1 keeps NGSA's engine as GTF2 as tested.

(6) Joint Venture: pass. The condition is met through code 7, and the weighted value is at least 0. The gear and GTF Advantage core enter as P&W-owned, P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer. With GTF2 live, the commit adds no new R&D, and the fold write-off is max(0, 2.00 - 2.00) = $0.

(7) Dividend and envelope: not applicable. The 2035 outlay is GTF2's last $0.33B (5.6% of about $6B), and the commit adds $0. No stretch is used.

(8) Declared premium: not needed; premium_b is 0.

Committed airframe and Premature exit do not apply, because no launch or cancel was ordered.

recommendations.text: Public statement: tighten one line. 'The partners hold equal shares, and each partner's own development work counts toward its own share' reads as terms already agreed. Rolls-Royce has not committed and has asked for terms that 'credit the technology we bring'. Present them as the terms P&W offers, for example 'on our terms, the partners would hold equal shares'. The rest of the statement passes: it claims no Rolls-Royce commitment, formed Joint Venture or Joint Venture date, gives GTF2's date as launch + 6 and names no NGSA EIS. This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.

Durability before EIS, and the calendar. The next Board round is 2045, after GTF2's 2036 ready year and NGSA's 2037 EIS, so no package will reach the Board before entry into service. Eddy's planned 2040 re-test also falls between rounds. Governance and Public Policy should therefore take the GTF2 durability report directly, at certification and again before NGSA's EIS. The report should show the severe-environment campaign complete, core and gear on test, and all life-limited parts at full life. The margin is one year nominal, and -1.0 to -0.5 years after the derivative slip prior. If GTF2 slips, the date gives and Airbus is told early. Under T1, no Rolls-Royce content enters the NGSA engine before 2041.

Joint Venture terms in any negotiation. The gear and the GTF Advantage core stay P&W-owned, P&W-built modules, with no licence or transfer. Keep Mitchill's ground-3 conditions: no balancing payment for technology, no carrying of Rolls-Royce's share, modules at standard terms, a P&W share not below half, and no money before formation. The GTF risk-sharing partners, who carried 49% of the 2023 charge, keep their proportions behind P&W's half. Book no partner money until it is signed. Bring the terms to the Finance Committee as a significant transaction before formation.

Hold the NGSA seat on readiness. S2, Airbus moving to code 5, is the low end of every row: -16.22, which is $14.69B below S1. No order prices it, and this is Airbus's last round to change the code. Hold the seat on the durability record and standard terms, with no launch-style discount or free upgrade; a rival's discount does not move the answer. Count no Joint Venture value in an S2 world.

Capital allocation after 2035. GTF2's development spend ends with this year's $0.33B, and the commit adds none. From 2036 the freed envelope follows the Board's order: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks as the fill-in. Any GTF2 production-ramp spend should be gated on fleet spares and shown against a buyback. No stretch has been used, and the one-time stretch stays in reserve.

Capitalise objective: say it plainly. The booked number is -1.53 (S1). The objective is met only in S3 (+0.40) and S4 (+0.68), a 0.20 chance on the governing weights. The Board asks for no spend and no premium to chase it. Long-term shareowner value is served by carrying GTF2 into service and keeping a commitment that costs nothing in any column.

board_review.note: The Board approves `jv_with_rr: commit` beside the carried GTF2. Against `hold` it is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.21, worth +0.22 on Mitchill's governing weights and never negative. It adds no R&D, and the fold write-off is $0. The Joint Venture condition is on the public record: live NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. Formed in 2035, the engine is ready in 2036 on the folded GTF2, ahead of the 2037 EIS, and Eddy passes durability and parts. Neither Mitchill nor Eddy vetoes, `overrides` is empty and the premium is $0. The Board endorses carrying GTF2. Three cautions: no Board round falls before the 2037 EIS, so Governance and Public Policy takes the durability report directly; the statement should present equal shares as our offer, not agreed terms; and the 2045 package must test the standing commitment. The Board believes this is right for shareowners over the long term.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development on its own clock. Entry into service no earlier than 2037, and only when it is mature. rolls_royce.rationale:
So, the decision. ORDERS: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (continue to ready in 2037), `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. Grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': +10.54 / -4.16 / +14.34 / +12.82 / +10.45 / +10.45 (S1-S6). This is my framing proposal unchanged. Both memos recommend it, McCabe co-signs and Watson raises no veto.

WEIGHTS. S1 0.60, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.05, on the ExCo rule because nothing new is on the record. McCabe confirms them. Submitted row +9.67 expected. Hold row 'UltraFan NB: hold' +9.44.

THE ONE BOARD ITEM: `jv_with_pw: commit`. Measured against 'UltraFan NB: hold', column by column: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00.
- Expected: +0.23. Stress tests: +0.11 with S4 halved (S1 0.65, S4 0.05), +0.23 with S2 doubled (S1 0.50, S2 0.20), and +0.11 on McCabe's guide-low set (S1 0.60, S2 0.20, S3 0.05, S4 0.05, S5 0.05, S6 0.05).
- Worst column: 0.00, against a $4B bill. The item is at least 0 under any weights, so there is no premium and no narrowbody premium.
- The submitted row's own worst column is -4.16 (S2, the unselected column). That comes from the Solo, and keeping still beats cancelling there.
- Partner alignment: P&W's commitment is NOT on the public record. P&W is silent on the Joint Venture, has its own GTF2 and competes on standard terms. NGSA, live and not yet in service with EIS 2037, carries code 7, which includes P&W. That is the Board's named alternative ground, and it passes.

WHY COMMIT NOW, THE TIMING. Under rules.md the Joint Venture forms in the first round in which both partners are committed.
- If P&W commits, its commitment becomes public only after this round.
- By 2045 our Solo is ready and fully spent.
- So 'we will commit once they do' would capture nothing. The +2.28 (our narrowbody money cut from $8.0B to $5.7B) exists only if both of us commit in 2035.
- Round 1's reason to wait was a Joint Venture with no airframe, at -4.00. That reason has gone.
This changes the line, not the strategy [RX-0098]: we go Solo, and partnership is the preference, not a need [RX-0118], on terms that credit the technology we bring [RX-0072]. The first commit is company doctrine applied to this board (inference), not my record. My record is thin on Joint Venture terms, so I take McCabe's test as the evidence on cash and the downside.

WHY CONTINUE THE SOLO. Keeping beats cancelling in every column, S2 included: -4.16 kept against -6.28 cancelled.
- The cancel item is -16.82 / -2.12 / -20.62 / -16.82 / -16.82 / -16.82, -15.73 expected.
- Its worst column, -20.62, is far beyond its own $5.71B write-off.
- A cancel would write off $5.71B to save $2.29B.
- It breaks the rule against cancelling a programme a live airframe flies [R-1573]. NGSA's code 7 includes RR, and UltraFan meets its EIS.
This is the last round a cancel is possible, and NGSA's code is fixed after it. Struck.

STRUCK WIDEBODY ITEMS.
- `t1000_upgrade: launch`. Item -6.03 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.03 / -5.88 / -5.88, -6.01 expected. Its worst column is three times its $2B bill, and the gap is beyond the $3B cap. It breaks the red line of no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (to 2037). McCabe withholds her co-signature, and that is binding.
- `ultrafan_wb: launch`. Item -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6, -8.80 expected, far beyond the $1B sub-cap. No Re-engine is on the record. It breaks the red line against UltraFan WB beside the Solo unless both are selected. McCabe's veto is binding.
Both items carry the $5B strain. The grid already includes it, and I do not deduct it again. My profile's default for the upgrade ('regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]) gives way to the strain the live Solo fixes on this board.

THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN NARROWBODY AND WIDEBODY, STATED PLAINLY.
- What $8.0B of narrowbody money buys: NB share of 29.9% in 2045 and 32.3% in 2050 (7.5% in S2, 49.7% in S3).
- The price on the widebody side: with a narrowbody programme on the record, any widebody programme pays $5B of strain for the life of the Solo, because the cancel that would remove it is closed.
- The upgrade would buy 4.8 pp of widebody share (to 60.0% in 2050) for $6.01B, about $1.25B a point. We decline it.
- UltraFan WB would reach 64.8% only in S5-S6, at -6.96 there.
- The core holds at 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042 in every column, 5.2 pp above the 50% line, defended by time on wing inside the envelope.

NARROWBODY MONEY AND THE CAPITAL FRAME (McCabe).
- $5.71B spent to date ($8B x 5/7).
- About $2.29B still to go to 2037: about $1.14B, or £0.84bn, a year at 1.36 $/£, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance.
- The $4B narrowbody bound is NOT met: $8.0B is committed, or $5.7B only in S4 with the commit, still $1.7B over. We accepted that breach on a selection in 2030, and I state it openly.
- Free cash flow funds it: no equity, no borrowing, the 30-40% payout intact, redeployed inside the R&D envelope or the envelope rebased openly through the Board.

VETO CHECKS.
- McCabe co-signs the commit. At her test it is above 0 with no column below 0. At her veto check it needs no equity and no leverage, and the payout stays intact.
- Her binding vetoes are all respected, and none of these items is in the orders: the upgrade, UltraFan WB, and any concession or inducement packaged with the commit. The commit is on standard terms.
- Watson: no Civil veto. Ready by EIS for the commit passes only through the fold. Formation + 6 = 2041 would miss NGSA's 2037 EIS. The folded Solo is ready in 2037 at the latest, at zero margin. In the other five columns nothing forms and the Solo stands at 2037.
His conditions are all met:
- (1) the support plan is restated with partner MRO shops by 2032, spares, repair and suppliers by 2035, and the EIS support team and early-service intervention by 2036 (private move);
- (2) the gearbox wording now reads 'narrowbody gearbox sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test (2028) before any launch';
- (3) if the Joint Venture forms, the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs, with no shortening;
- (4) 'we will commit once they do' is replaced, not kept alongside;
- (5) no Joint Venture date, and no internal wording in public moves.

RED-LINE FLAGS. McCabe flagged the upgrade, UltraFan WB and a cancel. Watson flagged the upgrade and UltraFan WB. I confirm all of them, and none is in the orders. No flag stands, and `overrides` is empty.

MATURITY. No test setback is on the record, and ready 2037 stands on the full seven years. Zero margin is a pass with a note. I cite no UltraFan 30 ground-test result that neither of us can source: the report goes to the Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Actually, I've seen this movie before on Trent 1000 dates. I discount my own dates and lean on Rob for them. The public line says 'no earlier than 2037, and only when it is mature'.

OFF-GRID RISK AND EXIT. A standing commitment outlives this round. If P&W commits only in 2045, the Joint Venture forms on a finished, fully spent engine and only equalises shares. McCabe books that at 0 with an unpriced downside. Control: in 2045 we test `withdraw` against commit column by column and bring it to the Board unless commit pays. No options management [RX-0051]: once a commitment has no use, it goes.

Her binding withheld co-signatures on the upgrade and UltraFan WB are respected, and so is her conditional veto on any concession packaged with the commit: standard terms only. Rob passes Ready by EIS for the Solo, at zero margin with a note, and for the Joint Venture only through the fold, since formation + 6 = 2041 misses NGSA. He raises no Civil veto. I confirm and strike his red-line flags on the upgrade and UltraFan WB. His lean to partnership agrees with the commit. On dates I defer to him.

recommendations.text: Continue UltraFan NB and bring no cancel. NGSA flies it, and the grid shows the Solo is worth keeping in every column, including S2 where Airbus drops us (-4.16 kept against -6.28 cancelled). After this round NGSA's code is fixed, because its EIS (2037) comes before the 2045 round, so S2 is the last selection risk. The protection against it is maturity and support delivered on time, not price. Standard terms and no concessions.

Joint Venture: weigh a commit this round, and set out the timing in `rationale`. The grid's saving (+2.28 in S4, our narrowbody money cut from $8.0B to $5.7B) exists only if both partners commit in the same round. P&W's commitment would become public only after this round, and by 2045 the Solo is ready and fully spent, so 'commit once they do' would then capture nothing (inference from rules.md). If the ExCo commits, it needs McCabe's co-signature and Watson's date check. The public line should change from 'we will commit once they do' to a standing commitment on terms that credit our technology, with no date. The ExCo should also plan the exit: put `withdraw` to us in 2045 if P&W has not committed and a later formation would only equalise shares on a finished engine (inference). If the ExCo holds, that is its call, and we will not press it.

Maturity, support and capacity. Watson's maturity watch should report the 2028 UltraFan 30 ground test and gearbox sizing, with the support move's wording corrected to 'proven before any launch', as we asked in round 1. It should also confirm the support milestones (partner MRO shops by 2032; spares, repair technology and suppliers by 2035; an EIS support team by 2036). Airbus certifies 'in sequence as each one matures', and GTF2 is ready in 2036, so we will be judged on maturity on day one, not on the date. The narrowbody ramp (257 engines in 2040, about 960-1,200 a year from 2044) is about five times our widebody volume. It needs partner MRO and capacity at high-performing suppliers, and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee should see the readiness plan.

The widebody core. No widebody programme this round. While a narrowbody programme is on the record, the $5B strain is permanent: only a cancel before the engine is ready removes it, and that cancel is closed to us. Any later upgrade or UltraFan WB therefore carries the strain. RR widebody share holds at 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042 in every column, above 50%, so the widebody franchise test does not trigger. Defend the franchise through time on wing inside the envelope. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the record, bring a widebody case to us in 2045, with the strain counted and any shortfall declared within the caps. Watch S5, where the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 30.2% of widebody airframes by 2050.

The capital frame and the narrowbody bound. McCabe should report narrowbody spend to date ($5.71B at 2035), the remainder to 2037 (about $2.29B, roughly £0.84bn a year) and the objective's status ($8.0B against the $4B bound: not met; $5.7B only in S4 with a commit). She should confirm that it is funded from free cash flow inside a redeployed or openly rebased R&D envelope, with no equity, no leverage for distributions, and the 30-40% payout untouched. Any guidance change comes through this Board before release.

Disclosure. Keep the statement short and conditional: UltraFan NB on its own clock, no date earlier than 2037, and nothing on Airbus's, Boeing's or P&W's dates or programmes. Give no Joint Venture date: formation plus 6 is 2041, and anything earlier exists only through a folded programme, which we do not publish. 'We won't do anything not profitable' stands.

(2) For each row A-E: the item value against its hold row, column by column; the expected gain; and the worst column against the item's own bill. My figures:

frame.asks_ops:
Rob, I need eight things. Your maturity watch goes to the Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee [RG-0049].

(1) Maturity watch. What was the result of the 2028 UltraFan 30 ground test? Was narrowbody gearbox sizing proven? Correct the support wording to 'proven before any launch', as you and the Board asked. Has any test setback turned zero margin against NGSA's 2037 EIS into compressed maturity in fact? If so, say it now. The choice is continue or cancel, not move the date.

(2) Readiness. UltraFan NB ready 2037 against NGSA 2037 (zero margin): still a pass? Against an fps 10-yr EIS of 2045 in S3, eight years in hand.

(3) Joint Venture: Ready by EIS for an unconditional commit. If it forms in 2035, formation + 6 is 2041 and misses NGSA. It is ready in 2037 or earlier only through our folded UltraFan, or through a partner programme that is further along. Pass or fail? Confirm that no Joint Venture date is disclosed, and that the public line stays consistent with a commit.

(4) The support plan against its dates. Partner MRO shops on the Singapore model by 2032: in place? Spares, repair technology and suppliers by 2035: on track? EIS support team and early-service intervention by 2036? With a Joint Venture, how much of the gap do P&W's GTF shop network and gearbox close?

(5) Capacity. Give me your advice on the narrowbody ramp: 7 engines (2037), 257 (2040), 487 (2041), 713 (2042), about 960-1,200 a year from 2044. That is about five times our 188-197 widebody engines a year. I need the high-performing suppliers and partner MRO needed, and the supplier risk [RX-0279, RX-0286].

(6) Strain and load. Confirm $0 strain under A and B, and that any upgrade or UltraFan WB now costs $5B for the life of the Solo. Confirm the engineering can carry the Solo to 2037, and a Joint Venture integration if it forms, beside Trent time-on-wing work.

(7) Widebody. Our share against the 50% line in 2040, 2045 and 2050 for each row: 58.0% / 55.2% / 55.2% in every column under A and B, 60.0% with the upgrade. Does any column threaten the franchise? Watch S5, where the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 30.2% of widebody airframes by 2050. What does time on wing inside the envelope protect?

(8) Your Civil veto check, binding or not, on each row. Flag any red-line breach you see.
frame.initial_lean:
So, my proposal.

ORDERS: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (continue to ready in 2037), `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. Grid row: 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV'.

THE NUMBERS:
- Row: +10.54 / -4.16 / +14.34 / +12.82 / +10.45 / +10.45, +9.67 expected.
- Commit item: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00, +0.23 expected, worst column 0.00.
- It is the PV-best plan in every column, so the premium is $0.
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold (0.60). Best plan there is a tie between A and B at +10.54.

WHY CONTINUE. NGSA flies our engine. Keeping it beats cancelling in every column, S2 included. A cancel would write off $5.71B to save $2.29B. We don't cancel what an airframer flies [R-1573].

WHY COMMIT NOW. Partnership is our preference, not a need [RX-0118]. It derisks, and we bring the technology [RX-0072]. The round-1 reason to wait, a Joint Venture with no airframe (-4.00), has gone. NGSA is live on code 7, which includes P&W. Our engine is two years from ready, and that is our leverage. The saving exists only if both of us commit in the same round, and 'once they do' would capture nothing in 2045. The strategy has not changed [RX-0098]: we go Solo, and we prefer a partner. Only the line changes, from 'we will commit once they do' to a standing commitment on terms that credit our technology. No date. If P&W has not come to the table by 2045, the commitment has no use, and we bring a `withdraw` to the Board then [RX-0051, RX-0050]. The first-commit call is doctrine applied to this board (inference), not my record.

CONDITIONS. Helen's co-signature, and Rob's pass on the Joint Venture's readiness through the fold and on the UltraFan maturity watch. If either is withheld, I fall back to A, all hold. That costs $0.23B expected and $0 in five of six columns.

TRADE-OFF, STATED PLAINLY:
- Narrowbody entry: 29.9% in 2045, 32.3% in 2050.
- The price: $8.0B against the $4B bound ($5.7B only if P&W joins now).
- The widebody side: with the Solo on the record, any widebody programme pays the $5B strain for life. The upgrade would lift us to 60% but costs $6.0B, so we decline it.
- The core holds at 55.2%, above 50%, through time on wing.

OTHER MOVES: the maturity watch report; support milestones to 2036; the capacity plan for the ramp; standard terms, no concessions; the capital frame from free cash flow.

DRAFT PUBLIC LINE: 'So, UltraFan for the narrowbody is on its own clock, entry into service no earlier than 2037. Our preference is partnership: Rolls-Royce has made a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. We don't need it for capability. Widebody is our core, and our focus there stays on time on wing. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.'
