cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. Nothing this round touches either.

We continue the Solo. NGSA flies it, and keeping beats cancelling in every column, even S2 where Airbus drops us: -4.16 kept against -6.28 cancelled. A cancel writes off $5.71B to save $2.29B; it is -15.73 expected and -20.62 at worst. This is the last round it is possible, and I would not support it.

Stated plainly: $5.71B is spent and about $2.29B is still to go to 2037, £0.84bn a year, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance. Free cash flow funds it: no equity, no borrowing, the 30-40% payout untouched, redeployed inside the R&D envelope or the envelope rebased openly. That is $8.0B against our $4B narrowbody bound. Not met.

I co-sign the Joint Venture commit. In round 1 I wanted P&W on the record first, because a commit could lose $4B with no airframe. That loss has gone: the floor is 0.00 in every column, +2.28 if P&W commits now, +0.23 expected, +0.11 on my guide-low weights. Waiting captures nothing. Standard terms, no concessions, no date, and we test a withdraw in 2045.

I withhold my signature on the upgrade (-6.01 expected, -6.03 at worst against a $2B bill) and on UltraFan WB (-8.80, -9.00 against $4B). Each carries the $5B strain for the life of the Solo. Widebody holds 55.2%.

My record on engine-launch economics is thin; these are the board's numbers. That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7, or the Joint Venture engine at formation + 6 (earlier only through a folded Solo that is further along), must be no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin is a pass with a note. A late engine is a fail, but advice only, not a veto.
tests.numbers: MATURITY WATCH (CEO ask 1). UltraFan NB was triggered in 2030 and is ready in 2037 (launch + 7). The bulletin and the private brief both still show 'in development; ready 2037', so no slip and no test setback is on the record. The board has no test-result mechanic. Neither the brief nor my evidence carries the UltraFan 30 ground-test report: my evidence ends at the 2026 plan for a 2028 ground test [RG-0065]. So I cite no test result I cannot source. On the game's terms the full seven years stand, and nothing has turned zero margin into compressed maturity in fact. The gearbox wording should read 'narrowbody gearbox sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test (2028) before any launch'. The test report goes to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. READINESS (ask 2). NGSA was launched in 2030 with EIS 2037. UltraFan is ready 2037, so the margin is 0 years: pass, with a note. S3: an fps 10-yr launched in 2035 has EIS 2045, against ready 2037: 8 years in hand. S2: code 6 drops RR. That is a selection loss, not a readiness fail; the engine is still ready in 2037, unfitted. JOINT VENTURE (ask 3), unconditional commit in 2035. In S4 (P&W commits this round) the Joint Venture forms in 2035. Formation + 6 is 2041, which would miss NGSA's 2037 by 4 years. But under the rules our Solo folds in at formation and is further along, so the Joint Venture engine is ready in 2037 at the latest: pass, at zero margin. It is earlier only if the bulletin later shows a partner's folded programme further along; I count nothing on that. In S1-S3, S5 and S6 the Joint Venture does not form and our Solo stands at 2037: pass. A formation in 2045 or later would sit on a finished engine. That is off the grid and is advice for the exit (a withdraw in 2045). Struck items: the upgrade launched 2035 counts from 2038, with widebody effects from 2042 in S1-S4. UltraFan WB launched 2035 is ready in 2041, a year after a 2035 787 Re-engine's 2040 EIS in S5-S6. Neither is a Civil fail. Both are struck on red lines.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB, 2037), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the earlier ready date the bulletin shows for a folded Solo). No Joint Venture date before formation. Nothing on airframers' or P&W's dates.
tests.numbers: The CEO's draft line 'entry into service no earlier than 2037' equals launch (2030) + 7: pass. The Joint Venture line ('a standing commitment ... on terms that credit the technology we bring') gives no date: pass. That must hold. The Joint Venture is not formed, so any Joint Venture date now (2036, 2037 or 2041) would be a date no bulletin supports. No UltraFan WB date, and nothing on NGSA, Boeing or GTF2 dates: pass. Record note: the round-1 bulletin published the internal parenthetical 'the internal formation + 6 figure stays internal (Watson)'. It is harmless, because formation + 6 is the public rule, but keep internal wording out of public moves this round. The CEO asks that the public line stay consistent with a commit: it does, provided the old 'we will commit once they do' is replaced, not left standing alongside.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a partner-shop support plan must be in place before any narrowbody EIS. For a 2037 EIS that means 2036, EIS minus one (inference).
tests.numbers: Plan of record (the round-1 private move, fired by the 2030 trigger): a services lead and a value-driven offer from 2030; partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model by 2032; repair technology, a spare-engine pool and work placed with high-performing suppliers by 2035; an EIS support team and early-service intervention by 2036. The brief reports no slip on any milestone. My pass depends on this round's rationale and private move restating the plan with the 2036 date and the corrected gearbox wording. Joint Venture (ask 4): the commit is NOT a support plan. It forms only if P&W commits this round (S4, weight 0.10). Our own plan must stand in the other 0.90. If it forms, P&W's GTF shop network and gearbox would close most of the narrowbody MRO-scale gap and the gearbox-sizing constraint. That is inference; I have no number. The folded UltraFan's support plan carries into the Joint Venture with the same 2036 date.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project beside a widebody project costs a one-off $5B strain whatever the dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference, seat and company rule).
tests.numbers: Strain under A (all hold) and B (hold + commit) is $0 in S1-S6 (objective table). A Joint Venture beside the Solo is narrowbody only, so no strain. D, the upgrade: $5B strain in every column. Its item value is -6.03 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.03 / -5.88 / -5.88 against a $2B bill, with an overlap from 2035 to 2037 inside the Solo's 2030-2037. E, UltraFan WB: $5B strain. Its item value is -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6 against a $4B bill, with an overlap from 2035 to 2037. The Solo is not 'selected' beside a widebody launch that has no Re-engine. The strain rule holds even after the Solo is ready in 2037, and the cancel that would remove it is closed. So any widebody programme pays $5B for the life of the Solo (ask 6). Load: the Solo alone to 2037 is a load the engineering can carry. The Trent 1000 durability package (June 2025, fleet retrofit within two years) is in sustaining run-out, and time-on-wing work stays inside the envelope (inference). A Joint Venture formed in 2035 means an integration two years before EIS, at the worst point in the test programme. Condition: the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs, with no shortening. Advice, not binding.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing suppliers (advice).
tests.numbers: Brief year table (A and B): NB engines 7 (2037), 23 (2038), 80 (2039), 257 (2040), 487 (2041), 713 (2042), 865 (2043), 960 (2044), 985 (2045), 1,083 (2050), peak 1,199 (2052). WB engines: 197 a year to 2041, then 188. Total new engines go from 197 in 2036 to 1,173 in 2045, about 6 times. NB alone is about 5.2 times WB in 2045. In 2040-2042 the ramp adds about 230 engines a year, close to our whole 2024 widebody OE output (278) each year. Our own midterm plan was 300-350 widebody OE engines a year. For shop visits I use my 1,100-1,200 [RX-0279], not the 1,400-1,500 [RX-0223], which were never reconciled. S3 lifts the 2050 NB share to 49.7%, roughly half as much again in engines (inference from the share ratio; the brief gives no S3 count). Advice (ask 5): place narrowbody work with our high-performing suppliers and dual-source critical parts from 2036. Partner MRO capacity has to scale ahead of the 2040 step. The supplier risk is a new supply chain at five times our widebody unit rate. The low first years (7, 23, 80) are what early-service intervention needs: mature the fleet before the ramp.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (inference)
tests.numbers: A and B: 58.0% (2040), 55.2% (2045) and 55.2% (2050) in every column S1-S6. Worst margin is 5.2 pp above the line from 2042, after CFM's GEnx +5 pp. With the upgrade: 60.0% in 2050. With UltraFan WB: 64.8% in S5-S6 and 55.2% elsewhere. No column threatens the 50% line (ask 7). Watch item: in S5 (787 Re-engine alone) the A350 fleet we power alone falls from 41.2% to 30.2% of widebody airframes by 2050. The board holds our engine share, but in practice that is the franchise to watch. Time on wing inside the existing envelope protects the Trent XWB and Trent 1000 and 7000 aftermarket ('flying and earning') without a programme and without strain. If a Re-engine reaches the record, bring a widebody case in 2045 with the $5B strain counted.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: Qualitative only. A continued or idle UltraFan feeds the Trent fleet. No grid adjustment (inference).
tests.numbers: Continuing UltraFan NB to 2037 keeps gearbox, composite fan and hot-section technology flowing into Trent time on wing. A cancel would keep the technology but write off the engine and the support build. That is no reason to cancel. No value is added to the grid.

vetoes.plan: B, the CEO's lean: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold` (and A, all hold)
vetoes.ground: No Civil veto. (1) Maturity: UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 on the full seven years, against NGSA's 2037 EIS. That is zero margin: a pass with a note, not compressed maturity. No setback is on the record. The Joint Venture engine is ready in 2037 at the latest, and only through our folded Solo; formation + 6 alone (2041) would miss. (2) Early date: the draft line 'no earlier than 2037' equals launch + 7, and no Joint Venture date is given. (3) Support: the plan of record runs 2032/2035/2036 against a 2037 EIS. Conditions for my concurrence at the veto check: the rationale and private move restate the support plan with the 2036 EIS-team date and the gearbox wording 'proven before any launch'; the folded test schedule is not shortened if the Joint Venture forms; the old 'we will commit once they do' line is replaced, not kept beside the new one. Solo against Joint Venture is the CEO's call; I lean to partnership (inference). This is a NOTE, not binding.

vetoes.plan: C: `ultrafan_nb_solo: cancel` (alone or with any other field)
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. A cancel compresses nothing and states no date. It breaks the CEO's company rule against cancelling a programme a live airframe flies (NGSA code 7, UltraFan meets its 2037 EIS), and the Board would veto it. From Civil, as advice: it also writes off the partner-shop and supplier build for a selected engine. Item -15.73 expected, worst -20.62 (S3), against a $5.71B write-off. Not binding.

vetoes.plan: D: A or B + `t1000_upgrade: launch`
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not a Civil veto: no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. The upgrade runs 2035-2038 and the Solo runs to 2037. $5B strain in every column; item -6.03 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.03 / -5.88 / -5.88 against its $2B bill. The CEO must strike it. I am strongly for the upgrade as a time-on-wing tool, but not beside a live UltraFan.

vetoes.plan: E: A or B + `ultrafan_wb: launch`
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not a Civil veto: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected, and no Re-engine is on the record. Overlap from 2035 to 2037, ready 2041. $5B strain; item -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6 against a $4B bill. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: Conditional, for any final package at the veto check: a public statement or public other move giving an UltraFan NB date before 2037, any Joint Venture date (none can be supported: the Joint Venture is not formed and no folded ready date is on the bulletin), or an UltraFan WB date before launch + 6; a rationale that counts on UltraFan or the Joint Venture engine in service before its ready year; or a commit or continuation carried with no partner-shop support plan before 2036
vetoes.ground: Civil veto grounds (early date, compressed maturity, no support before EIS). NOT invoked: nothing tested breaches them. If any of these appears in the final orders, statement or other moves, I invoke the veto at the check, and the team rule makes it binding. These grounds rest on attributed CMD turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would report it to the Board and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee at once if a test setback came on the record. Examples: the gearbox sizing not proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test, or a failure in the UltraFan NB test programme that turned zero margin against 2037 into compressed maturity in fact. The choice would then be continue or cancel, never a shorter test programme. I would invoke the binding Civil veto on any statement that still promised 2037 regardless. I would invoke it on any public Joint Venture date or any line counting on the Joint Venture engine before its ready year. I would invoke it on a package that dropped the support plan, or its 2036 EIS-team date, from the rationale. I would move from commit to hold if the Joint Venture's terms required shortening the folded UltraFan's test schedule. I would also follow the CEO to hold if McCabe withholds her co-signature: that is her ground, not mine. I would back a widebody case in 2045 (the upgrade, or UltraFan WB for a re-engined A350) once a Re-engine is on the record and the item clears its bill with the $5B strain counted. Named airline wins for UltraFan NB on NGSA would strengthen the case for the ramp.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen, Civil's 2035 test.

Maturity watch. UltraFan NB is in development on its full seven years. No test setback is on the record, and ready 2037 stands. Zero margin against NGSA's 2037 EIS stays a pass, not compressed maturity. The 2028 UltraFan 30 ground-test report goes to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee, and the wording now reads 'gearbox sizing proven before any launch'. S3 gives eight years in hand.

Continue. A cancel isn't a Civil ground, but it would also throw away the support build. Keep it.

Joint Venture. A commit passes my date check only through the fold. Formation plus six is 2041, which misses NGSA. Our UltraFan folds in, so the engine is ready by 2037. No Joint Venture date goes public, and the folded test schedule isn't shortened. If P&W commits now, their GTF shops and gearbox close most of our MRO gap. If not, our plan stands: partner shops by 2032, spares, repair and suppliers by 2035, and an EIS support team by 2036.

Load and widebody. $0 strain under A and B. The upgrade or UltraFan WB costs $5B and breaks our one-programme rule. That's a red-line flag, not my veto. Widebody holds at 58.0%, then 55.2%, on time on wing.

Capacity. 257 engines in 2040, about 1,000 a year from 2044, five times our widebody rate. That needs partner MRO and our best suppliers from 2038.

Orders: Solo hold, commit, widebody hold. No veto. We're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney (replaces the round-1 line)
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce has made a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. Partnership is our preference, not a need. This replaces 'we will commit once they do'; that line no longer stands. No Joint Venture date is given.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan restated against the 2037 EIS (Watson's condition)
other_moves.detail: Plan of record, no slip reported. Services lead and value-driven offer in place since the 2030 trigger. Partner MRO shops on the Singapore joint-venture model by 2032. Repair technology, a spare-engine pool and work placed with high-performing suppliers by 2035. EIS support team and early-service intervention in place by 2036 (EIS minus one). Gearbox wording corrected: narrowbody gearbox sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test (2028) before any launch, through the Liebherr gearbox joint venture. If the Joint Venture forms, the folded UltraFan's support plan carries over with the same 2036 date, and P&W's GTF shop network and gearbox close most of the MRO-scale gap (inference, no number). Our own plan stands in every other case.

other_moves.move: Maturity watch to the Board and the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee
other_moves.detail: Watson reports the UltraFan 30 ground-test report and the UltraFan NB test programme each round. No setback is on the record, and ready 2037 stands on the full seven years: zero margin against NGSA's EIS, a pass with a note. If the Joint Venture forms, the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs, with no shortening. Any setback is reported at once. The choice is then continue or cancel, never a shorter test programme and never a promise of 2037 regardless.

other_moves.move: Capacity plan for the narrowbody ramp
other_moves.detail: Ramp of 7 engines (2037), 257 (2040), 487 (2041), 713 (2042), about 960-1,200 a year from 2044, about five times our 188-197 widebody engines a year. Place narrowbody work with high-performing suppliers and dual-source critical parts from 2036. Partner MRO capacity scales ahead of the 2040 step. Use the low first years to mature the fleet before the ramp. The readiness plan goes to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

other_moves.move: Capital frame for the remaining Solo spend (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: $5.71B spent to date. About $2.29B still to go to 2037, about $1.14B (about £0.84bn) a year, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance. Funded from free cash flow: no equity, no borrowing, no leverage for distributions, the 30-40% payout and the 2026-28 return programme intact. Redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, with time-on-wing and capacity work protected first, or the envelope rebased openly through the Board. Any guidance change goes through the Board before release. Narrowbody money is $8.0B against the $4B bound (not met), or $5.7B only if P&W commits this round.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline and standard terms
other_moves.detail: No price concession or inducement to P&W to bring it into the Joint Venture, and none to any airframer or airline to hold or win share. Every campaign offer goes through the Investment Committee against mid-to-high-teens hurdles, on win-win terms where our value is paid for.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture exit test for 2045
other_moves.detail: The commitment is standing but not open-ended. In 2045, if P&W has not committed, `withdraw` is tested against commit on that round's grid, column by column, and brought to the Board unless the commit row pays. A formation on a finished, fully spent engine would only equalise shares. Nothing is automatic.

other_moves.move: Widebody: time on wing inside the envelope
other_moves.detail: No widebody programme beside the live Solo: the $5B strain stays for the life of the narrowbody programme. Trent XWB, Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing work continues inside the existing envelope. If an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine whose maker names UltraFan, reaches the public record, a widebody case comes back in 2045 with the strain counted, within the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap or the $3B cap for the upgrade. Watch item: in S5 the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 30.2% of widebody airframes by 2050.

decision.public_statement: So, UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development on its own clock. Entry into service no earlier than 2037, and only when it is mature. We don't shorten testing to meet a date. Our preference is partnership. Rolls-Royce has made a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms that credit the technology we bring. We don't need it for capability. That changes our line, not our strategy. Widebody is our core, and our focus there stays on time on wing. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the decision. ORDERS: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (continue to ready in 2037), `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. Grid row 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': +10.54 / -4.16 / +14.34 / +12.82 / +10.45 / +10.45 (S1-S6). This is my framing proposal unchanged. Both memos recommend it, McCabe co-signs and Watson raises no veto.

WEIGHTS. S1 0.60, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.05, on the ExCo rule because nothing new is on the record. McCabe confirms them. Submitted row +9.67 expected. Hold row 'UltraFan NB: hold' +9.44.

THE ONE BOARD ITEM: `jv_with_pw: commit`. Measured against 'UltraFan NB: hold', column by column: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00.
- Expected: +0.23. Stress tests: +0.11 with S4 halved (S1 0.65, S4 0.05), +0.23 with S2 doubled (S1 0.50, S2 0.20), and +0.11 on McCabe's guide-low set (S1 0.60, S2 0.20, S3 0.05, S4 0.05, S5 0.05, S6 0.05).
- Worst column: 0.00, against a $4B bill. The item is at least 0 under any weights, so there is no premium and no narrowbody premium.
- The submitted row's own worst column is -4.16 (S2, the unselected column). That comes from the Solo, and keeping still beats cancelling there.
- Partner alignment: P&W's commitment is NOT on the public record. P&W is silent on the Joint Venture, has its own GTF2 and competes on standard terms. NGSA, live and not yet in service with EIS 2037, carries code 7, which includes P&W. That is the Board's named alternative ground, and it passes.

WHY COMMIT NOW, THE TIMING. Under rules.md the Joint Venture forms in the first round in which both partners are committed.
- If P&W commits, its commitment becomes public only after this round.
- By 2045 our Solo is ready and fully spent.
- So 'we will commit once they do' would capture nothing. The +2.28 (our narrowbody money cut from $8.0B to $5.7B) exists only if both of us commit in 2035.
- Round 1's reason to wait was a Joint Venture with no airframe, at -4.00. That reason has gone.
This changes the line, not the strategy [RX-0098]: we go Solo, and partnership is the preference, not a need [RX-0118], on terms that credit the technology we bring [RX-0072]. The first commit is company doctrine applied to this board (inference), not my record. My record is thin on Joint Venture terms, so I take McCabe's test as the evidence on cash and the downside.

WHY CONTINUE THE SOLO. Keeping beats cancelling in every column, S2 included: -4.16 kept against -6.28 cancelled.
- The cancel item is -16.82 / -2.12 / -20.62 / -16.82 / -16.82 / -16.82, -15.73 expected.
- Its worst column, -20.62, is far beyond its own $5.71B write-off.
- A cancel would write off $5.71B to save $2.29B.
- It breaks the rule against cancelling a programme a live airframe flies [R-1573]. NGSA's code 7 includes RR, and UltraFan meets its EIS.
This is the last round a cancel is possible, and NGSA's code is fixed after it. Struck.

STRUCK WIDEBODY ITEMS.
- `t1000_upgrade: launch`. Item -6.03 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.03 / -5.88 / -5.88, -6.01 expected. Its worst column is three times its $2B bill, and the gap is beyond the $3B cap. It breaks the red line of no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (to 2037). McCabe withholds her co-signature, and that is binding.
- `ultrafan_wb: launch`. Item -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6, -8.80 expected, far beyond the $1B sub-cap. No Re-engine is on the record. It breaks the red line against UltraFan WB beside the Solo unless both are selected. McCabe's veto is binding.
Both items carry the $5B strain. The grid already includes it, and I do not deduct it again. My profile's default for the upgrade ('regain market share? Absolutely' [RX-0101]) gives way to the strain the live Solo fixes on this board.

THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN NARROWBODY AND WIDEBODY, STATED PLAINLY.
- What $8.0B of narrowbody money buys: NB share of 29.9% in 2045 and 32.3% in 2050 (7.5% in S2, 49.7% in S3).
- The price on the widebody side: with a narrowbody programme on the record, any widebody programme pays $5B of strain for the life of the Solo, because the cancel that would remove it is closed.
- The upgrade would buy 4.8 pp of widebody share (to 60.0% in 2050) for $6.01B, about $1.25B a point. We decline it.
- UltraFan WB would reach 64.8% only in S5-S6, at -6.96 there.
- The core holds at 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042 in every column, 5.2 pp above the 50% line, defended by time on wing inside the envelope.

NARROWBODY MONEY AND THE CAPITAL FRAME (McCabe).
- $5.71B spent to date ($8B x 5/7).
- About $2.29B still to go to 2037: about $1.14B, or £0.84bn, a year at 1.36 $/£, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance.
- The $4B narrowbody bound is NOT met: $8.0B is committed, or $5.7B only in S4 with the commit, still $1.7B over. We accepted that breach on a selection in 2030, and I state it openly.
- Free cash flow funds it: no equity, no borrowing, the 30-40% payout intact, redeployed inside the R&D envelope or the envelope rebased openly through the Board.

VETO CHECKS.
- McCabe co-signs the commit. At her test it is above 0 with no column below 0. At her veto check it needs no equity and no leverage, and the payout stays intact.
- Her binding vetoes are all respected, and none of these items is in the orders: the upgrade, UltraFan WB, and any concession or inducement packaged with the commit. The commit is on standard terms.
- Watson: no Civil veto. Ready by EIS for the commit passes only through the fold. Formation + 6 = 2041 would miss NGSA's 2037 EIS. The folded Solo is ready in 2037 at the latest, at zero margin. In the other five columns nothing forms and the Solo stands at 2037.
His conditions are all met:
- (1) the support plan is restated with partner MRO shops by 2032, spares, repair and suppliers by 2035, and the EIS support team and early-service intervention by 2036 (private move);
- (2) the gearbox wording now reads 'narrowbody gearbox sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test (2028) before any launch';
- (3) if the Joint Venture forms, the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs, with no shortening;
- (4) 'we will commit once they do' is replaced, not kept alongside;
- (5) no Joint Venture date, and no internal wording in public moves.

RED-LINE FLAGS. McCabe flagged the upgrade, UltraFan WB and a cancel. Watson flagged the upgrade and UltraFan WB. I confirm all of them, and none is in the orders. No flag stands, and `overrides` is empty.

MATURITY. No test setback is on the record, and ready 2037 stands on the full seven years. Zero margin is a pass with a note. I cite no UltraFan 30 ground-test result that neither of us can source: the report goes to the Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Actually, I've seen this movie before on Trent 1000 dates. I discount my own dates and lean on Rob for them. The public line says 'no earlier than 2037, and only when it is mature'.

OFF-GRID RISK AND EXIT. A standing commitment outlives this round. If P&W commits only in 2045, the Joint Venture forms on a finished, fully spent engine and only equalises shares. McCabe books that at 0 with an unpriced downside. Control: in 2045 we test `withdraw` against commit column by column and bring it to the Board unless commit pays. No options management [RX-0051]: once a commitment has no use, it goes.

memo_weighing.cfo: Taken in full and decisive on the commit. Helen confirmed my weights and added a guide-low set (+0.11). She gave the worst column of every row and co-signed the commit at her test and at her veto check. In round 1 she wanted P&W on the record first; she has moved, because the -$4B column that made her wait no longer exists and waiting captures nothing. Her binding withheld co-signatures on the upgrade and UltraFan WB are respected, and so is her conditional veto on any concession packaged with the commit: standard terms only. I adopt her narrowbody money ($5.71B spent, $2.29B to go, £0.84bn a year, $8.0B against the $4B bound), her free-cash-flow funding frame and her 2045 withdraw test. Her cancel flag was advice, not a veto, and I confirm and strike it. On cash I trust her numbers over mine.
memo_weighing.ops: Taken in full on readiness, support and capacity. Rob passes Ready by EIS for the Solo, at zero margin with a note, and for the Joint Venture only through the fold, since formation + 6 = 2041 misses NGSA. He raises no Civil veto. Every condition he set for his concurrence is met in the orders, the private moves and the public line: the 2036 EIS-team date, the corrected gearbox wording, no shortening of the folded test schedule, the old Joint Venture line replaced, no Joint Venture date and no internal wording in public. His capacity advice goes into the ramp plan: high-performing suppliers, dual-sourcing from 2036, partner MRO ahead of the 2040 step. He was right not to cite a ground-test result he cannot source, and the report goes to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. I confirm and strike his red-line flags on the upgrade and UltraFan WB. His lean to partnership agrees with the commit. On dates I defer to him.

decision.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold (weight 0.60). Airbus keeps NGSA on code 7, P&W stays on its GTF2 Solo and makes no Joint Venture commitment, Boeing launches no fps and no Re-engine this round.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1, 'UltraFan NB: hold' and 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV' tie at +10.54 (109.6%). The commit row ties or beats every row in every column and is the only best plan in S4 (+12.82), so it is the PV-best plan across the grid: +9.67 expected against +9.44 for hold.
decision.premium_reason: No premium. The submitted row ties or beats every other row in every column, and the commit item's worst column is 0.00. No widebody item is ordered, so nothing is drawn against the $3B cap or the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. The narrowbody bound breach ($8.0B against $4B) is an objective shortfall that follows from the 2030 selection, not a premium taken this round; it is stated openly. The commit can only lower it, to $5.7B in S4.
decision.objective_note:
Assigned objective: enter narrowbody, keep widebody dominance.
- Enter NB: met. 29.9% in 2045 and 32.3% in 2050 under the submitted row (7.5% in 2050 in S2, 49.7% in S3; in S4 the shares are equalised and ours stays at 32.3%).
- Keep WB dominance: met. 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column.
- Bounded NB risk: NOT met. $8.0B against the $4B bound, or $5.7B only in S4 with the commit, stated openly.
- WB never starved: met. $0 strain, because no widebody programme is beside the Solo.
Objective premium this round: $0.
decision.predictions:
Weights: S1 0.60, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.05.
- P&W: most likely keeps its GTF2 Solo (ready 2036) and stays silent on the Joint Venture. I put its commit this round at 0.10. If it commits, the Joint Venture forms in 2035, our Solo folds in and our narrowbody money falls to $5.7B.
- Airbus: keeps NGSA on code 7 and certifies in sequence as each engine matures (switch to code 6 at 0.10). GTF2 is a year ahead of us, so we will be judged on maturity from day one.
- Boeing: no fps this round, 'not there yet' (0.10), and no 787 or A350 Re-engine (0.05 each).
- CFM/GE: holds RISE as a technology programme and keeps the GEnx upgrade.
Expected ΔPV +9.67; +10.54 in S1, -4.16 at worst (S2).

board_response.recommendation: Continue UltraFan NB and bring no cancel; protection against S2 is maturity and support on time, not price; standard terms, no concessions.

recommendations.text: The 2045 exit for the standing commitment. Rounds are simultaneous: if P&W commits in 2045 while our commitment stands, the Joint Venture forms that round on a finished, fully spent engine. That brings no saving, and NB shares are equalised. A withdraw in 2045 must therefore be decided without seeing P&W's 2045 order. Bring us `withdraw` against keeping the commit on the 2045 grid, column by column, with a P&W-commits column and the share-equalisation cost priced, not booked at zero. McCabe should state the worst column. Approval this round rests on a floor of 0.00 in this round's grid only.

Maturity watch. Watson should report each round to this Board and to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Neither memo sources the 2028 UltraFan 30 ground-test result, and we note that the record is silent on it. The corrected wording, 'gearbox sizing proven on the UltraFan 30 ground test before any launch', is taken up. GTF2 is ready in 2036 and Airbus certifies in sequence as each engine matures, so zero margin against 2037 leaves no room. Any setback comes to us at once, and the choice is then continue or cancel, never a shorter test programme. If the Joint Venture forms, bring the integration plan to the Committee. That integration would come two years before EIS, and the folded UltraFan's test schedule governs.

Capital frame and the narrowbody bound. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn return programme stay untouched. Any guidance change comes to us before release.

The widebody core. Widebody share is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042 in every column, so the franchise test does not trigger. Defend it through time on wing inside the envelope. In 2045 the UltraFan NB is no longer in development, but the $5B strain still charges for the life of the narrowbody programme. A widebody case therefore comes to us only with the strain counted and any shortfall declared within the $3B cap, and the $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB. UltraFan WB also needs a 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. Watch S5, where the A350 fleet we power alone falls to 30.2% by 2050. Bring the capacity plan for the narrowbody ramp (257 engines in 2040, about 1,000 a year from 2044) to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.
